detail.abstract: This dissertation examines the relationship between fiscal policy and central bank independence in Suriname over the period 2000–2025, with particular emphasis on the role of fiscal dominance. Using a multidimensional framework that combines institutional analysis, central bank balance sheet indicators, and macroeconomic variables, the study investigates how fiscal deficits and public debt influence monetary policy autonomy and macroeconomic stability. Employing OLS, ARDL, VAR, and structural break models, the findings provide strong evidence that fiscal imbalances have historically increased reliance on central bank financing, contributing to monetary expansion, inflationary pressures, and exchange rate depreciation. The results indicate that fiscal dominance has constrained the effective operational independence of the Central Bank of Suriname, despite legal safeguards. The study concludes that central bank independence in Suriname has been predominantly de jure rather than de facto, and that sustainable fiscal policies, credible fiscal rules, and stronger institutional frameworks are essential for preserving monetary credibility and macroeconomic stability. The findings contribute to the literature on fiscal-monetary interactions in small commodity-dependent economies and offer policy recommendations for strengthening economic resilience.

title: Effects of Parents' Health on the Economic Outcomes of Children: Evidence in Korea
affiliations: National Pension Research Institute and St. Lawrence University

detail.title: Effects of Parents' Health on the Economic Outcomes of Children: Evidence in Korea

declarations.declarationOfInterest: no conflicts of interest

detail.abstract: This study examines how unexpected parental health shocks when children are aged between 15 and 20 affect children's labor market and social outcomes, using data from the Korea Labor and Income Panel Study (KLIPS). To address potential selection bias and identify causal effects, we employ the Heckman two-step selection model that controls for unobservables. Our findings show that parental health problems have a statistically significant negative impact on children's four-year college enrollment and graduation, employment status, and future wages. Interestingly, these effects vary by birth order and gender; firstborn children, in particular, suffer a greater penalty as they step in to fill the caregiving gap. These findings suggest that unexpected household health shocks can induce inequality among siblings and serve as a key mechanism that hinders intergenerational socioeconomic mobility.

title: The Klip Disconnect Magnitude II (KDM-2): A Two-Axis, Persistence-Weighted, and Survival-Calibrated Framework for Detecting Institutional Cognitive Capture in Late-Cycle Equity Manias
affiliations: Universidad Anahuac Mexico

detail.title: The Klip Disconnect Magnitude II (KDM-2): A Two-Axis, Persistence-Weighted, and Survival-Calibrated Framework for Detecting Institutional Cognitive Capture in Late-Cycle Equity Manias

declarations.declarationOfInterest: Declaration of interests: The author received no external funding for this work and has no financial or non-financial relationships with any organization that could be construed as influencing it. The Micron Technology prediction stated in the prior paper (KDM 1.0) remains open at the time of writing; the author may discuss publicly traded securities mentioned herein but provides no investment advice. AI-assisted tools were used for drafting and editorial refinement, as disclosed in the author’s note.
declarations.ethicsApproval: This paper names a publicly traded company (Micron Technology) and states a falsifiable prediction of a price decline. It is offered for hypothesis-testing only, is not investment advice, and analyzes institutional incentives rather than imputing bad faith to any individual analyst.

detail.abstract: This paper introduces KDM-2, a substantially revised indicator of late-cycle cognitive capture in equity markets that addresses three structural weaknesses in the original Klip Disconnect Magnitude1 (KDM 1.0): its reliance on a single-day snapshot, its blindness to the terminal phase of a mania, and its lack of a base rate. KDM-2 makes four changes. First, it generalizes the binary rating gate into a continuous bullishness weight. Second, it adds a persistence weight, so that a disconnect counts only insofar as it survives the time analysts need to update. Third, and most important, it adds a second axis—the revision disconnect—defined as the growth of analysts’ own price targets in excess of the growth of their own forward earnings estimates. This second axis is shown to equal the rate of multiple expansion that analysts embed in their targets, and it remains informative precisely when the first axis collapses. Fourth, all components are standardized crosssectionally, placing the base rate inside the metric. Finally, the paper reformulates the indicator as a set of time-varying covariates in a Cox proportional-hazards model for the event of a large peak-totrough drawdown, a formulation that forces the construction of a control group and yields falsifiable, out-of-sample hypotheses. The transition of Micron Technology between May 26 and June 15, 2026—during which the original KDM fell from 0.2851 to roughly 0.20 even as the mania intensified, because analysts raised targets faster than price—is presented as a live illustration of exactly the failure mode KDM-2 is built to capture.

title: The Spatial Support Problem in Public Spending Data: Evidence from Defense IT Procurement

detail.title: The Spatial Support Problem in Public Spending Data: Evidence from Defense IT Procurement
detail.abstract: The evaluation of regional economic policy and spatial analysis heavily relies on how geographic data is extracted and assembled from public administrative systems before any interpretation occurs. Such records routinely embed more than one geographic field, each produced for a distinct institutional purpose, so that the selection among administratively valid geographies is an analytical decision rather than a clerical detail, with measurable consequences for county-level totals, rankings, and the spatial structure of the resulting fields. The argument is developed in the setting of U.S. federal procurement, where prime-award records report both a recipient county and a reported place-of-performance county. Using Department of Defense contract actions in NAICS 541511 (Custom Computer Programming Services) for fiscal years 2019-2022, the paper introduces the Spatial Divergence Index (SDI), a 0-100 bounded measure of the normalized absolute difference between recipient-side and reported-performance obligations at county-year support, and a signed counterpart D that distinguishes recipient-hub from performance-importer countyyears. In the canonical continental U.S. analytic file, USD 13.08 billion in positive obligations are used for measurement. Of these dollars, 40.8 percent are assigned to different counties and 33.9 percent to different states under the two administrative geographies. The selection also reorders the procurement geography itself: recipient-and performance-based county totals exhibit a Spearman rank correlation of 0.462, and 75.0 percent of counties change decile. Complete divergence (SDI = 100) is common in the baseline panel but concentrates in low-activity county-years; restricting to county-years with at least ten counted transactions reduces the SDI = 100 share from 46.0 to 7.5 percent. The principal contribution is this dollarweighted reallocation and rank-shift evidence, which is robust to the activity-threshold and accounting-measure audits reported below. A complementary and deliberately exploratory spatial analysis shows that the signed field D carries small (Moran's I point estimates 0.08-0.13), statistically detectable, but specification-sensitive positive autocorrelation in fiscal years 2020-2022 under k-nearest-neighbor weights with Benjamini-Hochberg correction, and that the directional classification of counties is highly persistent from year to year. The performance-importer (High-High) local clusters are strongly associated with the presence of major Department of Defense installations-80 percent of these clusters host one, against 14 percent of non-clustered counties-confirming the administrative-reporting interpretation of the directional measure. The spatial autocorrelation attenuates under Queen contiguity and under restriction to high-activity county-years and is therefore reported as a secondary, exploratory characterization rather than as the load-bearing result. The contribution is conceptual rather than algebraic: SDI is a county-year application of the normalized absolute difference from the dissimilarity-index family, and the paper documents its empirical and spatial behavior when applied to administrative procurement records where geography selection is consequential and currently unaudited.

title: Built on Fault Lines: Mandatory ESG Disclosure and the Discovery of Value
affiliations: , Central Bank of Chile, affiliation not provided to SSRN and

detail.title: Built on Fault Lines: Mandatory ESG Disclosure and the Discovery of Value

declarations.declarationOfInterest: No conflicts of interest
declarations.ethicsApproval: No human subjetcs
declarations.funderStatement: Fondo de Investigacion con Impacto, School of Business Universidad Adolfo Ibanez

detail.abstract: Mandatory ESG disclosure improves firm profitability. We establish this causal claim by exploiting Chile's NCG 461 regulation-which imposed ESG reporting requirements on listed firms above discrete asset thresholds-in a sharp Regression Discontinuity Design across multiple cutoff years. The staggered implementation generates a natural temporal experiment: a pre-treatment placebo (2021) validates the design, the main treatment year (2023) identifies the causal effect, and a persistence test (2024) confirms that gains endure. Using administrative IFRS data from Chile's financial regulator (CMF) for 268-293 non-financial listed firms, we find that firms just above the disclosure threshold exhibit higher Return on Assets and higher Return on Equity, and a lower cost of debt, than firms just below it-profitability effects that are positive, statistically significant, and robust across specifications, and a cost-of-debt effect that is negative, significant, and robust. These effects are absent in the placebo year, emerge at the treatment cutoff, andin the persistence test-broaden into eighteen significant coefficients spanning contemporaneous, lagged, and two-year-lagged horizons. The temporal gradient is the signature of a causal mechanism. Simultaneously, treated firms cut intangible investment sharply, both before and after disclosure, while improving returns on existing assets: the operational efficiency channel. Three identification tests-McCrary density at every cutoff, MSE-optimal bandwidth diagnostics, and a battery of bandwidth-kernelpolynomial-selector variations-confirm that the design is not driven by manipulation, sample size, or specification choice. Wave 1 firms (above the 20 million UF threshold) show lower cost of debt but no profitability gain; Wave 2 firms (above the 1 million UF threshold) show both. Two mechanisms coexist-information asymmetry and operational efficiency-operating on different firms through different pathways. The evidence challenges the view that ESG regulation in emerging markets imposes net costs on firms: in an OECD member with IFRS accounting, credible enforcement, and an institutional investor base, mandatory disclosure pays for itself through the inefficiencies it forces firms to discover. A battery of seven functional-form and bandwidth specifications, evaluated across lagged, contemporaneous, and forward horizons, demonstrates that the plausible profitability effects are robust-the lagged measurement-channel effects most of all-while the largest contemporaneous return-on-equity estimates are not.

detail.abstract:
This paper introduces Sociotopography, a multi‑dimensional framework for modelling behavioural fragility and systemic pressure. The framework is grounded in established research across behavioural economics, cognitive psychology, systems theory, complexity science, and resilience studies. It proposes that behaviour should be understood as both trait and state, shaped by an individual’s position within a dynamic behavioural landscape.

The landscape is defined by three core dimensions: Economic Capacity (EC), Time and Cognitive Load (TCL), and Psychosocial Stress (PSS). These dimensions create a behavioural terrain with basins, ridges, and cliffs that influence how individuals respond to pressure.

Using a case study of South African taxi commuters before and after a diesel price shock, the paper demonstrates how Sociotopography reveals hidden fragility and population movement that traditional metrics fail to capture. The analysis shows that average scores may remain stable even as the underlying behavioural terrain shifts, increasing the risk of sudden behavioural change.

The paper outlines practical applications for organisations seeking to understand and anticipate behavioural instability. It argues that Sociotopography provides a more accurate representation of behaviour in complex environments and offers a foundation for improved decision‑making, policy design, and predictive modelling.

title: Mapping the Global Evolution of Environmental, Social, and Governance Regulations: A Comprehensive Institutional Analysis
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN, and Central Bank of Chile

detail.title: Mapping the Global Evolution of Environmental, Social, and Governance Regulations: A Comprehensive Institutional Analysis

declarations.declarationOfInterest: No conflicts of Interest
declarations.ethicsApproval: No human Subjects
declarations.funderStatement: Fondo de Investigacino con Impacto, Shcool of Business Universidad Adolfo Ibanez

detail.abstract:
This study presents the first comprehensive global analysis of Environmental, Social, and Governance (ESG) regulatory frameworks, examining 226 regulations across 58 countries from 2001 to 2024. Grounded in institutional theory (DiMaggio & Powell, 1983), we identify three phases: Early (2001-2010), Growth (2011-2019), and Acceleration (2020-2024). Europe leads with 51.8% of regulations, followed by Asia-Pacific (27.9%); mandatory frameworks dominate at 71.2%. Kaplan-Meier event history analysis of projected ISSB adoption (66 countries, 40 expected adopters, 26 right-censored) confirms the Brussels Effect: EU member states show substantially higher projected ISSB adoption than non-EU countries (log-rank χ² = 18.08, p < 0.001), confirming coercive isomorphism as the primary diffusion mechanism. Findings advance understanding of transnational regulatory convergence and inform ISSB harmonisation through 2030. 
Practitioner Points
  ESG regulation has crossed an institutional threshold from which there is no return. The 2019-2020 structural break marks a qualitative regime change, not a cyclical upturn: 83.2% of all global ESG regulations were enacted in just five years. Organisations still treating ESG as a reputational exercise or voluntary commitment are operating on an outdated model of the regulatory environment. 
 Mandatory disclosure is the norm, not the endpoint. Across all three phases of ESG regulatory development, binding requirements dominated from the outsetvoluntary frameworks appeared only as complements to mandatory ones, never as precursors. Corporate governance structures, audit processes, and board oversight mechanisms should be designed around mandatory disclosure as the baseline, not as an eventual destination.

title: AI-Assisted Works: Copyrightability in the United States, China, and the EU , and Implications for Academic Integrity

detail.title: AI-Assisted Works: Copyrightability in the United States, China, and the EU , and Implications for Academic Integrity
detail.abstract: This article explores the legal aspects of the copyrightability of AI-assisted works in the U.S., China, and the EU, within the context of a fundamental principle shared across these jurisdictions: only creations involving meaningful human creative choices are eligible for copyright protection. The article also presents comparative insights from court rulings – including those in China and the U.S. – that reinforce the requirement of human authorship for copyright protection and the legal and ethical implications of using generative artificial intelligence (AI) in academic work, with a focus on academic integrity, authorship, and copyright compliance. It analyzes recent developments in legislation, case law, and internal university regulations in jurisdictions including the European Union, the United States, China, and selected EU Member States. The central thesis is that AI-generated content cannot be regarded as an outcome of independent scholarly work if it replaces the creative process – particularly the development of a research concept and first draft. While AI tools offer efficiency and support in technical tasks such as grammar correction or literature searches, their unauthorized or undisclosed use in substantive academic writing constitutes a breach of academic ethics and may lead to the invalidation of academic degrees. Moreover, it emphasizes the growing need for universities to adopt AI detection policies that respect the presumption of innocence and align with data protection law. Ultimately, the article argues for preserving academic authorship as an intellectual process that cannot be outsourced to machines – lest scientific credibility itself be undermined.

detail.abstract: Citizen science biodiversity surveys generate spatially extensive datasets but are structurally prone to compounding observer biases—spatial undersampling of remote habitats, taxonomic over-representation of conspicuous species, and heterogeneous observer skill—that limit their direct utility for ecological analysis and evidence-based policymaking. We present a two-stage, open-source R pipeline and multi-format dataset derived from the National Breeding Bird Survey of Japan (2016–2021), designed to address these challenges without dependency on external GIS infrastructure. Stage 1 performs encoding sanitization, standalone mathematical decoding of six-digit second-order regional mesh codes (JIS X 0410; ∼20 km × 20 km) into WGS 84 bounding box coordinates, and application of an Inverse Mesh Frequency (IMF) rarity-weighting algorithm adapted from the information-theoretic TF-IDF framework to objectively identify grid cells harboring locally rare taxa that conventional species richness counts suppress. Stage 2 deploys the pre-compiled outputs in a lightweight Shiny–Leaflet WebGIS application enabling dynamic species richness filtering and clickable IMF-ranked species popups via leafletProxy differential updates, stable on free-tier cloud infrastructure. Curated outputs are distributed in three complementary formats—CSV (cross-platform tabular), RDS (R-native binary), and GeoPackage (OGC spatial vector; EPSG:4326)—archived at Zenodo (https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.20739666; CC BY 4.0) with a live interactive map at https://moteki.shinyapps.io/avian_diversity/. The standalone mesh decoding logic and IMF pipeline are immediately transferable to any Japanese administrative grid dataset, providing a generalizable template for reproducible spatial analysis in social science, regional planning, and biodiversity informatics.

title: States, Not the FDA, Are Winning the Drug War

detail.abstract: President Trump's January 2026 executive order directing federal agencies to finalize the rescheduling of cannabis from Schedule I to Schedule III marks a watershed moment in American drug policy-and one whose lessons reach well beyond cannabis. This essay argues that the cannabis story exposes a misconception that has guided much of the psychedelics field: that the surest route to federal drugpolicy reform runs through the FDA's approval pipeline. Drug rescheduling can follow two distinct paths: the "FDA backdoor," under which agency approval of a specific formulation triggers rescheduling of that product alone (as with Marinol, XYWAV, and Epidiolex), and a federalist track in which state-level deregulation generates the political and empirical evidence base that eventually moves federal law. Cannabis ultimately moved on the federalist track, not the medicalized onedespite Marinol's FDA approval nearly forty years ago. Drawing on the early data from Oregon's, Colorado's, and New Mexico's state psilocybin programs, and on the FDA advisory committee's 2024 rejection of MDMA-assisted therapy, the essay argues that psychedelic-policy reformers should treat state experimentationnot FDA approval-as the primary lever for substantive drug-policy change, with the medicalized pathway serving as a complementary rather than a leading strategy.

title: Attracting Talent to General Practice through Financial Incentives
affiliations: Charles III University of Madrid - Department of Business Administration, University of Barcelona and

detail.title: Attracting Talent to General Practice through Financial Incentives
detail.abstract: Shortages of general practitioners (GPs) strain healthcare systems worldwide. We test whether wage incentives can attract higher-ability physicians using a 2022 reform in Catalonia, Spain, that granted incoming GP residents unconditional salary supplements of 26% to 47% of base pay across three tiers. Using administrative data on medical residency choices nationwide and a synthetic difference-indifferences design, we document two effects. First, the reform raised entrants' standardized exam scores by 0.067 standard deviations on average (0.174 in the highest subsidy tier) and increased the international resident share by nearly 30 percentage points. Second, GP vacancies emerged nationwide after 2022 but rose 4.4 percentage points less in Catalonia, drawing lower-scoring candidates to the newly filled slots and mechanically diluting the average score gain. Lee bounds correcting for this compositional shift raise the estimated effects to 0.088 and 0.191 standard deviations in a fully cleared market. Our findings show that salary supplements can improve the allocation of medical talent to shortage occupations, though their effectiveness depends on local labor-market tightness and physician supply.

title: AI Adoption, Workplace Collaboration, and Mean Field Games

detail.title: AI Adoption, Workplace Collaboration, and Mean Field Games
detail.abstract: This paper studies generative AI adoption inside firms as a finite-type network mean field game with adaptive expectations. Workers are heterogeneous agents whose states-AI capability and task-specific human capital-evolve through own AI use, learning, and collaboration with AIcapable coworkers. Types summarize positions in the workplace collaboration structure, such as degree, team role, or exposure to AI-capable peers, and a row-stochastic mixing matrix maps type-level distributions into local peer environments. Managerial clarity enters through the perceived return to AI-enabled output and the speed of belief updating. The model yields a backward Hamilton-Jacobi-Bellman equation for each worker type, a forward Fokker-Planck equation for the type-specific distributions, and consistency conditions linking optimal policies to aggregate AI capability, collaboration, and perceived returns. A numerical exercise provides an illustrative finite-population network approximation designed to isolate the mechanism implied by the model. Managerial clarity can operate like a control parameter, shifting collaboration as an order parameter and accelerating convergence to the AI-capability frontier.

title: Artificial Intelligence, Misinformation, and Ideological Bias: Evidence From a News Classification Experiment

detail.title: Artificial Intelligence, Misinformation, and Ideological Bias: Evidence From a News Classification Experiment
detail.abstract: This paper investigates how ideological bias and classification errors vary across AI-mediated information environments. We conduct an incentivized laboratory experiment in which participants classify news items as true or false across three withinsubject phases: a human-written baseline, an AI-generated misinformation phase in which the role of AI is not made explicit, and an AI-detection phase in which participants receive an explicit AI probability signal. Average classification accuracy does not differ significantly across phases. The central result is instead that errors are strongly structured by ideological congruence: participants are more likely to accept congruent false news as true and to reject incongruent true news as false. The AI-detection phase suggests greater skepticism toward information, reflected in a higher false-negative rate. This skepticism seems to be selectively applied: the relation between congruence and classification errors becomes stronger when AI is introduced explicitly. The analysis of detector responsiveness points to non-selective partial mistrust of AI signals. Overall, AI-based verification does not mechanically correct ideologically structured classification errors.

title: From Funding Gap to Governing Rationalities: Six Archetypes of Resource Mobilisation for Climate and Biodiversity Action
affiliations: and Utrecht University - School of Economics

detail.title: From Funding Gap to Governing Rationalities: Six Archetypes of Resource Mobilisation for Climate and Biodiversity Action

declarations.funderStatement: This research has been carried out within the NATURESCAPES project. The NATURESCAPES project is funded by the European Union under Grant Agreement No 101084341. Views and opinions expressed are those of the authors only and do not necessarily reflect those of the European Union. detail.abstract:
The dominant ‘funding gap’ narrative for climate and biodiversity action foregrounds market-based
resource mobilisation logics while underplaying non-monetary, cross-sectoral, and place-based
resourcing strategies. This integrative literature review develops six resource mobilisation archetypes,
aimed at sub-national actors - hybrid, multi-scalar, policy-led, revenue-based, cross-sectoral and mosaic
– that can support long-term urban transformations. We characterise each archetype by its governing
rationality and evaluate its potential for long-term outcomes. We document, for each of them, the
diverse structural tensions between the enabling conditions required to realise a resourcing strategy and
the strategy's effectiveness for long-term transformation. The archetypes most distant from market-
based logic (mosaic assemblages and cross-sectoral reconfigurations) show the strongest evidence for
ecological adequacy and distributional equity, yet receive the least policy attention. Resource
mobilisation processes durably reshape sub-national governance, and sequencing matters: building
institutional foundations for more relational archetypes may be a precondition for ensuring external
capital serves locally defined outcomes. Our framework offers a diagnostic tool for aligning resourcing
strategies for sub-national climate and biodiversity action with long-term transformation objectives -
rather than the short-term objective of capital volume.

title: Chess Signatures of Play
affiliations: University of Chicago - Booth School of Business and University of Chicago

detail.title: Chess Signatures of Play
detail.abstract: A game of chess is a stream: a time-ordered sequence of moves, each carrying an engine evaluation, a measure of accuracy, a measure of position complexity, and a clock reading. We model a game as a multivariate path and apply the signature transform of rough-path theory to obtain a reparametrization-invariant, graded feature set that records the order and interaction of in-game events without a parametric likelihood. We show that a player's law of play is identifiable from the expected signature up to tree-like equivalence, construct a signature-kernel two-sample test on path space, and recast cheating detection as an anytime-valid sequential test: a signature conformance score becomes an e-process whose error is controlled for every sample size at once by Ville's inequality, with fluctuations calibrated on the moderate-deviation scale. The discriminating information lives in the signature's Lévy areas, which measure whether accuracy rises precisely when positions become hard, the fingerprint of engine assistance that aggregate match-rate statistics discard. In a controlled study the test holds exact type-I control and detection power rises from negligible for subtle assistance to 0.98 for blatant assistance, with a median detection time matching the growth-rate prediction log(1/α)/c. Calibrated to Magnus Carlsen's documented elite accuracy, the monitor does not flag world-champion-level play; and we exhibit cheating strategies that leave every aggregate statistic, including the best-move-frequency z-score of the Regan system, exactly unchanged yet are caught cleanly by the signature, making precise how an order-aware, anytime-valid test strengthens the prevailing approach to chess anti-cheating.

title: Model-Adjusted Volatility Proxy for ARMA-GARCH Forecast
affiliations: Finance and Risk Engineering, NYU Tandon School of Engineering

detail.title: Model-Adjusted Volatility Proxy for ARMA-GARCH Forecast
detail.abstract: Since asset price volatility is a latent variable and its forecasting accuracy depends on "imperfect volatility proxies" (Patton, 2011), we suggest that using standalone volatility models is unproductive for two related reasons. First, the conventional volatility proxy, i.e., realized volatility (RV), is calculated using equally-weighted price shocks for some past, arbitrarily chosen (though popular) time periods, which ignores nonstationary nature of financial time series. Second, the standalone volatility models neglect possible price autocorrelation effects and, hence, may yield biased estimates. In our view, volatility is just another feature of the price dynamics models. Comparative accuracy of these models (e.g., ARMA-GARCH) should be tested out-of-sample using observable variables, i.e. returns. Then, the relevant RV (called here model-adjusted RV (MARV)) can be calculated for the past time period where the optimal ARMA-GARCH model has non-zero ARMA lags. Here, we offer an example of this approach using the AIC-based and BIC-based optimal ARMA-GARCH and ARMA-GJR-GARCH models for the S&P 500 returns in all one-year periods within 2000-2024. We found that the MARV-based EWMA can be a more accurate volatility proxy than the MARV itself for the samples with pronounced autocorrelations.

title: MacroModelClaw: An AI-Collaborative Workflow for DSGE Model Development
affiliations: City University of Macau and The Chinese University of Hong Kong (CUHK)

detail.title: MacroModelClaw: An AI-Collaborative Workflow for DSGE Model Development
detail.abstract: Translating a macroeconomic theory into a numerically solvable DSGE model is a persistent bottleneck in quantitative macroeconomics. We introduce MacroModelClaw, a multi-agent workflow for Claude Code that enforces information barriers across the full DSGE development pipeline. The user supplies a single structured model document (model-doc.md); ten specialized agents—named after foundational economists—parse, calibrate, code, solve, run, validate, and review the model without sharing each other’s instructions. The paper makes three contributions: (i) a Dynare workflow architecture that encodes practitioners’ tacit knowledge as an enforced multi-agent system, including automatic timingconvention checking and Blanchard-Kahn error routing; (ii) a self-accumulating knowledge base of Dynare error diagnostics with confidence scoring and modelcontext indexing; and (iii) a numerical solver library covering seven algorithm families for nonlinear steady-state systems, with automatic selection and fallback sequencing. We demonstrate the approach on three applications of increasing complexity: a New Keynesian model, a two-sector housing DSGE, and a partial HANK steady-state computation.

title: Learning the Central Bank's Inflation Response in Financial Markets

detail.title: Learning the Central Bank's Inflation Response in Financial Markets
detail.abstract: Using nominal Treasury yields and Treasury Inflation-Protected Securities inflation compensation, this paper estimates a daily market-based index of how investors perceive the Federal Reserve's inflation response. The index allows for term, convenience, liquidity, and relative liquidity components, and is validated with professional forecasts, household expectations, maturity-specific event reactions, and Federal Open Market Committee surprise measures. The perceived response is low in 2021 and 2022, rises during the tightening cycle, and remains stable when the 20-year maturity is excluded. A stronger perceived response is associated with lower long-run professional inflation expectations, lower household inflation expectations at short and medium horizons, and lower disagreement; event-specific revisions also comove positively with clean monetary policy surprises. The results imply that marketbased policy benchmarks are conditional on beliefs about how the central bank reacts to inflation, so fixed-rule interpretations can confound credibility learning with other market components.

title: Same Firms, Different Verdicts: ESG Rating Choice and the Measurement of Greenwashing
affiliations: New York University Stern School of Business and

detail.title: Same Firms, Different Verdicts: ESG Rating Choice and the Measurement of Greenwashing
detail.abstract: This paper investigates the Aggregate Confusion hypothesis (Berg, Kölbel, and Rigobon, 2022) at the firm level by measuring the Disclosure-Performance Gap (DPG), defined as the standardised divergence between a firm's voluntary environmental disclosure ("Talk") and its realised emissions performance ("Walk"). The sample comprises 200 large European firms drawn from the Energy, Materials, Industrials, and Utilities sectors of the STOXX Europe 600 in fiscal year 2023, the final cross-section of the voluntary reporting era before the Corporate Sustainability Reporting Directive. The estimated model is identified through a systematic six-stage model selection process, namely candidate assembly, Pearson correlation screening, multicollinearity filtering by Variance Inflation Factor, stepwise forward search across five variable pools under the corrected Akaike Information Criterion, Cook's distance influence screening, and HC3 re-estimation, which evaluates 421 candidate specifications. The selected model is estimated by ordinary least squares with HC3 robust standard errors on the full sample of 200 firms. The strongest predictor of a wider gap is flagship index membership (β = +0.78, p < 0.01), consistent with institutional ceremonial conformity; Task Force on Climate-related Financial Disclosures (TCFD) endorsement is also positive (β = +0.86, p < 0.05) but is identified off a small group of non-supporting firms and is read as directional rather than as a precise magnitude. Two substantive commitments significantly narrow the gap, renewable energy use (β =-0.31, p < 0.01) and environmental capital expenditure (β =-0.22, p < 0.05), consistent with signalling theory. Governance and monitoring variables carry no explanatory power. The core findings are stable under influence trimming, under a rank-based recoding of the ordinal disclosure score, and when the TCFD variable is removed. Replacing the CDP Climate Score with the LSEG Environmental Pillar Score on the identical firms eliminates the index-membership effect while the renewable-energy effect survives, showing that detected greenwashing is conditional on the rating lens applied.

title: The Effect of School Disruptions on Parental Labor Supply: Evidence from Canadian Panel Data
affiliations: Ohio State University (OSU) - Department of Human Sciences, San Diego State University - Department of Economics, Dalhousie University and Dalhousie University

detail.title: The Effect of School Disruptions on Parental Labor Supply: Evidence from Canadian Panel Data
detail.abstract: This study explores the effects of COVID-19 school closures on labor market outcomes of Canadian parents of school-aged children. Using newly collected data on grade-level-specific school closures across 141 Canadian cities along with individual-level panel data from the Labour Force Survey, difference-in-differences estimates provide robust evidence that restrictions on in-person schooling reduced employment among partnered mothers of school-aged children by approximately 2 percentage points. For fathers, labor supply adjustments are much weaker and concentrated on single fathers. Finally, auxiliary analyses using administrative tax records provide suggestive evidence that school closures increased public benefit receipt among single parents.

title: Minimum Fisher Information, Geometric Priors and the Horseshoe
affiliations: University of Chicago - Booth School of Business and

detail.title: Minimum Fisher Information, Geometric Priors and the Horseshoe
detail.abstract:
Four threads in sparse Bayesian estimation — Mallows’ conjecture on minimum Fisher information for discrete normal-location mixtures, the Bickel-Collins theorem, the Mukherjee-Johnstone minimax predictive density, and the horseshoe prior — are unified by a single variational principle: minimise the Fisher information of the induced mixture density over a structured prior class subject to a variance constraint. The minimiser is the geometric distribution on the lattice and the half-Cauchy in the continuous global-local setting. 
The core of the paper is a four-way equivalence theorem (Theorem 3.13): within the lattice-mixture class, the geometric prior simultaneously minimises Fisher information, minimises integrated posterior variance (via the Tweedie formula), minimises the expected KL divergence from posterior to prior (the inverse Sanov theorem), and maximises KL predictive difficulty. Each of these four characterisations gives a distinct operational interpretation of why the geometric distribution is extremal, and the inverse Sanov perspective — that the geometric prior is the one from which data reveal the least, in the KL sense — is the deepest.
 Beyond the equivalence theorem we contribute: a corrected proof of Mallows’ conjecture addressing a gap in Bickel and Collins (1983); a complete Fisher information–KL duality for all variance ratios r > 0; a proof that geometric decay is necessary as well as sufficient for minimax KL optimality; and a demonstration that the horseshoe prior is the continuous realisation of the same four-way equivalence.

title: Disentangling Generative AI and Monetary Policy Shocks in the AI-Electric Vehicle Nexus
affiliations: Ecole Superieure des Sciences Economiques et Commerciales de Tunis (ESSECT),  Université de Tunis

detail.title: Disentangling Generative AI and Monetary Policy Shocks in the AI-Electric Vehicle Nexus
detail.abstract: This paper disentangles the effects of two concurrent macro-technological shocks, the Federal Reserve tightening cycle and the launch of ChatGPT, on systemic connectedness within the artificial intelligence and electric-vehicle (AI-EV) financial nexus. Using daily data on eight variables spanning May 2018 to June 2026, we identify three structural regimes via Bai-Perron break tests: a pre-ChatGPT baseline (P1), a monetary-tightening era (P2), and a generative-AI era (P3). The Diebold-Yilmaz generalized forecast-error variance decomposition reveals high systemic integration across all regimes, with a total connectedness index of approximately 7.7 percent in the baseline period. To capture distributional heterogeneity, we apply the quantile VAR framework of Ando, Greenwood-Nimmo and Shin (2022). At the median market state, the GenAI shock reduces connectedness roughly four times more than the monetary shock (-0.76 versus-0.18 percentage points). Monetary dominance re-emerges at the right tail, where the Federal Reserve effect reaches +1.40 percentage points against-0.56 for GenAI, suggesting that systemic stress amplifies the role of conventional macroeconomic policy. A horse-race difference-indifferences design confirms that the ChatGPT event dummy outperforms the Federal Reserve dummy in magnitude across all equity specifications. These results indicate that the AI-EV nexus is primarily governed by technological-regime shifts under normal market conditions, while monetary forces reassert themselves during episodes of tail risk. The findings carry implications for innovation forecasters, ESG portfolio managers, and policymakers navigating the concurrent transitions in energy and artificial intelligence.

title: Themes and Trends in Artificial Intelligence in Finance: A Bibliometric and Multi-Method Topic Modelling Analysis
affiliations: , The University of Texas at Arlington and University of Texas at Arlington - Department of Finance and Real Estate

detail.title: Themes and Trends in Artificial Intelligence in Finance: A Bibliometric and Multi-Method Topic Modelling Analysis
detail.abstract: This study maps the intellectual structure and evolution of artificial intelligence (AI) research in finance using a corpus of 1,579 articles indexed in the Web of Science between 2012 and 2025. We combine bibliometric analysis with three complementary topic modeling approaches-Latent Dirichlet Allocation (LDA), BERTopic, and Bunka-to identify the dominant and emerging themes shaping the literature. The bibliometric evidence documents rapid growth in AI-finance research, led primarily by the United States and China, with increasing concentration in topics related to machine learning, sustainability, FinTech, and large language models. Across the three topic modeling approaches, we identify 39 distinct research themes and nine consensus themes consistently detected across all methods, including sustainability and green finance, natural language processing and sentiment analysis, cryptocurrency markets, investment management, auditing, and labor-market effects of AI adoption. The findings indicate that AI-finance scholarship has evolved beyond traditional applications such as credit risk prediction and fraud detection toward broader questions involving governance, digital transformation, and human-AI interaction in financial services. Cross-method comparison further shows that probabilistic, neural, and LLM-augmented topic models provide complementary perspectives on the field's intellectual structure. We also identify several underexplored areas, including AI governance and regulation, behavioral dimensions of AI adoption in finance, emerging-market applications, and causal research designs. The study contributes to the growing literature on AI and finance by providing an integrated map of the field's thematic evolution and by outlining directions for future research.

title: Privacy-Protected Spatial Pipeline and Pedestrian Crash Risk Landscape Dataset Derived from Administrative Traffic Accident Records: Tokai City, Aichi Prefecture, Japan
affiliations: Nanzan University

detail.title: Privacy-Protected Spatial Pipeline and Pedestrian Crash Risk Landscape Dataset Derived from Administrative Traffic Accident Records: Tokai City, Aichi Prefecture, Japan

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no competing interests.
declarations.ethicsApproval: Not applicable
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no specific grant from funding agencies in the public, commercial, or not-for-profit sectors.

detail.abstract: Pedestrian-vehicle traffic accidents pose a persistent urban safety challenge in Japan, yet directly applying raw administrative records to local risk analysis raises concerns about stochastic noise, privacy exposure, and complex data taxonomies. This study presents a spatial data pipeline implemented in R that transforms the 2021 National Police Agency (NPA) open traffic accident dataset into two outputs for Tokai City, Aichi Prefecture. The first is a masked attribute dataset in RDS format for secondary statistical analysis; the second is a privacy-protected GeoPackage representing a continuous pedestrian crash risk landscape for deployment in desktop GIS environments. Privacy is operationalized through spatial abstraction: individual accident locations are dissolved into 500-meter buffer zones, making reverse identification structurally impossible while preserving macro-level risk distributions. The deliberate use of FY2021 data provides a further ethical safeguard, reducing psychological and legal risks to those involved. The resulting dataset is designed for data-driven policy formation in public safety, community safety workshops, and spatial overlay analyses with local demographic or infrastructure data. The pipeline and dataset together provide an ethically grounded model for regional pedestrian crash risk assessment applicable to other municipalities using administrative traffic accident records.

title: The Labor Market Effects of Expanding Overtime Coverage
affiliations: University of Southern California

detail.title: The Labor Market Effects of Expanding Overtime Coverage
detail.abstract:
This paper examines the labor market effects of overtime coverage in the United States, where salaried workers are covered for overtime if their base pay falls below a legislated salary threshold. Using an event-study design with administrative payroll data and state-level threshold changes from 2014-2021, I find evidence against conventional models of overtime. Contrary to the historical intent of policymakers, firms do not increase employment by substituting more workers for fewer hours. However, contrary to compensating differential models, firms also do not offset the costs of overtime by lowering workers' base pays. Instead, employers raised salaries above the threshold to keep workers exempt from overtime, indicating that monitoring and adjusting workers' hours is costly for firms. Taken together, these results suggest that expanding overtime coverage increases workers' earnings without negatively impacting employment.

Institutional subscribers to the NBER working paper series, and residents of developing countries may download this paper without additional charge at www.nber.org.

title: Huber, Sanov and Shannon, Merging Robust Statistics with Information Theory
affiliations: University of Chicago - Booth School of Business and

detail.title: Huber, Sanov and Shannon, Merging Robust Statistics with Information Theory
detail.abstract: We show that the Huber distribution f c is the unique fixed point of four information-theoretic minimisation principles over the ε-contaminated normal class F ε : Shannon minimax KL risk (Polson, 1988), Kolmogorov description length, Wallace's Minimum Message Length (MML), and Rissanen's Normalised Maximum Likelihood. An eleven-way Equivalence Theorem shows all four reduce to one Fisher-entropy duality: f c simultaneously minimises Fisher information and maximises Shannon entropy over F ε. The saddle-point equality is established via Sion's theorem with an explicit O(log n/n) rate from the Polson-Clarke-Barron expansion (Polson, 1988, 1992; Clarke and Barron, 1990). The MML equivalence is new: strict MML estimation under F ε is exactly Huber M-estimation, threshold determined by the Wallace-Freeman constant. Via the inverse Sanov theorem of Ganesh and O'Connell (1999), f c generates the flattest posterior large-deviation rate simultaneously across the BvM, moderate-deviation, large-deviation, and Cramér-Chernoff regimes. A universal theorem covers TV balls, Hellinger balls, Wasserstein neighbourhoods, and exponential family contamination. A simulation study confirms finite-sample threshold convergence and near-oracle MSE.

title: Can the Anomaly Zoo Speak with One Voice? Consensus, Reliability, and Expected Returns
affiliations: Rutgers Business School - Rutgers University

detail.title: Can the Anomaly Zoo Speak with One Voice? Consensus, Reliability, and Expected Returns
detail.abstract: Using 212 signed Chen-Zimmermann/Open Asset Pricing predictors, this paper studies whether the anomaly zoo contains a common real-time expected-return signal and whether that signal has measurable reliability states. The empirical design starts in 1963, uses expanding training windows with fixed twelve-year validation windows, and predicts returns from 1985 through 2024. The robust consensus, denoted C * , aggregates a family of legitimate consensus makers rather than selecting a single winning model. C * predicts next-month stock returns in Fama-MacBeth regressions and value-weighted portfolio sorts. A value-weighted high-minuslow portfolio earns an FF5-plus-momentum alpha of 1.06 percent per month. The premium is systematically conditioned by model agreement, signal-profile shape, support quality, higher moments, attention, information resolution, limits-to-arbitrage states, and the location of information across industries and peers. The evidence shows that high-dimensional anomaly information is organized by both consensus and reliability. The anomaly zoo contains a common expected-return component, and the reliability state behind that component changes how the signal should be interpreted in asset-pricing tests and portfolio choice.

title: Forecast Loss or Portfolio Loss? Objective Reliability in High-Dimensional Expected-Return Portfolios
affiliations: Rutgers Business School - Rutgers University

detail.title: Forecast Loss or Portfolio Loss? Objective Reliability in High-Dimensional Expected-Return Portfolios
detail.abstract: This paper studies whether high-dimensional expected-return portfolios should be selected by stock-level forecast loss or by portfolio-level payoff objectives. Using 212 Chen-Zimmermann/Open Asset Pricing characteristics, delisting-adjusted CRSP returns, and an annual validation-refit design for target years 1985-2024, I compare objective rankings across long-short, long-only active, and proxy-residualized long-short portfolio maps. Forecast loss is difficult to beat in unconstrained long-short portfolios: the validation-selected rule earns 45.9 percent annually, while the forecast-loss benchmark earns 47.7 percent. Portfolio objectives affect selection, objective-family dispersion, and implemented portfolio composition more when the map changes the payoff object, although they do not uniformly improve average returns. The contribution is to make objective reliability, the transfer of validation-window objective rankings into target-year portfolio outcomes, an empirical object of asset-pricing validation.

title: Fair Hearings: Accuracy First
affiliations: University of Oxford - Faculty of Law and

detail.title: Fair Hearings: Accuracy First
detail.abstract: There are two conflicting approaches to fair hearings in English law. One line of cases says that fairness or justice requires a hearing only when it stands to contribute to a more accurate overall decision. The other says that fairness requires a hearing independently of its contribution to an overall decision. Recently, many commentators have championed the second approach, usually based on an appeal to non-instrumental process values, such as respect and autonomy. Here we defend the first, accuracycentred approach. Others who do so tend to deny that there are process values. Our strategy is different: we show that the existence of process values is consistent with an accuracy-centred approach.

title: The Global Flow System: A Genetic Description of a Dynamic Structure Temporal Warfare I

detail.title: The Global Flow System: A Genetic Description of a Dynamic Structure Temporal Warfare I

This paper is independent scholarly work representing the author's own analysis alone, not the position of the Hungarian Defence Forces or any other institution. The author has no commercial or financial relationship bearing on this study and declares no competing interests.
declarations.ethicsApproval: This paper is a theoretical and analytical study in geostrategy and international political economy. It involves no human or animal participants, no clinical or experimental data, and no personal data. Ethics approval is therefore not applicable.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no specific grant or funding from any agency in the public, commercial, or not-for-profit sectors. It was conducted independently by the author.

detail.abstract: This paper describes the Global Flow System not in one of its states but through its genesis, on the premise that a dynamic system can be described truthfully only through the way it came to be: its present shape is a cross-section of an ongoing motion, not a separate, standing object. The account begins from the field-nature of the political unit. Community, Country, and State are not solid bodies but fields at different degrees of organization, and the fixed border is the most derivative term of all, the frozen imprint of two State-fields meeting where neither could expand further. From this ontology the paper derives the constitutive role of flow, the Neolithic proto-valve, the field-law, the growth axiom, and the historical pattern of the valve. The genesis runs into the present structure: three flow-constitutions, four interlocking layers, a single measuring layer that prices everything as the price of time, and a saturated field. One law holds at every scale. A flow-organized system fills its field, the filling saturates it, and in the saturated field tension seeks release; within closed space release is destructive, and only an extensive opening is not, until the new space fills in turn. The paper fixes the system's dynamic nature and its genesis, and hands the elaboration to the remaining chapters of the cycle.

title: Disrupting the Inevitability of Autonomous Vehicles
affiliations: Technische Universität München (TUM), Department of Science and Technology Studies, UCL and University College London

detail.abstract: Autonomous vehicles (AVs) have become central to visions of urban mobility. While AVs are often portrayed as an inevitable disruption, ongoing experiments reveal their unfinished nature and raise questions of responsible governance. In this chapter, we explore the implications of AVs and AV experiments for urban life and ask: what is meant to be disrupted, which mobility regimes are destabilized, and who participates in shaping the future trajectory of mobility innovation? We argue that current developments are not disruptive enough to transform unsustainable and unjust patterns of urban mobility. Rather than demonstrating inevitable autonomous systems, experiments could instead serve to open debate on the often ignored social, infrastructural, and regulatory dimensions of AVs, as well as on alternative options. Prioritizing local mobility needs over assumptions of universal scalability has the potential to make AVs beneficial for a broader public. We conclude that responsible governance in experiments and beyond needs to reconsider how AVs might disrupt incumbent mobility regimes.

title: Capacity-Constrained Demand Pressure as a Parsimonious Predictor of Inflation: An Occam's Razor Approach
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Capacity-Constrained Demand Pressure as a Parsimonious Predictor of Inflation: An Occam's Razor Approach

declarations.declarationOfInterest: None at present time
declarations.ethicsApproval: No studies were conducted involving patients / participants in the development of this paper. I would like to outwardly disclose that Claude Opus 4.6 was utilized throughout the research process, in every instance - the input data, frameworks and prompts were entirely my own and no external proprietary / confidential data was incorporated in the process.

detail.abstract: This paper introduces the Capacity-Constrained Demand Pressure (CPDP) model as a parsimonious, single-factor leading indicator for U.S. inflation as measured by the Personal Consumption Expenditures (PCE) price index. In contrast to the multi-factor Phillips Curve variants, DSGE frameworks, and machine learning ensembles that dominate contemporary inflation forecasting, the CPDP model exploits a single structural insight: inflation is fundamentally a capacity utilization phenomenon with a transmission lag. The model's predictive power is strongly regime-dependent: using 162 realized monthly forecastoutcome pairs from November 2012 through April 2026, the post-COVID subsample (2020-2026) achieves R2 = 0.440 (block bootstrap p = 0.049), while the preceding lowvariance period (2012-2020) yields R2 = 0.171 (p = 0.09), not statistically distinguishable from noise at conventional levels. A Chow test confirms a structural break at March 2020 (F = 52.40, p < 0.001), with the capacity-to-inflation transmission coefficient rising from β = 0.18 pre-COVID to β = 0.53 post-COVID. The pooled full-sample relationship (73.3% correlation, 53.7% R2, block bootstrap p = 0.002) benefits substantially from the highvariance inflation cycle and should be interpreted as a statistical average over two distinct regimes rather than a stable structural parameter. The CPDP model subsumes the unemployment gap's predictive content in the full sample and post-COVID regime: in a bivariate Phillips Curve comparison (N = 153), adding the unemployment gap to CPDP yields a statistically insignificant improvement (ΔR² = 0.003, F = 1.09, p = 0.30), while adding CPDP to the Phillips Curve yields a massive gain (ΔR² = 0.528, F = 173.4, p < 0.001). However, this subsumption is regime-specific: in the preCOVID low-volatility period (N = 79), the Phillips Curve retains independent predictive  content (R² = 0.283) above CPDP (R² = 0.207), and the unemployment gap adds significantly to CPDP (F = 12.07, p < 0.001). The 'sufficient statistic' characterization applies primarily to the post-COVID regime and full sample. The effective independent sample size of approximately 10 non-overlapping 16-month forecast windows - spanning roughly 1.5 inflation cycles of meaningful amplitude - represents a fundamental limitation on generalizability claims. The model is best understood as a conditional forecasting tool: it identifies the direction and magnitude of capacity pressure with high accuracy during regime shifts, but its signal-to-noise ratio deteriorates in low-volatility environments where all parsimonious models struggle. We argue this represents an Occam's Razor result: the simplest model consistent with the data should be preferred, particularly when complex alternatives offer marginal improvement at the cost of interpretability, robustness, and real-time applicability.

title: Is Immigration a Problem for Europe?

detail.title: Is Immigration a Problem for Europe?
detail.abstract: This article examines whether immigration constitutes "a problem" for Europe on the basis of evidence published in academic journals. Priority is given to meta-analyses, literature reviews, reforms, assignment rules, discontinuities, and other designs capable of distinguishing causal effects from selection. The evidence supports neither the view that immigration is harmless nor the view that it automatically produces benefits. Average effects on native wages and employment are generally small, but local and short-run losses occur among closely substitutable workers, and some quasi-experimental shocks produce sizeable declines in local employment. Skilled immigration can expand firms, capital, productivity, and innovation, although this evidence is concentrated in particular flows and regions. Refugees exhibit larger employment gaps and higher initial fiscal costs; employment bans, administrative delays, dispersal policies, and the nonrecognition of credentials causally aggravate those gaps. At the meso level, housing, schools, health care, and public safety display heterogeneous effects: housing may become more expensive where supply is rigid; high school concentration can impair outcomes; and although reviews find no uniform increase in total crime, several European designs detect increases in property or violent offences under unemployment, exclusion, or refugee inflows. At the macro level, immigration raises total output and may improve output per capita, employment, and demographic indicators, but fiscal conclusions depend fundamentally on age, employment, wages, household composition, time horizon, and accounting rules. The aggregate evidence on asylum is too narrow to support a universal claim. The balance is conditional and asymmetric: there is no basis for describing all immigration as an intrinsic general burden on Europe, but neither is there a basis for assuming that every volume or composition will be benign. The most robust problems are distributive, territorial, transitional-fiscal, and institutional; their magnitude depends on which flow arrives, how rapidly, where it settles, and under which housing, employment, education, legal-status, and municipal-financing rules.

title: Artificial Intelligence: What Drives Adoption in EU Countries?
affiliations: ,  and

detail.title: Artificial Intelligence: What Drives Adoption in EU Countries?

declarations.funderStatement: Financial support for this research was provided by Neoma Business School “Business Dynamics, Productivity, Employment, and Human Resources” research chair

detail.abstract: This paper uses results from successive waves of the Eurostat survey on 'ICT usage and e-commerce in enterprises' to study the determinants of AI adoption in a country/industry/time panel covering 17 countries and 24 industries of the European Union over 2021-2025. We relate adoption to several potential drivers: the perceived obstacles to adoption, the business environment (such as investment in organizational capital), the policy context (such as policies affecting the capabilities and incentives to adopt and use AI technologies) and demography (shares of different age groups within employees). We summarize some of the potential drivers using Principal Components Analyses and take a diff-in-diff approach to highlight how the influence of nationwide drivers of adoption differs depending on industry exposure to them. We find robust statistical associations of both adoption and the extent of AI use (at least three AI technologies) with mismatch obstacles (data availability, expertise, technological incompatibility, or AI's perceived lack of usefulness for the firm) whose significance has increased over time, as well as with costs and personal concerns (legal uncertainty, ethical and privacy concerns) whose significance has decreased over time. Human capabilities (such as ICT skills and organizational capital) and innovation policies are positively related to AI adoption, while policies curbing either workforce flexibility or competition in industries that are key providers of intermediate inputs are inversely related to adoption. Finally, we find evidence of an inverted U-curve between workforce age and AI adoption, with adoption being weaker where the age distribution is tilted towards young or elderly workers; however, higher AI exposure in an industry moderates these demographic effects, perhaps due to skillleveling effect of the new technology.

title: Fairness-Accuracy Trade-offs and Calibration Mechanisms in Machine Learning-Based Subprime Credit Scoring
affiliations: George Washington University, Renming University of China and

detail.title: Fairness-Accuracy Trade-offs and Calibration Mechanisms in Machine Learning-Based Subprime Credit Scoring
detail.abstract: The use of machine learning in subprime loans has significantly improved the ability to detect default, but it can also amplify structural differences between groups in the process of approving and pricing. Using real world business data from a US subprime auto lender, we have compiled some 120,000 application and repayment samples to compare the fairness and prediction performance of logistic regression, random forest, XGBoost, and multilayered perceptrones.This study uses AUC, KS, default detection rate, and portfolio returns as assessment measures to measure demographic equity, equal opportunities, and individual equity. The results indicate that XGBoost has the best prediction precision, but shows the greatest differences between races, ages, and sexes; logistic regression has a lower overall precision but shows a relatively stable equity performance.Addressing the high retraining and deployment costs associated with traditional fair constraints, a correction strategy is proposed that combines group-specific threshold adjustment with postprocessing calibration. With no change in the structure of the core model, this approach reduces the difference metrics by 27.4%, but the AUC is reduced by only 0.3 percentage points, and the aggregate gain remains substantially the same. This approach is more suitable for rapid deployment in existing loan schemes than for a simple modification of the loss function or the application of a single threshold. The results of the study show that equity and profitability are not mutually exclusive, and a more robust balance between risk control, profitability, and compliance can be achieved by appropriate calibration.

title: Predictive Minimaxity, the GLX Connecting Formula and the Horseshoe Prior
affiliations: Virginia Tech, University of Chicago - Booth School of Business, George Mason University and

detail.title: Predictive Minimaxity, the GLX Connecting Formula and the Horseshoe Prior
detail.abstract: Zhai and Ročková (2026) prove that the horseshoe is the first continuous prior to achieve the exact Mukherjee and Johnstone minimax KL predictive constant in the sparse Gaussian sequence model. We develop a framework (the George, Liang and Xu (GLX) connecting formula and the Datta Polson, Sokolov and Zantedeschi (DPSZ) Moderate Deviation Principle) that simultaneously simplifies their proofs, extends their results to the horseshoe+ prior, and weakens their conditions. The GLX formula equates excess KL predictive risk to α 2 times excess quadratic estimation risk; it converts the noise-case argument to a one-line bound, identifies horseshoe spectroscopy as conditional GLX plus Jensen, and eliminates three of their four adaptive lemmas. We prove the horseshoe+ achieves the same exact constant with a strictly faster sub-leading correction governed by its log-squared spike. The theta-min condition is weakened  to the MDP detection threshold and shown to be the sharpest achievable condition for any adaptive continuous-prior predictor. All results extend to sparse regression via SVD reduction.

title: GDP Nowcasting in Mauritania using Machine Learning and Satellite Data
affiliations: Economist at the Central Banque of Mauritania

detail.title: GDP Nowcasting in Mauritania using Machine Learning and Satellite Data
detail.abstract: This paper examines the role of satellite data and machine learning techniques in improving the nowcasting of real GDP in Mauritania, a context characterized by limited data availability and delays in official statistics. By combining traditional macroeconomic indicators with satellite-based variables such as Nighttime Lights and the Normalized Difference Vegetation Index (NDVI), the study develops a framework capable of capturing real-time economic dynamics. The results show that the inclusion of satellite data improves predictive accuracy, particularly when using non-linear models such as XGBoost. In particular, XGBoost records a reduction in RMSE from 0.019 to 0.017 and an increase in R² from 0.372 to 0.483 when satellite variables are included. Nighttime Lights are strongly correlated with economic activity, while NDVI exhibits more limited explanatory power. Overall, the findings highlight the potential of integrating alternative data sources and machine learning methods to enhance economic monitoring and support decisionmaking in data-constrained environments.

title: Survival-Implied Cost of Capital: An Unlevered Ku from Sectoral Business-Mortality Curves, with an Illustrative Application to U.S. Establishment Data

detail.title: Survival-Implied Cost of Capital: An Unlevered Ku from Sectoral Business-Mortality Curves, with an Illustrative Application to U.S. Establishment Data
detail.abstract: Standard estimation of the cost of equity for privately held targets - a routine requirement in M&A and purchase-price-allocation work - leans on a beta that, for the great majority of such targets, is not observable. Practitioners typically substitute comparable-company betas or ad hoc build-up premiums. This paper develops an alternative: an unlevered cost of capital (Ku) derived directly from sectoral business-survival curves, fit with a two-parameter Weibull hazard model. We argue this quantity is conceptually distinct from beta - it prices total (business, Porterian) risk rather than covariance with a diversified market portfolio - and is therefore appropriate for the single-owner, undiversified-investor setting that characterizes most private-firm valuation, while remaining reconcilable with conventional WACC through standard unlevering/relevering (Modigliani-Miller Proposition II) and Adjusted Present Value (APV) machinery. We derive a closed-form survival-implied Ke, extend it to age-conditional survival (relevant because M&A targets are rarely newborn firms), and illustrate the approach on publicly available U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics Business Employment Dynamics (BED) establishment-survival cohorts. The illustration also surfaces an important data-granularity limitation: at the 2-digit NAICS sector level publicly available from BLS, cross-sector dispersion in fitted hazard parameters is compressed relative to what a finer, firm-registry-based table (e.g., 4-digit classification) would likely reveal. We discuss this limitation together with the paper's other simplifying assumptions and lay out an empirical validation agenda - testing the survival-implied Ke against realized private-market transaction multiples - reserved for future work.

title: Monetary Policy and Functional Income Distribution: Aggregate-Level Evidence from Türkiye's Negative Real Interest Rate Regime
affiliations: Bahcesehir University

detail.title: Monetary Policy and Functional Income Distribution: Aggregate-Level Evidence from Türkiye's Negative Real Interest Rate Regime
detail.abstract: The paper examines the aggregate-level transmission of monetary policy to functional income distribution in Türkiye. The mechanism operates through the interaction of low policy ratetriggered exchange rate movements, inflation, and the sluggish adjustment of nominal wages. A six-variable structural VAR is estimated on quarterly data for 1998Q1-2023Q3, with a recursive identification suited to the unconventional low and negative real interest rate (LNRIR) policy episode of 2017-2022, during which the Central Bank of the Republic of Türkiye cut the policy rate despite rising inflation. Results show that a 10% depreciation shock in currency reduces the labor share significantly, with the peak decline within four quarters; the response of the labor share is roughly 1.5 times larger in the LNRIR sub-sample. A 250 bps policy rate cut works in the same direction with a more modest magnitude. Real wages recover within six to eight quarters while the labor share remains depressed. Moreover, the historical decomposition indicates that most of the variation in the labor share is driven by output and price shocks rather than by monetary shocks. The aggregate-level mechanism rooted in nominal wage rigidity therefore captures only a limited transmission of monetary policy to the functional distribution of income. The persistent compression of the labor share instead points to a production-side channel operating through material costs examined in the author's PhD dissertation.

title: Job Security and Effort in Major League Baseball
affiliations: and University of Michigan

detail.title: Job Security and Effort in Major League Baseball

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The authors have no relevant financial or non-financial interests to disclose.

detail.abstract: This study uses Major League Baseball (MLB) player data to test for impacts of job security on worker effort. Using variation in job security across the duration of multi-year player contracts, prior studies have found mixed evidence, with recent studies finding an inverse relationship between job security and worker production. Prior studies use measures of worker production as proxies for effort, though production depends on effort, ability, and luck. With the advent of improved tracking technology with Statcast in baseball, more direct measures of player effort are now available. In this study we test for how job security impacts measures of production, effort, and luck by estimating player fixed effects regressions on a panel of MLB hitters from 2016 to 2024. In line with recent literature, we find that increased job security leads to diminished production. In advancing the literature, we also find evidence that increased job security leads to diminished effort. We do not find any evidence of job security influencing luck. These findings have implications for how teams may use player tracking to incentivize player effort in the face of high job security. The finding also has implications for employment settings outside of sport.

title: Stress Analyzer: A Machine Learning Approach to Predict Student Stress Levels for Early Intervention
