title: Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning with Biological Graph Architecture (BDH) for Multi-Echelon Supply Chain Optimization Under Disruptions

detail.title: Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning with Biological Graph Architecture (BDH) for Multi-Echelon Supply Chain Optimization Under Disruptions

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares that they have no known competing financial interests or personal relationships that could have appeared to influence the work reported in this paper.
declarations.ethicsApproval: Not applicable. Neither human nor animal experimentation was conducted in this study. The research relies purely on computational algorithms and secondary dataset simulations.
declarations.funderStatement: This research did not receive any specific grant from funding agencies in the public, commercial, or not-for-profit sectors.

detail.abstract:
Managing a multi-echelon supply chain under demand volatility and disruption risks is a complex sequential decision-making problem. Current Deep Reinforcement Learning (DRL) models relying on Multi-Layer Perceptrons (MLP) or Graph Neural Networks (GNN) often struggle to capture complex network topologies or suffer from oversmoothing and scalability issues in large-scale graphs. To overcome these limitations, this research proposes a novel Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning (MARL) framework integrating Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO) with the Dragon Hatchling (BDH) architecture as the core policy network. BDH is a biologically inspired, scale-free network model that leverages local neuron interactions and Hebbian working memory.
By modeling a two-echelon supply chain environment subject to stochastic demand and lead-time disruptions, the proposed BDH-PPO model enables agents to autonomously reason and adapt to supply shocks without relying on computationally expensive chain-of-thought processes. Through rigorous simulation, we demonstrate that the BDH-PPO model converges faster and outperforms static inventory policies (e.g., base-stock, (s, Q)) in minimizing total operational costs while effectively dampening the Bullwhip Effect.
Current State of the Art (The Gap): While Transformer-based models and traditional RL have been extensively used, BDH represents a novel "post-Transformer" architecture. To date, no existing Q1/Q2 Scopus literature has published the direct integration of BDH as the Policy Network in a MARL framework for supply chain inventory control. This project aims to be the pioneer in translating BDH's cognitive reasoning capabilities from NLP tasks into the domain of Control and Logistics.

title: Climate Regulation, Asset Stranding and Foreign Investors
affiliations: IE Business School and

detail.title: Climate Regulation, Asset Stranding and Foreign Investors
detail.abstract: Climate regulation is typically studied as a repricing event. We show it is also a sorting event, moving in opposite directions across the same market. Using Boston's 2013 building carbon mandate, we find regulation strands the bottom of the market while reallocating the top to foreign capital. Financially vulnerable buildings lose buyers entirely rather than simply repricing, forfeiting the energy upgrades that ownership changes enable, while the most valuable properties attract investors experienced in managing regulatory risk. A well-intentioned regulation fails because the buildings that most, not least, need to improve are locked out of the trading mechanism.

title: Mitigating Requirement-change Intrusion Spillovers in Software Development: Additional Task
affiliations: Fudan University, School of Management, Fudan University, University of Nottingham, Ningbo - University of Nottingham Ningbo China and Fudan University

detail.title: Mitigating Requirement-change Intrusion Spillovers in Software Development: Additional Task
detail.abstract: Requirement changes are common in software development and often prompt managers to reduce developers' remaining workload to help them cope with such intrusions. Yet the effects of requirement-change intrusions on other concurrent tasks have been largely overlooked in prior research. We argue that requirement-change intrusions leave residual cognition with the interrupted task, thereby impairing performance on other concurrent tasks. We further propose that assigning additional tasks can help developers redirect attention away from the interrupted task and toward actionable work. Using development log data from a software-as-a-service company and a difference-indifferences design, we find that requirement-change intrusions significantly reduce performance on concurrent work, providing evidence of spillover effects beyond the interrupted task itself. Furthermore, additional task assignment exhibits an inverted-U moderating effect: moderate assignment attenuates the negative impact of requirement-change intrusions, whereas excessive assignment reverses these benefits. Additional analyses show that the buffering effect of the additional task assignment is stronger when requirement uncertainty is high, suggesting a greater role for attention redirection, whereas the detrimental effects of excessive assignment are more pronounced when intrusions involve high-priority tasks, indicating heightened cognitive overload. The findings generate important theoretical and managerial implications for interruption management in software development.

title: The Bitter Pill: The Impact of Tendering on Nationwide Drug Shortages
affiliations: Rotterdam School of Management (RSM) Erasmus University Rotterdam, , Erasmus University Rotterdam (EUR) - Rotterdam School of Management (RSM) and

detail.title: The Bitter Pill: The Impact of Tendering on Nationwide Drug Shortages

declarations.declarationOfInterest: No
declarations.ethicsApproval: No
declarations.funderStatement: This research was supported by TKI Dinalog (No. 2024-1-364-TKI) and Helsevel; The Research Council of Norway (No. MIA:300867).

detail.abstract: This study examines the impact of tendering to procure drugs on nationwide drug shortages. While tendering can improve affordability, it is argued to threaten availability by putting suppliers’ margins under pressure, increasing market concentration, inducing switches in suppliers, and prompting suppliers to exit the market. To date, however, empirical evidence of this trade-off has been missing in the literature. We use three unique datasets from the Netherlands to examine this using a stacked difference-in-differences approach. Our results confirm that tendering substantially increases drug shortages. In the year after a tenderer initiates its first tendered contract for a drug, shortages increase by the equivalent of 9.9 additional days of nationwide shortage – a 36% increase relative to the average of 27.7 days in the year before. The impact aggravates in the long term and is particularly strong for drugs that (1) have few – but more than one – alternative suppliers, (2) have a fairly concentrated market, and (3) generate low revenues. Our study provides actionable insights on how to modify tendering or selectively apply it to reduce impacts on shortages.

title: The Environmental Impact of Multinational Firms
affiliations: University of British Columbia (UBC), University of Lausanne and University of Bologna

detail.title: The Environmental Impact of Multinational Firms

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The authors declare no conflict of interest.
declarations.funderStatement: F.N. acknowledges financial support from the Canada Research Chairs Program.

detail.abstract: Air pollution, deforestation, biodiversity loss, and climate change are among the most pressing global problems, but while environmental conditions are improving in many developed countries, environmental degradation is still widespread across the developing world. Multinational enterprises could play a central role in solving or fuelling these global environmental problems. On the one hand, they could help to transfer clean technologies and sustainable management practices to less developed regions, but on the other hand, they may contribute to the problem by shifting polluting production to developing countries or by lowering local environmental standards. Here, we use a unique geospatial panel of millions of multinational and domestic companies to quantify their impact on the environment in Africa. Our results show that an expansion of multinational activity causes severe loss of forest cover, erodes local crop diversity, and, to some extent, increases greenhouse gas emissions. They show further that the adverse environmental impact of multinationals is significantly larger than the impact of domestic firms, even after controlling for firm characteristics. Our results highlight the tradeoffs that many developing countries face. While multinationals contribute more to local economic activity than domestic firms, they also cause more environmental damage than their domestic counterparts. Our findings also suggest a solution to this dilemma. They show that governance in the parent corporation and the multinational affiliate's country plays an important role in reducing environmental damage.

title: Motivating Secure Behavior in AI-Enabled Public Organizations: Ethical, Inclusive, and Sustainable Transformation
affiliations: Wroclaw University, Faculty of Historical and Pedagogical Sciences, Institute of Psychology, Adam Mickiewicz University, University of Lower Silesia and University of Lower Silesia

detail.title: Motivating Secure Behavior in AI-Enabled Public Organizations: Ethical, Inclusive, and Sustainable Transformation

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The authors declare no conflict of interest.
declarations.ethicsApproval: This study used publicly available and anonymized data and did not require ethics committee approval under applicable regulations.
declarations.funderStatement: University of Wrocław, Institute of Psychology

detail.abstract: As AI-driven digital transformation advances, secure behavior in public institutions depends not only on technology but also on employee motivation. This study examines how Openness to AI (AIES-AI) and Perceived Development Barriers (AIES-DEV) relate to secure behavioral intentions (BIS-ACT) in publicsector organizations. Drawing on self-determination theory and protection motivation theory, we introduce and validate the CAIMOS model using survey data from 221 Polish public-sector employees. Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modeling (PLS-SEM) reveals that openness to AI is positively, though marginally, associated with secure intentions, while perceived development barriers show a small but significant positive relationship. The model explains 44% of the variance in secure intentions, indicating moderate explanatory power. Findings suggest that motivational dynamics in AI-enabled environments may operate through both activating and mobilizing mechanisms. The study provides a context-sensitive measurement tool and advances understanding of human-centered cybersecurity in the digital transformation of public organizations.

title: When Corporate Actions Do Not Lead to Purported Impact: Type II Greenwashing as a Barrier to Sustainability Mainstreaming
affiliations: EDHEC Business School, University of London - Royal Holloway and

detail.title: When Corporate Actions Do Not Lead to Purported Impact: Type II Greenwashing as a Barrier to Sustainability Mainstreaming

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The authors declare no conflicts of interest.
declarations.ethicsApproval: Not applicable – conceptual article, no human or animal subjects.
declarations.funderStatement: The research received no specific grant from any funding agency in the public, commercial, or not-for-profit sectors.

detail.abstract: To dispel suspicions of "greenwashing," many companies have adopted more rigorous corporate sustainability communication (CSC) practices, such as reporting an increased amount of numerical, third-party verified data. This has led to claims that greenwashing is declining. In this conceptual article, we propose a more nuanced diagnosis, arguing the importance of distinguishing between two types of greenwashing: Type I, i.e., CSC practices by which companies exaggerate the extent to which they engage in actions described as socially or environmentally desirable; and Type II, i.e., CSC practices by which companies falsely suggest that their actions contribute to the macro-level goal of sustainability. While Type I greenwashing may have declined, Type II greenwashing remains insufficiently conceptualized and countered, thus posing a major obstacle to mainstreaming sustainability. We identify key features of Type II greenwashing, theorize three discursive devices through which it operates, and outline ways to thwart it.

title: Here Today, Gone Today: First Evidence on European Zero-Day Options
affiliations: Independent

detail.title: Here Today, Gone Today: First Evidence on European Zero-Day Options
detail.abstract: This paper provides the first systematic empirical analysis of zero-days-to-expiry options on the EURO STOXX 50 and the DAX. Since their introduction on the Eurex in 2023, daily-expiry index options have grown rapidly, yet their European pricing and trading costs remain undocumented. Using intraday order-book data, four results emerge. Putcall parity holds tightly at quoted mid-prices, with cross-strike dispersion of the implied forward around a tenth of an index point for the EURO STOXX 50 and half a point for the DAX. This efficiency is, however, largely a mid-quote phenomenon: once the spread is crossed, the round-trip cost of a synthetic position is roughly fifteen to twenty times larger, near 10% and 13% of the at-the-money straddle premium, respectively. The proportional cost rises sharply into expiry, reaching roughly 40% and 70% of the straddle value in the final half-hour. Costs peak at the money, where the premium is thinnest relative to the spread, and are consistent across both indices. The market is thus priced most precisely where execution is most expensive, with trading costs concentrated in the final, thinnest-liquidity minutes of the session.

title: C.S. Lewis' Enduring and Unpretentious Lessons on Stepparent Child Custody Part 3: Communication, Preparation and the Best Interests of the Child

detail.abstract: In Part 1, we considered the personal and relational challenges C. S. Lewis faced as a newly formed stepfamily confronted impending loss, and in Part 2, we examined the legal framework that governs custody when a custodial parent dies. Together, these reveal both the human and legal tensions inherent in such cases. Part 3 turns to Lewis' responseexamining how his actions, decisions, and steady focus on the children's well-being offer practical guidance for stepparents navigating similarly difficult circumstances.

title: A Review of Payments Clearing Systems for Operations Researchers
affiliations: Central South University - School of Business, University of Toronto - Rotman School of Management, Payments Canada, University of Toronto - Rotman School of Management and Hefei University of Technology

detail.title: A Review of Payments Clearing Systems for Operations Researchers
detail.abstract: Payment clearing systems process trillions of dollars in transactions daily across interconnected banking networks, serving as the foundational infrastructure underpinning nearly all financial and commercial activity in modern economies. Despite their enormous scale and systemic significance, payment systems remain comparatively underexplored within the operations research and management science literature. This paper reviews the design and operations of such systems through an operations management perspective, centering on the fundamental trade-off between settlement risk and liquidity sourcing costs. Our core contribution lies in developing a unified analytical framework that decomposes payment systems into three interconnected components: (i) payments and liquidity input that capture stochastic payment flows and liquidity policy instruments; (ii) the clearing process characterizing clearing architectures and algorithms; and (iii) the performance objective that assesses system outcomes via a social cost function encompassing strategic policy costs and daily operational costs. Building on this framework, we structure the existing literature around two central design problems: liquidity policy design covering both strategic and operational choices that shape banks' liquidity endowment; and payment submission behavior and the clearing architecture design encompassing clearing timing, netting density and clearing algorithms. We demonstrate that these design dimensions jointly determine systemic stability and efficiency. We further synthesize extant studies highlighting how network interconnectedness and strategic delay incentives give rise to systemic vulnerability and payment gridlock. Finally, we identify prominent research gaps spanning dynamic optimization of clearing operations, endogenous payment network formation, and the joint calibration of complementary policy tools. We conclude that future advances in this domain call for dynamic, state dependent models that unify system design, participant incentives, and real-time operational dynamics, with the ultimate goal of enhancing both the efficiency and resilience of payments clearing systems.

title: Distortions, Efficiency and the Size Distribution of Firms
affiliations: Université de Sherbrooke - Department of Economics and Vancouver School of Economics, UBC

detail.title: Distortions, Efficiency and the Size Distribution of Firms
detail.abstract: We develop a model of firms' growth in which the tax and credit environments act as selection mechanisms. Such a model, parametrized and validated using a variety of data restrictions, can rationalize observations about input choices and size patterns typical of many developing countries. Using counterfactual experiments, we show that firms' optimal responses to the tax environment are effective in reducing efficiency losses. As a consequence, tax distortions only account for 13% of the gap in output per worker between an undistorted economy and the benchmark. Credit constraints account for 44% of this gap. However, the interaction between the cost of capital and credit constraints appears to be the most important source of misallocation and can explain up to 85% of the difference in output per worker between the benchmark and first-best.

title: The Unbuilt Capacity: Contractor-Side Claims Capacity in Pakistani Public-Sector Construction — A Diagnosis from the State of the Matter

detail.title: The Unbuilt Capacity: Contractor-Side Claims Capacity in Pakistani Public-Sector Construction — A Diagnosis from the State of the Matter

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author is an independent practitioner in Pakistani public-sector construction with professional experience across contractor, consultant, and employer-adjacent positions, including witness service in construction arbitration. The paper reflects that practitioner perspective. The author has no financial interest in any party or matter referenced. Drafting and structural assembly were supported by AI assistance under the author's direction; the analysis, the diagnosis, the weighing of causes, and the field readings are the author's own.
declarations.funderStatement: No external funding. The research was conducted independently by the author.

detail.abstract: In Pakistani public-sector construction, a contractor's entitlement to payment is a legal right under the Contract Act 1872 and the FIDIC-derived contracts that govern the work. Yet that right frequently fails to convert into payment through the contract's own machinery — notice, the Engineer's determination, the dispute board — and reaches resolution, if at all, through the courts. This paper diagnoses the failure as a present structural condition: contractor-side claims capacity, the specialised discipline of recording, notifying, and escalating entitlement before arbitration, is under-developed and under-practised. The diagnosis rests on three present signs: foreign contractors recover through the contractual machinery, under public-sector employers of the same class as local firms, without diplomatic intervention; disputes characteristically reach arbitration by judicial route rather than through the contract; and Pakistani firms lack an internationally-competitive contracting footprint. The paper distinguishes this core finding from its account of origin — the narrowing of the competitively-tendered field as work moves to state-associated entities — which it offers as the most probable explanation rather than as proof. It concludes that although the gains from building the capacity are positive-sum and accrue to the state, the concentrated cost of building it falls structurally on the contractor, who must build it claim by claim, regardless of who caused the deficit.

title: Does Regulation Bite at Gateways? Evidence from MiCA and Stablecoins
affiliations: LUISS University - Department of Economics and Finance and University of Surrey

detail.title: Does Regulation Bite at Gateways? Evidence from MiCA and Stablecoins
detail.abstract: Gateways are trading venues where regulation can change the assets investors can trade. We study this margin using MiCA-EU's Markets in Crypto-Assets Regulation-which led several exchanges to delist USDT pairs for European Economic Area users, while USDC obtained MiCA authorization. First, aggregate market shares and trading volumes barely move. Second, comparing Regulated-facing exchanges with globally oriented exchanges where MiCA is less likely to bind, we show that the crosssection shifts toward USDC-USDC share rises by 0.82 and relative trading volume by 0.54 pre-event standard deviations. Both reflect USDT trading contracting where it is delisted.

title: The Executive Order
affiliations: UC Berkeley School of Law

detail.title: The Executive Order
detail.abstract:
Executive orders have been a defining feature of the second Trump presidency. Hundreds of orders and proclamations have introduced sweeping policies and an exceptionally broad view of presidential control over the administrative state. Yet existing scholarship on executive orders offers only a partial view of this key presidential governance instrument. Scholars have largely focused on the constitutional and statutory underpinnings of executive orders and treated them as monolithic instruments within a broader toolkit of presidential administration. The structure of executive orders and how agencies interact with them have received far less attention. 

This Article offers a novel account of executive orders that focuses on how their internal structure determines agency implementation. Based on an original dataset of 1,982 executive orders issued between 1981 and late 2025, the Article identifies three distinct categories of executive order elements: (1) action-forcing elements that operate as mandates, (2) methodology-setting elements that impose trans-substantive regulatory requirements, and (3) policy-setting elements that merely articulate aspirational policy goals. The Article empirically examines additional structural features, including cited legal authority, domestic or foreign policy orientation, and the relationship between those elements and an order’s composition.

The Article argues that each category of elements interacts with agencies and White House oversight in fundamentally different ways, shaping the likelihood, form, and intensity of agency implementation. Action-forcing elements are likely to trigger substantial agency implementation efforts. They are significantly correlated with citations to statutes, not just vague invocations of Article II authority. Policy-setting elements are highly susceptible to bureaucratic pushback, inattention, and indecision. Methodology-setting elements often have robust White House backing, but methodological ambiguity and resource constraints hamper their implementation. Orders that rely heavily on policy-setting and methodology-setting elements—like many of President Trump’s recent orders—are therefore subject to important limitations on the President’s ability to generate agency compliance.

title: Individual and Collective Academic Freedom

detail.title: Individual and Collective Academic Freedom
detail.abstract:
Amidst unprecedented attacks on higher education in the United States, the leading defenders of academic freedom cannot agree on what academic freedom means. Most converge in their understanding of individual academic freedom: the longstanding principle that university teachers and researchers should be allowed to pursue those activities freely, subject only to the standards of their discipline and the judgments of their disciplinary peers. But individual freedom to teach and research, necessary as it is, can hardly be sufficient: it does little good if the individual’s courses, funding, or entire department is cut by administrators or politicians acting without the benefit of shared governance, which takes into account the collective opinions and expertise of faculty.  

Prominent critics and campus speech organizations have recently worried that when it comes to issues like DEI initiatives, institutional speech, and academic boycotts, calls for shared governance reduce academic freedom principles to majoritarian decision-making. This Essay argues instead that collective decisions on these issues are unavoidable, and best left to the faculty; meanwhile, the potential dangers of collective academic freedom are already familiar in the disciplinary judgments on which individual academic freedom depends. Avoiding these genuine dangers requires us to see both individual and collective academic freedom as an ethical practice in which the categorial rules some critics seek are unlikely to prove helpful.

title: Ontological Politics and the Limits of Recognition in Northeast India

detail.title: Ontological Politics and the Limits of Recognition in Northeast India
detail.abstract: This paper examines the intersection of Indigenous epistemologies and politics of recognition in Northeast India. The politics of recognition is viewed as not only a legal or political process but an epistemological as well. Although usually understood as the act of granting visibility and legitimacy of existence to marginalised groups by the state, recognition is inherently tied to struggles between different epistemological and ontological orders. The struggles of indigenous people for autonomy and self-representation were historically based on demanding recognition from the state. Yet, these demands become limited when the idea of autonomy becomes confined to the frameworks of bureaucracy or legislation. The notion of ontological politics helps us understand recognition in terms of both its potentialities and its limitations. On one hand, recognition provides indigenous people with security, visibility, and institutional legitimation. On the other hand, it is also part of a classificatory regime that fixes the dynamic and complex realities of Indigenous societies within the framework of administrative categories. In this context, recognition can work against the process of self-representation and put restrictions on it via epistemological constraints, as it may impose external definitions and limitations on how indigenous identities and knowledge systems are understood and expressed. While challenging the framework of liberal multiculturalism, the paper aims to understand the political aspirations of indigenous people, not just as a demand to be included in the already existing order but as a fight for the right to exist politically and epistemologically differently.

title: Can Unbiased Predictive AIs Amplify Bias?
affiliations: Queen's Economics Department

detail.title: Can Unbiased Predictive AIs Amplify Bias?

detail.abstract: I analyze a model of unbiased predictions mediated by biased humans, showing that a bias-neutral precision gain (e.g. from AI adoption) is not generally bias-neutral in its effects. Expected victims of bias are discriminated-group applicants with qualifications warranting approval under a counterfactual unbiased standard but not the stricter biased standard they face. For them, precision raises discrimination by reducing noise-driven chance approvals. Overall discrimination can also increase when precision shifts more realized predictions of discriminated-group applicants into than out of the between-standards interval. This isolates a new channel through which AI can exacerbate discrimination, distinct from biased design or data.

title: An Amplifier of Position, Not Competence: Why Hierarchy Emerges, What we Pay for It to Hold, and why its Cost cannot be Settled
affiliations: Independent Researcher

detail.title: An Amplifier of Position, Not Competence: Why Hierarchy Emerges, What we Pay for It to Hold, and why its Cost cannot be Settled

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author received no specific funding for this work and declares no competing financial or personal interests.
declarations.ethicsApproval: Not applicable. This study involves no human or animal subjects and uses only publicly available secondary datasets (ICIJ Offshore Leaks Database, GH Archive, Maddison Project Database); ethics approval was therefore not required.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding.

detail.abstract: A prior trilogy established that individual outcomes are dominated by the dispersion of the environment rather than of capability, formally Var(ln ρ eff) ≫ Var(ln k) at a global dominance ratio R ∈ [27, 134] [1, 2], but not where that dispersion comes from. We supply the mechanism: hierarchy as an amplifier, a multiplicative cascade that turns tiny, often capability-irrelevant initial differences into the large positional dispersion the trilogy measured, so that R becomes an output of structure rather than a fact about people. We microfound the feedback f (S) in Gould's deference model [4] (linear at the bottom, saturating at the top) and identify the Kesten reset [10] that creates the heavy tail with Boehm's reverse-dominance insurance [7], pinning the tail index in closed form, α = 1 + [δ + δ 2 + 2σ 2 p]/σ 2 , confirmed by a Clauset MLE [18]. The calibrated amplifier reproduces R at all four aggregation levels and requires a near-random-walk between-environment process. On the raw ICIJ Offshore Leaks officer network [24] the predicted heavy tail holds (global α ≈ 2.25), but no concentration metric tracks recording opacity across jurisdictions: that negative result vindicates the demarcation paper [3], since the quantity that would test the lever is hidden by construction. We then turn to a domain where position is logged, GitHub pull requests. On 113 895 closed pull requests, position multiplies the merge odds 3-7× at fixed diff size; a within-author design bounds the position premium at 12.6 pp (p = 2 × 10-18); and the cleanest design, a promotion holding author and project fixed, still finds acceptance rising +4.1 pp in the same repository at unchanged proposal size (p = 2 × 10-7), though even it cannot fully separate the badge from the competence that travels with it. The amplifier's gains are continuous and visible while its costs are rare, delayed and hidden, so hierarchy always appears beneficial and its net cost cannot be honestly settled.

title: Virtual Leadership Competencies in United States Health Care Organizations A Qualitative Inquiry of Health Care Leaders
affiliations: Capella University

detail.title: Virtual Leadership Competencies in United States Health Care Organizations A Qualitative Inquiry of Health Care Leaders

contentType.other: Peer reviewed by Capella University faculty as a pre-requisite for a doctoral degree in business

detail.abstract: The accelerated adoption of virtual and hybrid work has increased the importance of virtual leadership in health care organizations. This qualitative inquiry explored the perspectives of U.S. health care leaders regarding the competencies required to be effective virtual leaders and improve team performance. The specific business problem was that some U.S. health care organizations did not have adequate virtual leadership competencies critical to successful virtual leadership, contributing to reduced team performance. Using a generic qualitative inquiry design, data were collected through one-on-one semi-structured Zoom interviews with 11 U.S. health care leaders who had experience managing remote or hybrid teams. Data were analyzed inductively using Braun and Clarke's six-phase thematic analysis process. Four competency themes emerged. First, leaders can be effective virtual leaders when their competencies include clear, frequent, and timely communication, active listening, and personal engagement with their teams. Second, leaders can be effective virtual leaders when they possess competencies in trustbuilding, self-awareness, role modeling, transparency, vulnerability, and empathy. Third, leaders can be effective virtual leaders when their competencies include team inclusion in decisionmaking, setting and communicating clear goals, fostering ownership and accountability, and providing positive reinforcement. Fourth, leaders can be effective virtual leaders when they demonstrate adaptability, continuous learning, and technology proficiency. The findings align with existing e-leadership literature and extend practitioner knowledge by presenting virtual leadership as a set of observable, developable competencies rather than a purely personalitybased construct. The study has implications for leadership selection, development, performance management, and organizational support for virtual leaders in health care settings.

title: Federal Research Funding and STEM Education
affiliations: , World Bank and University of British Columbia, Sauder School of Business

detail.title: Federal Research Funding and STEM Education
detail.abstract: This paper examines how federal science and engineering research funding—although intended to advance research—affects degree production and programs offered in science, technology, engineering, and mathematic (STEM). Using data from 1971–2016, the study implements a triple-difference design that exploits variation across colleges, time, and fields of study. The findings show that federal grants generate 27.4 percent of doctorates and 14.7 percent of undergraduate science, technology, engineering, and mathematics degrees, as well as 6.3 percent of doctoral programs and 3.7 percent of undergraduate programs in STEM annually across 200 U.S. research universities. The impacts are concentrated in biology and engineering, aligning with the priorities of major funders such as the Department of Health and Human Services, the National Science Foundation, and the Department of Defense. These findings suggest that research grants to universities may generate a "double dividend," simultaneously expanding the supply of skilled labor in targeted fields while also advancing scientific discovery.

title: “I Was Well Informed. It Was a Great Advantage”: Pre-Arrival Information Seeking, Information Intelligence, and Immigrants’ Settlement
affiliations: CUNY Queens College and Western University

detail.title: “I Was Well Informed. It Was a Great Advantage”: Pre-Arrival Information Seeking, Information Intelligence, and Immigrants’ Settlement

publicationDetails.detailsText: Journal of Librarianship and Information Science, 0[10.1177/09610006261448918]

detail.abstract: This study reports on the role of pre-arrival information seeking and informed decision making in the settlement experiences of Bangladeshi immigrants in Canada. Despite the importance of immigrants in shaping Canada's future in innovation, economy, and population, this research shows a significant mismatch between immigrants' expectations and their actual settlement experiences, particularly in terms of their employment. This mismatch can lead to depression, frustration, and anxiety, affecting integration into Canadian society. While there has been a recent increase in immigrants' settlement information behavior research in LIS, most focus on post-arrival information needs and seeking. Research findings of this study contribute to understanding the effects of limited access to pre-arrival information and of post-arrival settlement challenges and of the role of active and proactive information seeking in helping newcomers make informed decisions about their lives in their adopted country. The study introduces the concept of "information intelligence" which describes how some newcomers cultivate and use their informational, social, and emotional competencies to gather a comprehensive picture of life before arrival, resulting in better settlement preparations and experiences. The study recommends that government-sponsored comprehensive pre-arrival informational sessions be mandatory for potential immigrants that share information about both benefits and challenges of moving to Canada. This approach ensures newcomers receive accurate and timely information to prepare for life in Canada, reducing reliance on informal or potentially unreliable sources. The study also recommends that these sessions include components to help potential immigrants identify public library programs and services that may benefit them and their families after arriving in Canada.

title: Something about the US -The 2026 Fifa World Cup's economic impacts
affiliations: DER SPIEGEL GmbH & Co. KG

detail.title: Something about the US -The 2026 Fifa World Cup's economic impacts
detail.abstract: Does the 2026 Fifa World Cup have an economic impact of 80 billion USD as promised by Fifa President Gianni Infantino? Should the three hosting countries expect a boost to their GDP from the event? This article studies whether the promises made by a Fifa commissioned analysis or if there is an independent way to measure the economic impact of the mega-sport event. This study based on World Bank and OECD data, uses economic effect studies to predict more reliable results. By introducing a macroeconometric economic growth model and regarding two scenarios, one OECD forecast before and one after the Iran War. For the United States, both scenarios show negative results in the range between-1.5 and-1.0 percentage points. For Canada, that only has two hosting cities, there is no statistically significant result. Mexico, which invested around 8 billion USD in stadia and infrastructure, the results are also small and insignificant, but slightly positive. Even though ex ante studies have their limitations, it gives a first outlook on what some economists and experts have already witnessed as indications.

title: Abel-Regularized Volterra Solvers for American Option Free Boundaries
affiliations: Department of Mathematics

detail.title: Abel-Regularized Volterra Solvers for American Option Free Boundaries
detail.abstract: We present a computational framework for single-and coupled Americanstyle free-boundary problems governed by nonlinear weakly singular Volterra integral equations. The free boundary is parameterized using B-splines, reducing the global continuous problem to a low-dimensional residual system in coefficient space. An Abel-type product-integration scheme isolates the neardiagonal Abel factor, yielding consistent residual quadrature and well-scaled Jacobian assembly. The residual system is solved by correction iterations based on AD full-Jacobian, AD full-Hessian, or reduced-Jacobian models. Numerical experiments on American puts, dividend-paying calls, and coupled choosertype contracts across standard and challenging parameter regimes demonstrate stable boundary reconstruction, accurate prices, and computational efficiency.

title: The Social and Statistical Construction of Race
affiliations: University of Chicago, University of Chicago - Booth School of Business, Louisiana State University, Baton Rouge and University of Chicago

detail.title: The Social and Statistical Construction of Race
detail.abstract: We examine the social construction of race in the United States, from Reconstruction to the modern day, and show how this affects statistical differences across and within racial categories. During the Reconstruction era, people with the same light brown skin tones, recorded by the Freedman's Bank (1865-1874), were more likely racialized as White or Mulatto in the 1870 Census if they were wealthier or literate. Racial assignment of descendants remained fluid through the 1940 Census. In modern data, self-reported race also varies with income and college completion among people with light brown skin tones. This endogenous racial assignment increases cross-race wealth gaps, which we show can be adjusted using sub-samples with data on skin tone or ancestry. Endogenous race also induces selection when controlling for race that, for example, attenuates the relationship between wealth and skin tone.

title: Configurations of Resilience in Inter-Organizational Networks
affiliations: Ca Foscari University of Venice - Department of Management, University of Padua, University of Udine and Luiss Guido Carli University

detail.title: Configurations of Resilience in Inter-Organizational Networks

publicationDetails.detailsText: Venice School of Management - Department of Management Working Paper No. 8
publicationDetails.journalName: Venice School of Management - Department of Management Working Paper Series

detail.abstract: This study examines how inter-organizational business networks build resilience in the face of crises. Prior research has mainly treated structural characteristics and coordination mechanisms as separate explanations of resilience. However, we still lack a clear understanding of how these elements combine to influence resilience outcomes across networks with varying characteristics. We adopt a configurational perspective and investigate how these elements jointly shape networks’ time to recovery after disruption. Using survey data on 224 Italian formal business networks (“contratti di rete”) and fuzzy-set Qualitative Comparative Analysis (fsQCA), we identify configurations associated with both resilience and non-resilience. The findings show that resilience consistently depends on the joint presence of resource complementarity and relational coordination, while the role of formal coordination variesacross network configurations. More specifically, we develop a scale-contingent view of interorganizational resilience: in small, vertically organized networks, resource complementarity and relational coordination can sustain fast recovery, whereas in large, horizontally organized networks, fast recovery requires formal coordination alongside relational practices. Overall, this study advances a configurational understanding of network resilience by showing that fast recovery depends on distinct combinations of network structure and coordination mechanisms, rather than on any one-size-fits-all network design.

title: India's Emerging Geoeconomic Architecture and the Pursuit of Strategic Sovereignty
affiliations: Indian Institute of Information Technology Lucknow, Indian Institute of Information Technology Lucknow, Indian Institute of Information Technology Lucknow, Indian Institute of Information Technology Lucknow

detail.title: India's Emerging Geoeconomic Architecture and the Pursuit of Strategic Sovereignty
detail.abstract: This paper explores how India has evolved from a passive participant in global trade to a crucial geoeconomic player that's actively pursuing strategic sovereignty in the face of growing trade fragmentation. By analysing data from the International Monetary Fund (IMF) Article IV consultations and focusing on three key areas-proactive industrial policies through Production Linked Incentive (PLI) schemes, digital public infrastructure (DPI) as a diplomatic asset, and strategic trade diversification-we illustrate how India is capitalizing on its domestic market size to reduce risks associated with weaponized interdependence while still achieving impressive growth. Our analysis shows that India's strategic engagement, rather than retreating into isolation, positions it to sustain a GDP growth rate of 6.6-7.3 percent through 2027, despite anticipated tariff shocks. By March 2025, India's PLI initiatives had drawn in ₹1.76 lakh crore ($21 billion) in investments across 14 sectors, leading to over ₹16.5 lakh crore ($191 billion) in production and the creation of 1.2 million jobs. Additionally, India's Unified Payments Interface (UPI) has emerged as the largest realtime payment system globally, handling over 250 billion transactions annually worth $3.4 trillion, which accounts for 50 percent of the world's digital transaction volume. These insights suggest that India's strategy could serve as a practical model for other emerging economies trying to navigate the complexities of great power competition while keeping their macroeconomic stability intact.

title: Gendered Language in Job Advertisements: A Linguistic Analysis of Bias in Recruitment Discourse

detail.title: Gendered Language in Job Advertisements: A Linguistic Analysis of Bias in Recruitment Discourse
detail.abstract: This article examines whether the language used in job advertisements is gender-neutral and discusses the linguistic mechanisms through which bias is produced in recruitment discourse. The starting point of the study is that job advertisements are not merely texts providing technical information about open positions, but also construct, through language, the type of employee that organizations are looking for, the personality traits they value, and the behavioral patterns they associate with the "suitable candidate." Within this framework, the main objective of the article is to identify masculine and feminine connotations in Turkish job advertisements, to reveal in which sectors and professional roles these expressions are concentrated, and to analyze how the texts construct an "ideal candidate" model. The research is designed based on a qualitative research approach; an interpretive method combining document analysis, qualitative content analysis, and discourse analysis has been adopted. The dataset consists of a total of 80 Turkish job advertisements selected from the fields of finance and banking, information and technology, sales and marketing, and administrative support and customer relations. During the analysis process, job advertisements were evaluated under categories such as recurring phrasing, agentic language, communal language, emphasis on leadership and authority, expectation of emotional labor, appearance and representationfocused discourse, and implicit exclusionary indicators. The findings show that masculine-coded qualities such as competition, resultsorientedness, leadership, initiative, high-paced work, and working under pressure are more prominent, especially in technical and managerial positions. In contrast, more communal and feminine-sounding qualities such as communication skills, adaptability, patience, friendliness, orderliness, representation ability, and appearance are more frequently emphasized in customer relations, front office, assistant, and support roles. Furthermore, the study reveals that in many advertisements that do not explicitly specify gender, an implicit but effective exclusionary mechanism operates through phrases such as "young and dynamic team," "adaptability to a fastpaced environment," "flexible working hours," and "will represent the organization well." In conclusion, this article argues that job advertisements are discursive structures that can reproduce gender norms. The study concluded that language recruitment is not merely a matter of corporate style; it is a crucial issue of equality that can impact candidates' sense of belonging, their desire to apply, and their access to the position. Therefore, a more inclusive and thoughtful job advertisement should be considered a factor that can strengthen not only the quality of communication but also fairness and diversity in recruitment processes.

title: The Citizens Standard: Empirical Validation of the Transactional Aggregate — Identifying M^T Independently of the Price-Stability Locus, and Testing Whether It Carries Goods-Inflation Information Beyond Simple-Sum M2
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: The Citizens Standard: Empirical Validation of the Transactional Aggregate — Identifying M^T Independently of the Price-Stability Locus, and Testing Whether It Carries Goods-Inflation Information Beyond Simple-Sum M2
detail.abstract: The Citizens Standard (CS) prices the price level off a transactional aggregate M^T — the transaction-active share of broad money — rather than off simple-sum M2. The framework's own exposition names this decomposition its largest single vulnerability: if M^T cannot be measured independently of the price-stability locus it is used to derive, the construction risks circularity, and if it carries no information beyond M2 it adds nothing. This paper turns that vulnerability into a testable empirical program. It does three things. First, it shows analytically that the decomposition is an accounting identity, not a theory: writing broad money as a transaction-active part plus an idle part, the quantity relation P·Y = M^T·V^T holds exactly, and the familiar instability of simple-sum velocity is, in part, the idle-share composition margin masquerading as velocity. Second, it locates CS in the documented death-and-revival of the monetary aggregates: the money–inflation link weakened in the late 1980s and was abandoned, then reappeared in 2020–2022, when a roughly 41% M2 expansion preceded a 9.1% CPI peak and money growth predicted the inflation that consensus models missed — with the honest caveat, now formalized as the two-regime view, that the link is strong only in high-inflation regimes. Third, it specifies an identification strategy: three independent constructions of M^T (composition-based, payment-flow-based, user-cost / Divisia-weighted), none of which is back-solved from the locus, evaluated out-of-sample against simple-sum M2, a Divisia benchmark, and an expectations baseline, with a pre-registered falsification condition. The claim is deliberately bounded: not that money forecasts inflation better than the central bank, but that an independently-weighted transaction aggregate carries more goods-inflation information than simple-sum M2, and that under CS full reserve the composition margin vanishes identically (M = M^T = M^0), so the incumbent-economy test is a conservative lower bound on the decomposition's validity. Price-level determinacy continues to be carried by the determinacy result (Neo-Solon 2026e, Proposition 7), not by aggregate forecasting. On a first execution of the registered protocol, the transaction-active aggregate carries four to five times the goods-inflation information of simple-sum M2 in high-money-growth regimes and statistically displaces it in a joint regression, while neither aggregate out-forecasts a naive inflation-persistence baseline — precisely the bounded result the design anticipates, leaving the falsification condition untriggered.

title: The Hidden Costs of Flexibility: Just-in-Time Scheduling and Turnover in a U.S. Restaurant Chain
affiliations: McDonough School of Business, Georgetown University  and University of Washington

detail.title: The Hidden Costs of Flexibility: Just-in-Time Scheduling and Turnover in a U.S. Restaurant Chain
detail.abstract: Just-in-time (JIT) scheduling, increasingly augmented by algorithmic tools, allows service firms to match labor supply with demand in real time. While effective in reducing labor costs, such systems often generate precarious schedules-particularly in retail and service sectors-raising concerns about employee well-being and long-run firm performance. Using granular shift-level data covering over 2.3 million hours worked by 2,400+ frontline employees across three years at a national casual dining chain, we examine how scheduling quality-along three dimensions: predictability (advance notice), consistency (temporal stability), and sufficiency (adequacy of hours)-affects worker turnover. Leveraging a Cox proportional hazards model with an instrumental-variables approach, we find that (1) a 10 percentage-point increase in the share of real-time (same-day) additions raises turnover risk by 7.5%, whereas short-notice additions made typically two days in advance have no detectable effect; (2) a 10 percentage-point increase in the volatility of shift timing raises turnover risk by 3.7%, whereas variation in weekly hours has no effect; and (3) each additional weekly hour worked lowers turnover risk by 2.1%. These effects are even stronger among low-hour workers and weekend shifts, where work-life conflict may be most acute. A calibrated economic-impact analysis shows the implied retention costs are financially material for the firm. Our findings reveal the hidden costs of flexibility-first scheduling, distinguish which forms of flexibility are most damaging, and offer evidence for ongoing debates over fair-workweek policy.

title: The Legal Regime of Public Private Partnership in Bangladesh: An Overview and Analysis

detail.title: The Legal Regime of Public Private Partnership in Bangladesh: An Overview and Analysis

publicationDetails.detailsText: BiLD Law Journal, Volume 1, No.1. Pp. 47-60,

detail.abstract: Infrastructure is the backbone of economic growth of a country. Export, import, supply of goods and energy depends on infrastructure. A country with a strong infrastructure attracts investment as the risk factors regarding business seems deductible. Infrastructural development itself requires investment. The Government of a country basically initiates the projects relating to the development. Mega scale projects require a huge amount of monetary investment as maximum of these projects generates income for a long period. The prospect of mega infrastructural development attracts entrepreneurs. Moreover, the huge monetary investment required for long term projects needs private investors as the Government may not always be able to bear the responsibility of the sole contributor. The concept of Private Public Partnership (PPP) originated to facilitate the infrastructural development of a country. This concept allows both the Public sector and the Private sector to work side by side as investors and contributors. Bangladesh has set up a goal to become a member of the second world country by 2021. The Government prepared its vision 2021 as a strategic paper and development of infrastructure through PPP is one of the top priorities. As a result, Bangladesh got its first PPP related legislation in 2015. This paper concentrates on the history, development and features of current PPP related laws and papers of Bangladesh.

title: Tax-Induced Emigration: Who Flees High Taxes? Evidence from the Netherlands
affiliations: Maastricht University, Erasmus University Rotterdam (EUR) - Erasmus School of Economics (ESE), Maastricht University and Maastricht University

detail.title: Tax-Induced Emigration: Who Flees High Taxes? Evidence from the Netherlands
detail.abstract: We study a policy change in the Netherlands that unexpectedly reduced the duration of preferential tax treatment for high-skilled migrants from specific countries. Using administrative data, we document substantial out-migration responses driven entirely by the top 1% of earners, with no detectable response below the 95th percentile. Among the 95-99th percentile, previously internationally mobile workers also leave sooner, particularly to countries offering tax breaks, consistent with tax shopping behavior and pointing to distortionary effects of international tax competition. Increased tax intake from remaining workers offsets revenue lost from departing high earners, making the policy fiscally cost-neutral.

title: The Indian Philosophical Discourses and Intangible Socio-Economic-Cultural Heritage: A Study of Eight Manufacturing Clusters of West Bengal, India
affiliations: , Rajatpur I. N. Vidyapith and

declarations.ethicsApproval: We have sincerely followed all the research ethics

detail.abstract:
The Indian Knowledge System (henceforth, IKS) refers to a vast and multifaceted corpus of intellectual traditions that evolved in the subcontinent over several millennia. Rooted in profound philosophical inquiry, it established the epistemological and ontological foundations for subsequent developments in scientific reasoning, artistic and cultural expressions, principles of governance, and broader socio-economic-political organisational forms. This eclectic intellectual heritage was transmitted across generations through tangible economic and cultural artefacts and intangible socio-economic-cultural traditions/institutions (heritage), thereby ensuring continuity within the civilisational transformations.

In this study, we identify Mahatma Gandhi and Gurudev Rabindranath Tagore as two of the most significant modern bearers of this great philosophical tradition and seek to enlighten our research with their intellectual legacies. We try to uncover the relevance of these great thinkers to the contemporary problem of inclusive and sustainable development in the Global South; we try to understand whether their ideas could offer an alternative to the present hegemonic bandwagon, in the context of the fundamental problem called development. Both Gandhi and Tagore positioned themselves in sharp contrast to the principles of neo-classical and neo-liberal thought. Their emphasis lay on village-centred development and small-scale production systems grounded in cooperation, reciprocity, and sharing of knowledge and a variety of resources across and over the generations.

However, under the neo-classical and neo-liberal regimes, policymakers in the developing nations of the Global South, including India, largely emulated the trajectories of their industrialised counterparts. This has resulted in exclusionary patterns of growth, generating vast pools of unemployed labourers who are absorbed into the unorganised/informal sectors, primarily comprising non-farm micro-small-medium enterprises. The majority of this sector remains excluded from the benefits of accumulation-driven growth, and consequently suffers from persistent economic and social vulnerabilities. In this context, the formulation of inclusive strategies aimed at strengthening micro-enterprises emerges as a crucial pathway toward sustainable and equitable development. And in this very context, we invoke Gandhi and Tagore as two great visionaries from the East.

As a long-term inclusive and sustainable development strategy for the non-farm sectors in developing countries, cluster-focused policies have been advocated, as clusters generate scale, synergies, collective efficiency, and competitive advantage, even for smaller firms under private ownership. In this regard, we are interested in studying micro, small, and medium enterprise (MSME) clusters, specifically the production organisation of firms, intra-cluster (inter-firm) interactions in the production plane, and the impact of inter-firm collaboration on firm performance.

Through rigorous empirical exercise, we have found that inter-firm collaboration positively impacts firm performance. Collaboration is the natural outcome of social embeddedness, maintained through informal arrangements, shared history, friendships, ethnic and religious identities, long-term relationships, social networks, and mutual trust.

title: Logistics Platforms as the Moderator of Information Sharing and Service Execution in Container Transport
affiliations: Erasmus University Rotterdam, Erasmus University Rotterdam (EUR) - Rotterdam School of Management (RSM) and Erasmus University Rotterdam (EUR) - Rotterdam School of Management (RSM)

detail.title: Logistics Platforms as the Moderator of Information Sharing and Service Execution in Container Transport
detail.abstract: We examine a situation where logistics platforms, through sharing digital information of multiple quality levels, determine the overall service reliability of container transport together with transport operators. By analytically modeling the interplay between information sharing and transport execution, we demonstrate that: (1) improving either information sharing or transport execution service individually could further improve the overall service reliability of the container transport chain, and (2) given a pre-defined requirement on deadline and reliability of the final customer, information service and transport service establish an efficiency frontier. We further show, with our game-theoretic analysis, that possibilities exist for coordination between logistics platforms and transport operators and propose a coordination mechanism such that both parties could maximize their individual profits while offering this combined service. Our results complement the current knowledge on the role of logistics platforms as an information sharing facilitator and shed light on possible competition between digital information sharing entities and physical logistics service providers, who individually maximize their profits given a predefined objective.

title: The Floating Balance Sheet. How Cargo Data Becomes Financial Infrastructure.
affiliations: Jagiellonian University and Atexxa Group AG

detail.title: The Floating Balance Sheet. How Cargo Data Becomes Financial Infrastructure.
detail.abstract:
A cargo event is also a financial event. No platform treats it that way. Visibility vendors track shipments for operations. The bank, the insurer, and the treasury team are left to price risk from slow, document-driven signals.

This white paper argues the gap is structural, not technical. No new feature closes it. The obstacle is who owns the data, and who profits from holding it back. The remedy is structural too: neutral, federated infrastructure. Each party keeps control of its own data. Only the financial consequence moves upward.

That missing layer is the Floating Balance Sheet. It lets cargo in motion be priced, financed, and insured while the goods are still moving. The argument draws on the USD 2.5 trillion trade finance gap and 25 interviews across five stakeholder groups. The window is 2026 to 2028, opened by EU rules forcing cargo-event data into machine-readable form.

title: Using a Two-step Clustering Approach to Examine Judiciary Efficiency in European Countries
affiliations: Faculty of Economics, Matej Bel University in Banska Bystrica, Slovakia and Faculty of Economics, Matej Bel University in Banska Bystrica, Slovakia

detail.title: Using a Two-step Clustering Approach to Examine Judiciary Efficiency in European Countries
detail.abstract: Panel data, also known as longitudinal data, is collected and analysed across various research areas. This type of data consists of statistical objects that are periodically observed over time. In comparison to cross-sectional data, there are significantly fewer clustering techniques available for panel data. Therefore, the main objective of the contribution is to present a two-step clustering approach. In the first step, the panel data are transformed into a static form using a set of proposed characteristics that capture time dynamics. In the second step, the objects are clustered using conventional spatial clustering algorithms, such as K-means clustering or hierarchical partitioning. The clustering performance of this approach is then compared to that of the well-known KML method using real panel data sets. These datasets include indicators that assess the effectiveness of courts at the first instance level. Factors like digitalisation in the public sector are affecting the judiciary's efficiency during this period. The methodology implemented allowed us to categorise European countries based on the efficiency of their courts while capturing the dynamic trends. This approach is generally helpful in assessing and comparing the efficiency of public spending and evaluating the quality of public institutions, including courts.

title: Fifty Years of Knowledge Management Research: A System-Level Analysis of Intellectual, Conceptual and Social Structures
affiliations: Academia Forţelor Terestre „Nicolae Bălcescu”, Academia Forţelor Terestre „Nicolae Bălcescu”, Academia Forţelor Terestre „Nicolae Bălcescu”, Academia Forţelor Terestre „Nicolae Bălcescu” and Lucian Blaga University of Sibiu

detail.title: Fifty Years of Knowledge Management Research: A System-Level Analysis of Intellectual, Conceptual and Social Structures
detail.abstract: Knowledge Management (KM) has evolved over the last five decades as a complex sociotechnical system shaped by interactions between organizational processes, technologies and social actors. This study maps the systemic evolution of KM research between 1975 and 2025 by examining its intellectual, conceptual and social subsystems. Using a largescale bibliometric science-mapping approach that combines performance indicators and network-based techniques, we analyze 33,153 documents indexed in the Web of Science Core Collection. The results reveal a pronounced post-1995 expansion of the field, marked by a consolidated core of specialized journals and influential scholars, alongside an increasingly global research network. The analysis shows that KM research is structured around four interdependent dimensions: organizational processes, strategic orientations, technological infrastructures and socio-cultural factors. More recent developments indicate the emergence of new system trajectories associated with digital transformation, knowledge governance and sustainability. Viewed through a system-level lens, these findings position KM as an evolving research system characterized by adaptive and cross-domain dynamics.

title: Improving Human-Algorithm Interaction with Causal Machine Learning-based Decision Support
affiliations: IESEG School of Management, Catholic University of Lille - IESEG School of Management, Catholic University of Lille - IÉSEG School of Management, Lille Campus, Research Institute of China Unicom (Shanxi) for New Industrialization and Ghent University

detail.title: Improving Human-Algorithm Interaction with Causal Machine Learning-based Decision Support

declarations.funderStatement: Maud Van den Broeke and Marijn Verschelde acknowledge financial support from the French National Research Agency through the project BALANCE (ANR-22-CE10-0006-01).

detail.abstract: This study demonstrates how causal machine learning (CML) can enhance human-algorithm interaction (HAI) in digital operations. In settings where algorithm aversion and algorithm appreciation shape human decision-making behavior, a key managerial challenge is determining when human decision-makers should override algorithmic decisions, and when they should not. Using Infrabel's digitized railway control room as our empirical setting, we examine the heterogeneous effects of controllers' overrides of algorithmic decisions on train punctuality. Specifically, we examine how override effects differ across operational contexts with distinct characteristics and how to design a CML-based decision support system (DSS) to improve HAI. Our empirical results reveal substantial heterogeneity in the override effects across traffic contexts. In particular, we find that zone-hour-specific workload is the primary driver of treatment-effect heterogeneity relative to other operational context characteristics included in the analysis. To translate these insights into managerial practice, we develop a prototype DSS based on an instrumental-variable forest approach that provides real-time, context-specific causal recommendations regarding override decisions under confounding. Counterfactual analysis shows that aligning decisions with DSS recommendations improves punctuality by 6.618 seconds per train section, exceeding the average observed delay change of 4.744 seconds and indicating significant potential for delay reduction. The study contributes to operations research by integrating causal inference and machine learning to support human decision-making in algorithmic operational environments.

title: A Review of Payments Clearing Systems for Operations Researchers
affiliations: , University of Toronto - Rotman School of Management, Payments Canada, University of Toronto - Rotman School of Management and Hefei University of Technology - School of Management

detail.title: A Review of Payments Clearing Systems for Operations Researchers
detail.abstract: Payment clearing systems process trillions of dollars in transactions daily across interconnected banking networks, serving as the foundational infrastructure underpinning nearly all financial and commercial activity in modern economies. Despite their enormous scale and systemic significance, payment systems remain comparatively underexplored within the operations research and management science literature. This paper reviews the design and operations of such systems through an operations management perspective, centering on the fundamental trade-off between settlement risk and liquidity sourcing costs. Our core contribution lies in developing a unified analytical framework that decomposes payment systems into three interconnected components: (i) payments and liquidity input that capture stochastic payment flows and liquidity policy instruments; (ii) the clearing process characterizing clearing architectures and algorithms; and (iii) the performance objective that assesses system outcomes via a social cost function encompassing strategic policy costs and daily operational costs. Building on this framework, we structure the existing literature around two central design problems: liquidity policy design covering both strategic and operational choices that shape banks' liquidity endowment; and payment submission behavior and the clearing architecture design encompassing clearing timing, netting density and clearing algorithms. We demonstrate that these design dimensions jointly determine systemic stability and efficiency. We further synthesize extant studies highlighting how network interconnectedness and strategic delay incentives give rise to systemic vulnerability and payment gridlock. Finally, we identify prominent research gaps spanning dynamic optimization of clearing operations, endogenous payment network formation, and the joint calibration of complementary policy tools. We conclude that future advances in this domain call for dynamic, state dependent models that unify system design, participant incentives, and real-time operational dynamics, with the ultimate goal of enhancing both the efficiency and resilience of payments clearing systems.

detail.abstract: Despite from growing democracy trends that has improved over the past few years, ongoing conflicts in Southeast Asia, particularly in Thailand and Myanmar, have undermined democracy, leading to a resurgence of conflict. This paper compares between the role of civil society and the military between these disputed countries, showing how their struggles challenge civilian governments and often engage in political violence. Using a qualitative comparative approach, this study focuses on how the matters that related to historical, institutional, and normative implications of the current literature on civil-military relations in Southeast Asia. The findings suggest that both militaries justified coups by defending democratic and cultural authority, such as the monarchy in Thailand and the concept of "consensus democracy" in Myanmar. Furthermore, weak civilian governance, elite polarization, and the strategic use of military-drafted constitutions to shape the division of power enable their continued political dominance. The study concludes that meaningful democratic civilian rule requires the dismantling of both formal constitutional privileges and informal elite networks that allow the military to repeatedly veto democratic processes.
