detail.abstract: Since the mid-twentieth century, international commercial arbitration has been widely recognized as one of the most important and appropriate mechanisms for resolving international commercial disputes. In this regard, many national legal systems have been updated in accordance with international conventions governing arbitration and the enforcement of arbitral awards. Nevertheless, due to the issuance of inconsistent arbitral decisions in certain cases, the confidence of both petroleum-producing states and international oil companies has occasionally been affected. In particular, some oil-exporting countries perceive the submission of disputes with foreign legal entities to international arbitration as potentially inconsistent with, or even weakening, their national sovereignty. In order to address such concerns and to reduce the possibility of biased or unfair decisions, the use of alternative dispute resolution (ADR) mechanisms has increasingly been recommended. This article seeks to examine in detail the various methods for resolving disputes arising from international upstream oil and gas contracts, with particular attention to ADR mechanisms.

title: A Multi-Dimensional Economic Stress Monitoring System: Identifying Economic Stress From 38 Macroeconomic Indicators
affiliations: Lexington High School

detail.title: A Multi-Dimensional Economic Stress Monitoring System: Identifying Economic Stress From 38 Macroeconomic Indicators
detail.abstract: This paper presents a continuous economic health monitoring system built on 38 macroeconomic indicators pulled from the FRED database. This system, unlike many other binary models, provides a continuous reading on the country's economic health. The system draws these 38 macroeconomic indicators from various different sectors with the attempt to cover most if not all economic conditions. These sectors include: labor markets, inflationary measures, financial conditions, trade and commodities. This system achieves its continuous economic health monitoring through the use of percentile-based analysis across multiple rolling lookback periods. Moreover, testing against all available US recessions since 1990 (2001, 2008-09, 2020) shows that the model correctly identified all 3 periods as recessionary events, with stress levels peaking at 84% to 88% across all recessions. Furthermore, sample testing was conducted on each crisis using information only available up to that recession. The tests were conducted and showed that the model identified 2 out of the 3 recessions correctly, with the near miss reaching a peak level of 66.9%, just below the 70% threshold. One of the biggest findings was the pre-recession acceleration analysis, which shows a stress acceleration averaging 10.9% quarter after quarter versus a change of-0.5% stress acceleration for non-recessionary quarters (Cohen's d = 1.04; p = 0.045; n = 3). Furthermore, the model was benchmarked against similar models and showed to lead the Sahm Rule by 4 quarters. As of Q1 2026, the system reads 32.1% at the 45th historical percentile, showing that the economy is near its long-run median without any elevated stress levels.

title: Contagious Polarization: How Divisive Shocks Reshape Legislative Behavior Across Policy Domains

detail.title: Contagious Polarization: How Divisive Shocks Reshape Legislative Behavior Across Policy Domains
detail.abstract: This paper examines how exogenous divisive shocks contribute to political polarization among U.S. legislators and influence legislative outcomes. Using roll-call vote data from the U.S. House of Representatives between 2005 and 2015, I study the effects of mass shooting events (MSEs)—salient but quasi-random shocks—on legislators’ behavior. Leveraging a difference-in differences design, I find that Representatives from affected districts significantly increase party discipline and reduce bipartisan cooperation. These effects extend across a wide range of cultural policy areas while leaving economic policy largely unchanged, revealing the contagious nature of polarization: a shock on one divisive cultural issue triggers partisan realignment across broader domains. To unpack these dynamics, I analyze congressional speeches and legislators’ ideological responses. Representatives from affected districts display stronger rhetorical polarization. I further show that this polarization arises from identity-based voter realignment rather than from changes in electoral incentives.

title: Board-Approved, Perfectly Legal: The NBFC Loophole Behind India's Predatory Lending Apps - From the Andhra Pradesh Microfinance Crisis to App-Based Digital Lending: A Regulatory History and Policy Analysis

detail.title: Board-Approved, Perfectly Legal: The NBFC Loophole Behind India's Predatory Lending Apps - From the Andhra Pradesh Microfinance Crisis to App-Based Digital Lending: A Regulatory History and Policy Analysis
detail.abstract: In October 2010, after roughly two hundred borrowers in Andhra Pradesh had reportedly died by suicide amid coercive collection by microfinance agents, the state government shut the industry down almost overnight and the Reserve Bank of India convened a committee under Y. H. Malegam to work out what had gone wrong. The committee's answer was, in effect, that price and conduct both needed hard limits: it recommended a 24% ceiling on the annualised rate an NBFC-MFI could charge and a 10 to 12 percent margin cap on top of the cost of funds. Those limits held, more or less, for a decade. Then, beginning with a June 2021 consultative paper and finalised in the 2022 microfinance framework, the RBI removed both caps and replaced them with a requirement that each lender's own board approve its pricing policy. This paper argues that the removal of the Malegam-era caps, layered on top of a licensing regime in which acquiring a dormant NBFC is markedly easier than registering a new one, has recreated-in app-based form-much of the price and collection dynamic that produced the 2010 crisis in the first place. Using RBI circulars, court judgments, NCRB and MeitY enforcement data, and documented harassment and suicide cases from 2022 through 2024, the paper traces how a small operator can lawfully acquire a licensed but inactive Base-Layer NBFC, launch a consumer lending app under that licence, disclose a rate that technically satisfies the Key Fact Statement requirement, and still extract an effective annualised cost running into the hundreds of percent once processing-fee deductions are accounted for. A comparative section examines how the United Kingdom (the FCA's 2015 price cap of 0.8% per day with a 100% total-cost ceiling) and Kenya (the Central Bank of Kenya's 2021 licensing power, which lets the regulator set pricing parameters directly rather than leave them to lender boards) addressed structurally similar problems. The paper closes with a set of specific, sequenced recommendations, the central one being a statutory all-in cost cap for small-ticket unsecured digital credit, restoring in substance what the Malegam Committee had recommended in 2011 and what the sector operated under until 2022. A July 2026 investigation by the business publication The Ken, drawing on Ministry of Corporate Affairs filings and lenders' own board-approved interest rate policy documents, independently corroborates this mechanism, naming specific NBFCs whose revenue grew by several hundred to several thousand times in a single year after acquisition.

title: The Impact of Microfinance and Financial Inclusion Tools on Household and Microenterprise Outcomes”
affiliations: , , ,  and

detail.title: The Impact of Microfinance and Financial Inclusion Tools on Household and Microenterprise Outcomes”
detail.abstract:
Financial inclusion is now a central policy mechanism in the promotion of household welfare, financial resilience, and microenterprise growth in the developing economies. The growth of microcredit, micro-savings and commitment savings products, digital payments, mobile money, digital credit, and micro-insurance over the last few years has changed the financial decision-making of low-income households. But the literature currently analyzes these tools to a great extent separately, which provides minimal information on how various financial tools collectively affect the outcomes of households and microenterprises.

The present research fills this gap by taking a composite framework to look at the relative impacts of key financial inclusion instruments on the household welfare, business performance and financial attitude. The research is based on a systematic literature review on both the experimental and quasi-experimental studies and on primary survey findings of 116 low-income households and on the owners of microenterprises. Likert-scale variables were used to capture the financial outcomes, business performance indicators, and attitudinal measures.

 The reliability analysis proves the high internal consistency of the measurement tool (Cronbach a = 0.850). With the non-normality of the variables, parametric statistical methods were used (robust and non-parametric) and that is one-way ANOVA with Welch corrections and chi-square tests of independence. The results show that the effects of financial inclusion instruments are very heterogeneous. Insurance cover comes with increased financial security, higher savings discipline, increased corporate stability and reduced loan-related stress.

The mechanisms of commitment savings seem to be better at encouraging financial discipline than credit based interventions, whereas digital payments seem to make transactions more convenient and responsive to shocks without necessarily improving long run welfare. The occupational factor turns out to be a major predictor of financial performance, and gender and age do not have a significant explanatory value.

In general, the findings demonstrate that the outcomes of financial inclusion are related to the design of tools, the characteristics of their users, and the underlying behavioral processes. The paper highlights the importance of concerted, well-planned financial inclusion policies and not single product-centered strategies.

title: What Is Freedom? New Liberal Economics

detail.title: What Is Freedom? New Liberal Economics
detail.abstract:
Man is born free, and everywhere he is in chains.” Since Jean-Jacques Rousseau established the foundational principles of the Social Contract, the historical trajectory of humanity’s pursuit of genuine emancipation has been set. Yet, why do these fetters remain perpetually unbroken? This article conducts an in-depth extension of Hayek’s neoliberal economics, systematically elucidating its theoretical premises, critiquing its limitations, and offering necessary conceptual supplements.

Although this endeavor inherits the true ethos of Hayek’s thought, it operates much like a physician prescribing a targeted remedy to cure a disease: while therapeutically necessary, the medicine is seldom palatable to the patient. Therefore, this work should ultimately be understood as a therapeutic inheritance—an inheritance driven by the intent to cure, rather than by mere reverence.

title: LRISK: Systemic Liquidity Risk in Mutual Funds
affiliations: Banque de France, Banque de France and CREST-ENSAE

detail.title: LRISK: Systemic Liquidity Risk in Mutual Funds
detail.abstract: This paper introduces LRISK, a forward-looking measure of systemic liquidity risk in mutual funds that quantifies the aggregate price pressure on financial markets conditional on a systemic redemption shock. The model captures the mechanics of fire sale spillovers by integrating three amplification channels: flow commonality, portfolio similarity, and endogenous declines in asset liquidity. Tracing the evolution of systemic liquidity risk from 2011 to 2024, we validate the predictive capabilities of LRISK at the asset, fund, and aggregate levels. At the asset level, LRISK-implied price pressure drives the cross-section of corporate bond returns during the COVID-19 crisis. At the fund level, higher LRISK exposure translates into underperformance during redemption shocks and helps explain funds' adoption of redemption in kind. At the aggregate level, LRISK serves as an early warning indicator, forecasting market distress up to two quarters ahead. Finally, a system-wide optimization exercise using the LRISK measure shows that a central planner could substantially reduce the spillovers generated by uncoordinated liquidations, suggesting that macroprudential tools can be designed to mitigate systemic liquidity risk.

title: The Everyday Cost of Paradise: Seasonal Grocery Inflation as a Tourism-led Externality
affiliations: University of Split, University of Zagreb - Faculty of Economics & Business and

detail.title: The Everyday Cost of Paradise: Seasonal Grocery Inflation as a Tourism-led Externality

declarations.funderStatement: This paper/research was funded by the European Union (NextGenerationEU) under the Croatian Recovery and Resilience Plan 2021–2026 (NRRP), through the University of Split institutional project “Tourism of Tomorrow: Resilience, Sustainability and Digital Transformation (TURBO; IP-UNIST-04)”, approved by the Ministry of Science, Education and Youth of the Republic of Croatia. Views and opinions expressed are however those of the author(s) only and do not necessarily reflect those of the European Union or the European Commission. Neither the European Union nor European Commission can be held responsible for them.

detail.abstract: This study conceptualizes tourism-led grocery inflation as a cost-of-living externality affecting everyday goods. Using retailer-published price microdata for Croatia, it aggregates 1.3 billion daily observations into monthly datasets covering May-October 2025. Prices are already higher in tourism-intensive coastal municipalities in May and then show additional coastal price growth over the summer, tracing an inverted U-shaped pattern that peaks in July-August and moderates by October. The pattern persists for essential goods and identical barcode-matched products. Retailer responses are heterogeneous: some chains show stronger coastal price increases during the peak season, while others show little or no coastal-inland differential. The findings identify a resident-facing tourism externality and support local cost-of-living monitoring to inform place-sensitive policy.

title: Storing Power or Projecting Influence? The Political Economy of Energy Storage Choice in Central Asia: Pumped Hydro versus Batteries through the Lens of Infrastructure Projection of Geopolitics
affiliations: and Kyrgyz State Technical University

detail.title: Storing Power or Projecting Influence? The Political Economy of Energy Storage Choice in Central Asia: Pumped Hydro versus Batteries through the Lens of Infrastructure Projection of Geopolitics
detail.abstract: The choice between pumped hydro energy storage (PHES) and battery energy storage systems (BESS) in Central Asia is conventionally framed as an engineering and cost-optimisation problem. This paper argues that it is, in fact, a geopolitical decision. Applying the author's framework of the Infrastructure Projection of Geopolitics (IPG) and its dysfunctional extension, Infrapopulism, we develop a three-axis analytical grid-projection, dependency, and narrative-to-reality gap-and apply it to the two dominant storage technologies. We show that BESS predominantly projects an external (largely Chinese) geopolitics and generates a novel, cyclical form of infranomic dependency, yet disciplines delivery and is therefore structurally resistant to infrapopulism; PHES can serve as an instrument of a small state's own infrastructural projection and secures infranomic sovereignty in operation, but is acutely vulnerable in financing and is the principal generator of infrapopulism in the region's energy sector. Engineering calculations of Kyrgyzstan's storage potential show that the Toktogul reservoir alone holds a seasonal storage potential of roughly 5,840 GWh, and a 60-year life-cycle comparison finds BESS roughly twice as costly as PHES for an equivalent duty owing to replacement cycles. No single technology dominates across all three axes. The optimum is a portfolio whose regulatory architecture neutralises the specific weakness of each technology, anchored in the common electricity market of the Eurasian Economic Union (Art. 79) and in tariff reform. The empirical anchor is the April 2026 final investment decision on the Mirny wind-plus-BESS project in Kazakhstan, read against the decades-long declaratory history of the Kambarata cascade in Kyrgyzstan.

title: The Geopolitical Blockchain: Infrastructural Power of Protocols and the Architecture of a Polycentric Order

detail.title: The Geopolitical Blockchain: Infrastructural Power of Protocols and the Architecture of a Polycentric Order
detail.abstract: This paper introduces the concept of protocol geoeconomics — an analytical framework in which the infrastructure of digital governance is treated as an autonomous instrument for the distribution of power amid the systemic crisis of the multilateral order. The central argument holds that as the traditional mechanisms of global governance lose their function as neutral arbiters, control over the rules of verification, enforcement, and sanctioning of international commitments becomes a key resource of geopolitical agency. Distributed Ledger Technology (DLT) in this perspective is not a replacement for diplomatic institutions but the next logical form of infrastructural power — the appropriation of political influence through the ownership of coordination protocols. The paper introduces two operational categories: the sovereign node (a national point of participation in a distributed ledger that cannot be unilaterally disconnected) and protocol Westphalianism (a digital-age analogue of the Westphalian system in which a state's sovereignty is defined by its capacity to maintain a verifying node in critical international coordination systems). A formal model of algorithmic stability is developed through a slashing function and quadratic weighting of influence, providing structural protection against unipolar capture of the system. The dynamic National Influence Index (NI) operationalises representation as a function of verifiable contribution rather than historical privilege. Three contributions emerge. First, infrastructural power is established as a self-standing analytical category describing power exercised through rules of computation rather than through resources or territory. Second, the sovereign node operationalises the concept of digital sovereignty, hitherto largely declarative in the literature. Third, protocol Westphalianism provides a structural exit from the false dichotomy between national sovereignty and global governance. The framework is positioned as the digital extension of Infrastructure Projection of Geopolitics (IPG, WP-IPG-2026-01), with strategic implications for Russia, BRICS+, and the Global South in the construction of Multipolar World Order 2.0.

title: The Algorithmic Screening Exam: EMTALA’s Blind Spot for AI Triage

detail.title: The Algorithmic Screening Exam: EMTALA’s Blind Spot for AI Triage
detail.abstract: Emergency departments across the country are deploying artificial intelligence triage systems that functionally shape, and in some cases substitute for, the medical screening examination that the Emergency Medical Treatment and Labor Act (EMTALA) requires. 1 The statute was written to prevent "patient dumping" by ensuring every person who presents to an emergency department receives a screening by qualified medical personnel. It never contemplated an algorithm performing that function. This Essay argues that AI triage systems create three unresolved EMTALA problems: (1) whether an algorithmically influenced screening satisfies the statutory requirement; (2) whether an AI system that diverts patients away from the emergency department triggers EMTALA's stabilization obligation; and (3) who bears liability (the hospital, the vendor, or both) when an AI triage failure results in an EMTALA violation. Current guidance from the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services is silent on all three questions, and the window for regulatory clarity is closing as adoption accelerates.

title: Infranomics: The Foundational Economic Stratum — A Canonical Definition with Operational Index

detail.title: Infranomics: The Foundational Economic Stratum — A Canonical Definition with Operational Index
detail.abstract: This paper presents the canonical definition of Infranomics — the foundational economic stratum that constitutes the lower level of the three-tier stratification (Infranomics → Classical Economy → Ultranomics) on which the author's research programme is built. The concept has been repeatedly deployed in prior work, but has not until now received a separate canonical formalization. The paper closes this methodological gap and simultaneously demarcates the political-economic concept developed here from the prior systems-engineering concept of the same name introduced by Gheorghe and Masera (2010, 2014). Infranomics in the political-economic sense is defined as the economic stratum in which physical and physical-adjacent infrastructure — energy networks, transportation systems, water systems, telecommunications, datacenters as physical objects — operates as the material foundation of all subsequent economic activity, and whose objects possess a structural power not reducible to their market value. Infranomics is not an industry or a sector; it is the lower economic level upon which the classical economy stands, and through it the ultranomic apex. The stratum is constituted by four features: (1) physical-territorial anchoring; (2) structural power not reducible to market value; (3) coercion of dependency; (4) sub-economic financing as constitutive. Together these features differentiate Infranomics from the classical economic stratum and justify it as a distinct theoretical category. The paper also introduces an operational instrument — the Infranomic Sovereignty Index (ISI) — a four-axis system for assessing the degree of infranomic sovereignty held by a state across its critical infrastructure sectors. The ISI evaluates four dimensions per sector: decision control, local financing share, technical standard origin, and political transferability. The instrument is applicable without specialized training and produces profiles comparable across countries and across sectors. The paper differentiates Infranomics from five adjacent concepts: from infrastructure economics as a mainstream subfield (sectoral, not structural); from systems-engineering Infranomics in the Gheorghe-Masera sense (decision-methodology, not stratum); from Infrastructure Political Geography (IPG) as an applied analytical framework operating on the infranomic stratum; from geo-economics as a foreign-policy concept; and from infrastructure studies in critical theory traditions (Easterling, Larkin, Mitchell, Khalili) which capture important dimensions but do not develop infranomics as a structural-economic stratum. Five anticipated objections are addressed within the text. The concluding section discusses three macro-consequences: the redefinition of sovereignty as infranomic control; infrapopulism as the predictable political pathology of infranomic dependency; and the hierarchy of structural conditioning under which the classical economy and ultranomics both depend on infranomic prerequisites.

title: From Wages to Watts: Energy as the Measure of Synthetic Labor in Two Emerging Economic Architectures

detail.title: From Wages to Watts: Energy as the Measure of Synthetic Labor in Two Emerging Economic Architectures

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The Citizen 5.0 framework discussed here is developed in full in the author’s forthcoming book, Citizen 5.0: A New Social Contract for Artificial Intelligence (CRC Press, an imprint of Taylor & Francis Group), and in companion papers (Galipeau, 2026a, 2026b, 2026c). This article draws on and refers to that work as a scholarly article, recasting its argument in new prose, quoting only brief attributed passages, and pointing readers to the book rather than reproducing it, and it gives credit to the Publisher and the Work accordingly. It is intended to complement, not to substitute for or compete with, the book.
declarations.ethicsApproval: Data availability. This is a conceptual paper and generated no datasets. All primary materials are the cited published works.
declarations.funderStatement: None. The author developed the Citizen 5.0 framework that is one of the two objects of comparison and has a clear interest in its reception. The paper attempts to mitigate this by applying symmetric scrutiny and by declining to rank the frameworks. Readers should nonetheless weight the self-comparison with this conflict in view. The author has no financial relationship with Roemmele or Read Multiplex.

detail.abstract: Two independent proposals now argue that the unit in which economic value is measured is shifting from the wage to the watt. Brian Roemmele's JouleWork prices the output of autonomous AI agents in an energy-denominated wage unit and runs it, in a live "Zero-Human Company," as a continuous thermodynamic payroll. The framework presented in Citizen 5.0: A New Social Contract for Artificial Intelligence (Galipeau, 2027; hereafter Citizen 5.0) makes the joule a unit of public account and an ecological budget, taxes the surplus that synthetic labor captures when it displaces human work through a Synthetic Labor Tax, and governs compute through a Joule Standard and a Metabolic Ledger. This paper compares the two on four dimensions held separate from any value judgment: their mathematical formulations, their methodological approach, their results to date, and their prospects for realization. The comparison finds that the frameworks measure different objects, an agent's energy-weighted output as against a firm's displacement surplus; that they operate at different layers, a firminternal wage as against a societal account; and that they rest on opposite governance logics, bottom-up market selection as against top-down fiscal deliberation, while converging on a shared thermodynamic premise and a shared token mechanism. Neither is implemented at scale, both are explicitly illustrative, and each supplies what the other lacks. Beyond the comparison, the paper offers one constructive result, stated formally as a falsifiable proposition: a firm running JouleWork-style accounting makes the Citizen 5.0 tax base directly observable, reducing its central measurement problem from three unknowns per task to one, and so positioning JouleWork as a candidate micro-foundation for the Citizen 5.0 architecture rather than a rival to it. The independent convergence of a builder and an institutionalist on energy-denominated value is read here not as a settled result but as a signal that the field is at its beginning. The paper closes with a research agenda.

title: Cognitive Dissonance at Scale: How Named-Individual Accountability Breaks Institutional Rationalisation

detail.title: Cognitive Dissonance at Scale: How Named-Individual Accountability Breaks Institutional Rationalisation
detail.abstract: This paper applies Festinger's (1957) theory of cognitive dissonance to institutional accountability at scale. The diagnosis it begins from-that responsibility dissolves when distributed across anonymous collective processes-is well established in political theory and organisational ethics, and the paper claims no originality for it. Its contribution is an instrument that acts on that condition: the Burgess Principle binary test, which asks whether a named human being applied their individual mind to the specific facts of a specific case before a significant decision issued, and which converts a diffuse structural problem into an attributable, citable, answerable record on demand. Drawing on a documented dataset of 80 interactions across 15 named institutions, the paper shows the test relocating accountability from the institution to an identified role-holder, who must evidence individual consideration (SOVEREIGN) or leave its absence on the record (NULL). Because the dataset is a single-author convenience sample, the paper treats it as a set of existence proofs rather than a population estimate, separates every classification from any contested legal allegation, and validates the rubric against two matters of public record-the Australian Robodebt scheme and the Post Office Horizon prosecutions-in which the author had no involvement. The paper also connects NULL to its cognitive microfoundations, drawing on Shaw and Nave's (2026) account of 'cognitive surrender' to artificial (System 3) outputs, and reads the binary test as a real-world device for reactivating the deliberative scrutiny that surrender displaces. A dedicated section sets out, and operationalises, the ethical limits the framework imposes on itself, including a correction and right-of-reply protocol, on the principle that a standard demanding attributable accountability must be answerable on the same terms. Individuals are identified by role, not name.

title: A Healthcare Analytic Framework for Lung Allocation Process Modeling Using Path Analysis
affiliations: Yarmouk University, affiliation not provided to SSRN and affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: A Healthcare Analytic Framework for Lung Allocation Process Modeling Using Path Analysis
detail.abstract: Lung allocation includes complex associations among clinical, immunological, and procedural factors, many of which reveal nonlinearity with post-transplant outcomes. Current studies often rely on linear or predictive approaches; these approaches either lack interpretability or fail to capture nonlinear relationships. In this study, we introduce an integrated path-analytic framework combining Structural Equation Modeling (SEM) with Bayesian neural network-based Universal Structural Modeling (USM) to analyze lung transplant outcomes using United Network for Organ Sharing (UNOS) data.  SEM is first used to construct clinically interpretable unobserved (or latent) representations of lung allocation factors. These unobserved constructs are then integrated into USM to discover nonlinear and interaction effects. Model performance is evaluated using censoring-aware survival metrics (Concordance index (C-index), area under the curve (AUC), and Integrated Brier Score (IBS)) and classification metrics for functional outcomes. Using 5-fold cross validation, the proposed framework shows improved discrimination and calibration compared with linear, non-linear, clinical-only, and Lung Allocation Score (LAS) baselines, while preserving structural interpretability. This work donates a validated integration of unobserved -variable modeling and nonlinear learning for associational analysis of lung allocation process.

title: Which livelihood capital matters most? Prioritizing drought resilience drivers for rural food security using the sustainable livelihood framework Authorship Statement
affiliations: Razi University and Razi University

detail.title: Which livelihood capital matters most? Prioritizing drought resilience drivers for rural food security using the sustainable livelihood framework Authorship Statement
detail.abstract: Droughts have severely affected rural livelihoods in Iran and endangered food security. Kermanshah Province, despite high agricultural potential, faces alarming food insecurity levels. This study prioritized livelihood capitals human, social, natural, physical, and financial in food resilience under drought using the sustainable livelihood framework. A survey of 384 rural household heads in Kermanshah was analyzed using PLS-SEM. Results showed that 65.8% of households were food insecure, more than double the national average. Livelihood capitals, except human capital, were critically low. Financial capital had the greatest impact on food resilience (β = 0.345), followed by social (β = 0.234), human (β = 0.162), natural (β = 0.145), and physical capital (β = 0.123). The five capitals explained 63.9% of the variance in food resilience. Rather than conventional education-extension approaches, policies should prioritize financial empowerment through local markets, eliminating intermediaries, and direct producer-consumer connections. Local cooperative networks for sharing drought adaptation experiences and replacing traditional crops with low-water-demand alternatives are recommended. The prioritization pattern depends on ecological conditions and drought severity, so a single model cannot be generalized to all regions. This research contributes to sustainable livelihood knowledge and offers practical solutions for drought adaptation.

title: When AI Agents Pay: The Viability Bound
affiliations: Erasmus University Rotterdam (EUR), Rotterdam School of Management (RSM)

detail.title: When AI Agents Pay: The Viability Bound

declarations.declarationOfInterest: No conflicts
declarations.ethicsApproval: N/A
declarations.funderStatement: This research is self-funded

detail.abstract: When should a task that includes payments be handed to an autonomous AI agent, and when should a human still own and execute it? This paper decomposes the cost of an autonomous agentic AI task into three parts: inference, verification, and settlement. The binding cost is verification, and it rises steeply with complexity, because a trustless auditor cannot re-run the task on chosen inputs and can reliably check only a bounded number of actions at once. A more capable verifier agent lowers this cost only modestly; only simplifying the task's interaction structure changes how fast it grows. The result is a bounded "Goldilocks zone'': agents beat humans only up to a threshold complexity, and humans should retain the most complex tasks.

title: Elevating Brands Through Intellectual Capital: Legal and Economic Synergies
affiliations: , University of Silesia in Katowice - Poland Faculty of Law and Administration and Mackenzie Presbyterian University

detail.title: Elevating Brands Through Intellectual Capital: Legal and Economic Synergies

declarations.funderStatement: This research was funded in whole by the National Science Centre in Poland, grant “Brand Abuse: Brand as a New Personal Interest under the Polish Civil Code against an EU and US Backdrop”, grant holder: Marlena Maria Jankowska-Augustyn, number: 2021/43/B/HS5/01156. For the purpose of Open Access, the author has applied a CC-BY public copyright licence to any Author Accepted Manuscript (AAM) version arising from this submission.

detail.abstract: The research explores how brands contribute to economic growth by fostering consumer loyalty, enabling premium pricing, and facilitating market differentiation. Additionally, the paper delves into the interplay between IP protection and brand management, emphasizing the necessity of robust legal frameworks to safeguard brand integrity and prevent abuse. Through a comparative analysis of different regulatory environments, the study identifies best practices in brand protection and leverages interdisciplinary insights from law, economics, and management. The intellectual capital approach broadens the understanding of brands, recognizing their role in enhancing intangible assets such as human capital, relational capital, and structural capital. This comprehensive perspective underscores the importance of strategic brand management in leveraging intellectual capital for sustained economic success. By integrating theoretical and empirical evidence, the study offers a holistic view of brands as dynamic entities that embody both legal protections and economic potentials. As a concrete illustration of these concepts, the paper will subsequently examine the M&M's brand to demonstrate how a well-managed brand leverages both IP frameworks and intellectual capital. The findings contribute to the ongoing discourse on the strategic importance of brands, providing valuable implications for policymakers, business leaders, and academics. Ultimately, this research advocates for a synergistic approach that aligns IP strategies with intellectual capital management to maximize the legal, economic, and organizational benefits of strong, well-managed brands.

title: The Impact of the Gaza War on Crime Rates in Muslim-Israeli Settlements
affiliations: Charles University in Prague - Faculty of Law

detail.title: The Impact of the Gaza War on Crime Rates in Muslim-Israeli Settlements
detail.abstract: This paper tests for differential crime rates between predominantly Muslim and non-Muslim Israeli settlements relative to the timing of the Gaza War using a difference-in-differences specification. I find that Muslim settlements experienced an additional 34.40 crime incidents per 100k residents in the average post-war quarter. The baseline effect is driven by security, public order, and against property offenses. The rise in public order offenses depends on localized social unrest (i.e., protest and riot events), whereas the effect on security offenses is suggestive of broader wartime enforcement. The increase in against property offenses is explained neither by localized social unrest nor socioeconomic status.

title: What is in a Bottle? Thirty Design Strategies for Luxurious Packaging, Transcending Intellectual Property to Embrace Intellectual Capital
affiliations: and University of Silesia in Katowice - Poland Faculty of Law and Administration

detail.title: What is in a Bottle? Thirty Design Strategies for Luxurious Packaging, Transcending Intellectual Property to Embrace Intellectual Capital
detail.abstract: This study explores the nuanced role of intellectual property (IP) and intellectual capital (IC) in the premium beverage industry, focusing on bottle design as a strategic asset. By analyzing the ways brands like Maker's Mark, Veuve Clicquot, and Glenfiddich differentiate themselves through unique bottle features, our study highlights how companies are building brand identity and consumer loyalty outside conventional IP protections. This approach emphasizes the importance of design strategy in the beverage industry and reflects broader trends in leveraging IC to create a competitive advantage. This study examines the strategic role of bottle design within premium and luxury beverage brands, aiming to uncover how companies use IC-such as design, brand equity, and consumer perception-to create value in areas not covered in traditional IP rights. The study examines how design elements shape consumer expectations and enhance brand prestige, illuminating the intersection of IP and brand identity. The study provides a novel perspective on the role of design strategy in the premium beverage industry, contributing to both academic and practical discourse on how brands build value outside traditional IP frameworks. It highlights how bottle design serves as an IC, shaping brand identity and consumer loyalty in ways that redefine value creation in competitive markets.

title: The Role of Digitalization in Early Internationalization Research: A Systematic Literature Review and Future Research Directions
affiliations: , University of Vaasa and Autonomous University of Barcelona

detail.title: The Role of Digitalization in Early Internationalization Research: A Systematic Literature Review and Future Research Directions
detail.abstract: The purpose of this research is to systematically collate and synthesize the literature on how digitalizationrelated antecedents influence the processes and outcomes of early internationalizing firms. To do so, the present study systematically reviews a total of 120 related articles published in a broad range of academic journals from 1994 to 2024. The review enables us to outline the development of major research areas in terms of themes, theoretical approaches, and methodological issues at the intersection of the early internationalization and digitalization research. We contribute by offering a model that delineates a more subsumed, multilevel explanation of the interface of early internationalization and digitalization. Further, we propose a number of future research directions based on the integration of the reviewed articles and inputs purposefully collected from surveyed scholars in the field.

title: Decarbonizing Long-haul Heavy-duty Electric Trucks with Co-optimized Corridor Charging Hubs
affiliations: Shanghai University of Electric Power, Shanghai University of Electric Power, East China Branch of State Grid Corporation of China, Shanghai University of Electric Power, University of Exeter, Durham University, Shanghai Normal University and Shanghai University of Electric Power

detail.title: Decarbonizing Long-haul Heavy-duty Electric Trucks with Co-optimized Corridor Charging Hubs
detail.abstract: The decarbonization of long-haul road freight is a major challenge because high-power charging, grid constraints and corridor-level heterogeneity jointly shape the cost and feasibility of heavy battery electric truck operations. Highway charging hubs can function as en-route charging stops that segment long trunk expressways into feasible charging corridors, but deciding where to build hubs and how large to build them remains difficult when land premiums, grid interconnection costs and time-of-use electricity tariffs vary sharply across space. Here we develop a corridor optimization framework that jointly plans charging-hub location and capacity, grid interconnection, and charging operations. Across 35 selected national trunk expressway freight corridors with one-way distances of 773-4,081 km, we find that optimized corridor planning brings operating costs close to diesel benchmarks, with a mean unit energy cost of about 2.62 CNY km^{-1}, and increases the share of economically competitive corridors from about 17% to 60%, corresponding to 6 to 21 routes. Environmental performance depends strongly on regional grid carbon intensity. Under baseline operations, only 15 of 35 corridors achieve net emissions benefits relative to diesel, whereas optimized planning reduces route-level emissions by about 0.3-50.4% relative to unoptimized HBET operations across all 35 corridors and expands the set of environmentally competitive routes from 15 to 32. Optimized planning also mitigates the payload penalty by reducing required onboard energy storage, with a 60-70% reduction on an ultra-long-haul corridor relative to unoptimized baselines.

title: A Hybrid Prior–Performance Monte Carlo Model for Forecasting FIFA World Cup Knockout Outcomes: Methodology and Retrospective Validation 1986–2026

detail.title: A Hybrid Prior–Performance Monte Carlo Model for Forecasting FIFA World Cup Knockout Outcomes: Methodology and Retrospective Validation 1986–2026

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no competing financial or personal interests.
declarations.ethicsApproval: Not applicable. This study used only publicly available aggregate sports statistics and did not involve human participants, animals, or personal data.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no specific grant from any funding agency in the public, commercial, or not-for-profit sectors.

detail.abstract: We present a Monte Carlo simulation framework for forecasting the champion of the FIFA World Cup from the first knockout round onward. Each surviving team is assigned a scalar strength rating that linearly combines season-long priors (FIFA ranking and aggregate squad market value), in-tournament group-stage performance (expected goals created and conceded, goals, and individual "star" production), and a pre-tournament goalkeeper/defensive-pedigree term. Strength differences drive a Poisson goal-scoring engine with extra-time and penalty-shootout resolution, and the fixed knockout bracket is simulated approximately 300,000 times to estimate each team's championship probability. The weight configuration was selected against six tournaments (2002-2022) under a relaxed objective requiring the eventual champion to rank among the model's most-probable title-winners. A key methodological finding is that adding an explicit goalkeeper/defensive-pedigree feature was necessary to capture defensively-anchored champions (notably Italy 2006 and Spain 2010) that goal-based signals systematically underrate. The final model ranks the eventual champion among its two most-probable title-winners in all ten tournaments examined (1986-2022) — a statement about which two teams are likeliest to win the trophy, not a prediction of first and second place — including a strict out-of-sample test on four pre-tuning tournaments (1986-1998) in which the champion was among the top two every time. Leave-one-tournament-out cross-validation on the modern set places the champion among the top two in five of six held-out folds. Applied prospectively to the in-progress 2026 World Cup from the Round of 32, the model identifies Argentina (28.0%) and Spain (21.1%) as the leading championship candidates. We discuss limitations, principally the small number of tournaments available for validation and the risk of in-sample weight selection.

title: Stablecoins under Stress in a National Economy: Transaction-Level Evidence from Austrian Crypto-Asset Service Providers
affiliations: IMT School for Advanced Studies Lucca, Oesterreichische Nationalbank (OeNB), , Oesterreichische Nationalbank (OeNB),  and

detail.title: Stablecoins under Stress in a National Economy: Transaction-Level Evidence from Austrian Crypto-Asset Service Providers
detail.abstract: Cryptoassets are increasingly entangled with the traditional financial system, and how this activity integrates into national economies and behaves under stress bears on financial stability and the design of public digital money. However, blockchain pseudonymity and the lack of geographic identifiers force existing work to rely on indirect proxies to infer and locate market participants. Here we use a regulatory registry that directly identifies the on-chain addresses of all crypto-asset service providers (CASPs) registered in Austria, reconstructing their on-chain transaction activity across Bitcoin, Ether, USDC, and USDT through May 2025, and separating retail-like from institutionally mediated flows. We find that Austrian CASPs intermediate roughly $30 billion with external counterparties and are integrated globally rather than domestically. In value, this activity is dominated by a few institutional counterparties; in number, by retail-like ones. Around three major shocks, the Terra-Luna collapse, the FTX bankruptcy, and the Silicon Valley Bank failure, the two groups respond through different mechanisms, and stablecoins do not act as a uniform safe haven. The clearest case is SVB, where retail-like deposits and institutional withdrawals are consistent with USDC's two-tiered redemption mechanism. These patterns are invisible in aggregate data. Registry-based, transaction-level measurement thus offers a reproducible, cross-jurisdictional basis for monitoring how cryptoasset markets transmit risk.

title: SNAP Purchasing Power and Household Time Allocation
affiliations: American University

detail.title: SNAP Purchasing Power and Household Time Allocation
detail.abstract: SNAP benefits are set uniformly across the contiguous United States, but geographic variation in food prices creates substantial disparities in the program's real purchasing power. This paper exploits this variation using a triple-difference strategy that compares SNAP-eligible to near-eligible households across 35 local markets. A 10-percent increase in SNAP purchasing power was associated with a 7-percent reduction in daily purchasing time and a 4-percent increase in leisure time, with no meaningful results on market work, home production, childcare, or sleep. Heterogeneity analysis reveals that these associations differ by gender and parental status. These findings suggest that geographic disparities in benefit adequacy affect not only what households can purchase but how they allocate their time.

title: Life After Divorce: Effects of Joint Custody on Parents and Children
affiliations: , , , Yale University, Stockholm University, Stockholm University, Ifo Institute,  and

detail.title: Life After Divorce: Effects of Joint Custody on Parents and Children
detail.abstract: Divorce reshapes family life, yet little is known about one of its most consequential features: the allocation of child custody. We study the impact of joint versus sole custody on both parents and children using rich administrative data from Sweden linked to over 25 years of newly-collected court custody rulings. To address selection concerns, we exploit random assignment of custody disputes to judges who differ sharply in their propensity to grant joint custody. For fathers, joint custody substantially raises earnings and improves mental health, consistent with sustained paternal involvement enhancing labor market attachment and psychological well-being. In contrast, there are no measurable labor market or mental health effects for mothers. Turning to children, joint custody increases standardized test scores and school quality without affecting mental health outcomes. Joint custody increases fathers' chances of remarriage, keeps separated parents in closer geographic proximity, and has no effect on intimate partner violence allegations against either partner. These findings inform longstanding debates over the role of child custody in shaping post-divorce family life.

title: COVID-19 Pandemic and Prosociality: An Experiment with Healthcare Professionals
affiliations: London School of Economics, Catholic University of the Sacred Heart of Milan, Catholic University of the Sacred Heart, Rome and University of Cologne

detail.title: COVID-19 Pandemic and Prosociality: An Experiment with Healthcare Professionals
detail.abstract: We study the extent to which exposure to COVID-19 relates to healthcare professionals' prosociality. Drawing on empirical evidence from an incentivized experiment and a companion survey of healthcare professionals (HCPs) at a large Italian hospital (N = 194), we find that different forms of exposure to COVID-19 predict their altruistic motivation in heterogeneous ways. HCPs who worked in COVID-19 wards or had a close relative or friend severely affected by the virus are more than 5 percentage points more likely to prioritize patient welfare over personal gain, with the association for professional exposure being mostly driven by female HCPs, especially nurses. Conversely, personally contracting COVID-19 is associated with a 6 percentage point decline in prosociality. Our results highlight that different experiences of need shape prosocial behavior in hospital settings

title: Freedom of Contract and Sustainability Considerations in the European Financial Sector
affiliations: Radboud University Nijmegen - Institute for Financial Law (IFR)

detail.title: Freedom of Contract and Sustainability Considerations in the European Financial Sector

keywords: Termination and suspension of the contract

publicationDetails.detailsText: European Banking Institute Working Paper Series No. 211
publicationDetails.journalName: European Banking Institute (EBI) Research Paper Series

detail.abstract: In the European financial sector, sustainability considerations increasingly restrict the contractual freedom of banks and other financial institutions. Using Dutch law as a case study for the impact of EU law on national contract law, this chapter examines these restrictions across three stages—the pre-contractual stage, the content of contracts, and termination or suspension of the contract—and assesses them against three criteria: legitimacy, proportionality, and consistency. It analyses statutory duties under the CSDDD alongside civil-law duties of care, arguing that duties of refusal towards upstream business partners can be regarded as proportionate, whereas a general downstream duty of refusal risks being disproportionate absent global acceptance. The chapter shows that EU sustainability regulation is being transformed: the second von der Leyen Commission's simplification agenda and the CSDDD2 amendments—notably abolishing the duty to terminate business relationships—signal a shift away from ever-stricter constraints towards reconciling sustainability objectives with European competitiveness.

title: Auditing in Crisis: Can External Auditing Capture Organisational Resilience or Does It Entrench Compliance-Driven Vulnerability?
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Auditing in Crisis: Can External Auditing Capture Organisational Resilience or Does It Entrench Compliance-Driven Vulnerability?
detail.abstract: This paper examines whether external audit practice can evaluate and foster organisational resilience. It argues that the compliance orientation, backward-looking temporal focus, and epistemological foundations of the prevailing paradigm create significant tensions with resilience as a dynamic, forward-looking, and transformative capacity. The study combines interpretive documentary analysis of International Standards on Auditing, INTOSAI auditing standards, and audit case evidence from COVID-19-era organisational collapses, the Ghanaian banking clean-up, and climate-related audit deficiencies, with thirty-six semi-structured interviews with senior audit partners, public sector auditors, audit committee chairs, and academic specialists in Ghana and South Africa. Three dimensions of audit-resilience tension are identified. Temporal tension describes how backward-looking financial statement verification appears insufficient for capturing prospective resilience dimensions. Epistemological tension describes how the commitment to verifiable quantifiable evidence appears to exclude relational, adaptive, and cultural resilience dimensions. Political tension describes how bilateral principal-agent accountability appears misaligned with the networked, multi-stakeholder accountability architectures that resilient systems require. Competing perspectives are presented and evaluated. The paper is primarily theoretical and interpretive, grounded in two African jurisdictions. The paper contributes a three-dimensional framework for understanding tensions between conventional audit epistemology and resilience, and proposes a resilience-oriented audit model with specific procedures, reporting implications, and assurance approaches.

title: Canada's Productivity Paradox and Minority Foreign Ownership: Boardroom Reconfiguration and the Branch Plant Transformation -Evidence from Keel Infrastructure

detail.title: Canada's Productivity Paradox and Minority Foreign Ownership: Boardroom Reconfiguration and the Branch Plant Transformation -Evidence from Keel Infrastructure

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares that there are no known competing financial or personal relationships that could have appeared to influence the work reported in this paper.
declarations.ethicsApproval: The research utilizes publicly available data sources and does not involve human participants or identifiable personal data. As such, formal ethics approval was not required.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding.

detail.abstract:
Canada’s digital economy faces a persistent structural tension: while strategic foreign investment can accelerate firm-level commercial scaling, it may also induce governance reconfigurations that weaken domestic innovation capacity. This study examines the micro-foundations of this “productivity paradox” through the 2024–2026 boardroom transition of Toronto-headquartered Bitfarms Ltd., initiated by U.S.-based competitor Riot Platforms, culminating in the firm’s redomiciliation to the United States as Keel Infrastructure Corp.

Adopting an abductive qualitative design grounded in the Gioia methodology, the study traces how foreign strategic investors can leverage sub-threshold equity accumulation to gain effective influence without triggering formal review under the Investment Canada Act. Anchored in New Internalization Theory, and drawing on Transaction Cost Economics and the Knowledge-Based View, the analysis shows that full acquisition is not always necessary to internalize a firm’s strategic assets. Instead, minority ownership positions can enable governance shifts that simultaneously support commercial expansion, such as the development of a 2.2 gigawatt high-performance computing pipeline, while contributing to what this study conceptualizes as a “branch plant transformation.”

The findings suggest that such transformations involve the reallocation of strategic decision-making and innovation capacity beyond domestic boundaries, with implications for long-term productivity and policy design. The study concludes by outlining potential avenues for incorporating behavioral and governance-based triggers into foreign investment review frameworks.

title: Adverse Social Behaviour at Work and Mental Health in the European Health and Care Workforce: Elevated Exposure Without Differential Vulnerability. A Cross-Sectional Study of 35 Countries in the European Working Conditions Survey 2024
affiliations: , , European University of Tirana and University of Shkodra "Luigj Gurakuqi"

detail.title: Adverse Social Behaviour at Work and Mental Health in the European Health and Care Workforce: Elevated Exposure Without Differential Vulnerability. A Cross-Sectional Study of 35 Countries in the European Working Conditions Survey 2024
detail.abstract:
Purpose. Health and care workers are disproportionately exposed to violence and harassment at work. It remains unclear whether they experience greater mental-health consequences from adverse social behaviour (ASB) than other workers. We examined whether the association between ASB and mental health differs between health and care workers and the rest of the European workforce.

Methods. Cross-sectional analysis of the European Working Conditions Survey 2024 (35 countries; n = 36,644). Health and care workers (n = 2,172) were identified from ISCO-08 major groups 22 and 32, and personal care workers (group 53) in human-health or residential-care industries. Exposure was eight forms of ASB (composite, count, and individual forms). Outcomes were WHO-5 wellbeing, emotional exhaustion, sleeping difficulties and anxiety. Weighted regression with country fixed effects estimated exposure-by-sector interactions; a severe-exhaustion threshold model tested for scale artefacts.

Results. ASB was more common among health and care workers than other workers (26.0% vs 17.0%). ASB was strongly associated with poorer mental health on every outcome (WHO-5: −10.85 points, 95% CI −11.53 to −10.16). The sector-by-exposure interaction was null for wellbeing, sleeping difficulties and anxiety; a nominally significant interaction for emotional exhaustion did not replicate on a severe-threshold specification (p = 0.15), indicating scale compression. Within the sector the wellbeing penalty was carried by psychological forms—bullying, humiliation and verbal abuse.

Conclusion. The elevated mental-health burden of the European health and care workforce reflects greater exposure to adverse social behaviour, not greater vulnerability to it. Prevention should prioritise reducing exposure rather than building individual resilience.

title: A Mid-Range Theory of Relational Distance and Curvilinear Value Realization in Organizational Combinations

detail.title: A Mid-Range Theory of Relational Distance and Curvilinear Value Realization in Organizational Combinations

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares that there are no known competing financial interests or personal relationships that could have appeared to influence the work reported in this paper.
declarations.ethicsApproval: Not applicable. This study is a purely theoretical and conceptual manuscript that does not involve any human participants, patients, or experimental animal subjects.
declarations.funderStatement: The author received no financial support for the research, authorship, or publication of this article

detail.abstract: This paper introduces a mid-range theory of relational distance to model the curvilinear path of value realization in organizational combinations. Aligning with the principles of engaged scholarship, this framework translates a critical real-world problem setting (the notoriously high failure rate of corporate combinations) into a rigorously defined theoretical area of concern. It proposes that combinations routinely fail because both extreme similarity and extreme difference tend to destroy value: similarity creates capability redundancy and cognitive lock-in, while extreme difference exhausts a firm's absorptive capacity, creating severe operational and cultural friction. Consequently, value is maximized at an optimal threshold (the "Zone of Optimal Tension" or "Goldilocks Zone") where resource novelty is fully leveraged before communication fatigue and integration friction trigger an exponential decline. Because managers often cannot eliminate this distance, they must match their chosen corporate vehicle (e.g., mergers and acquisitions, joint ventures, strategic alliances, etc.) to the existing relational distance, using the governance structure as an elastic filter to absorb friction. By bridging macroeconomic corporate strategy with the micro-foundations of organizational design, this paper explicitly delineates the constructs (What), their relationships (How), and the underlying psychological and economic mechanisms (Why), establishing a robust, value-added theoretical contribution.

title: What Keynes Would Say About Pakistan's IMF Programme

detail.title: What Keynes Would Say About Pakistan's IMF Programme
detail.abstract: John Maynard Keynes remains, nearly ninety years after the publication of The General Theory of Employment, Interest and Money (1936), the most consequential economist of the modern era-the architect of macroeconomics, the intellectual force behind the Bretton Woods institutions, and the theorist whose central insight, that aggregate demand rather than supply determines the level of output and employment, was rediscovered by policymakers worldwide during the 2008 financial crisis and again during the COVID-19 pandemic. I revisit here Keynes' intellectual legacy-his rejection of Say's Law, his theory of effective demand, his advocacy of counter-cyclical fiscal policy, and his role in designing the postwar international financial architecture-and apply it directly to a live policy debate: Pakistan's fiscal trajectory across its FY2025-26 and FY2026-27 federal budgets under the 2024 IMF Extended Fund Facility. Pakistan's Public Sector Development Programme was cut by PKR 173 billion in FY2025-26 and then held flat in nominal terms in FY2026-27 even as tax revenue targets rose 18 percent-while debt servicing fell by roughly PKR 383 billion, freeing fiscal space that was substantially redirected toward an 18 percent increase in defence spending rather than development. I argue that Pakistan's predicament has evolved from a simple austerity story into a more precise Keynesian expenditure-composition problem: newly available fiscal space is being allocated in ways whose long-run productivity consequences differ sharply, and that choice deserves more explicit scrutiny than Pakistan's domestic fiscal debate currently gives it. I am not arguing that Keynes offers Pakistan an easy alternative-external financing constraints and genuine security imperatives are real and cannot be wished away by domestic policy choice alonebut I do think the Keynesian question of how public expenditure composition affects long-run productive capacity is being asked too rarely in Pakistan's current fiscal debate, and deserves more serious attention than it currently receives.

title: One Law at Every Scale: A Scale-Invariant Theory of Institutional Stability

detail.title: One Law at Every Scale: A Scale-Invariant Theory of Institutional Stability
detail.abstract: This paper states the single dynamical object behind a four-part programme on institutional stability and shows that the firm-scale theory, its macroeconomic extension, the accompanying essays, the company, and the proposed legislation are not four themes that rhyme but one object observed at four magnifications. The object is a boundary-equilibrium bifurcation in an inclusion gain: a system tracks its own true state only while the people who hold that truth are inside the loop with power to correct it, and above a critical gain beta* it sits in a truthful basin while below it a self-reinforcing corrupted basin captures it. The paper sets out the substrate-free equations, instantiates them at the scales of a mind, a community, a firm, and an economy, and renders an honest renormalization verdict. The firm and the economy are the strongest rung, though not a Wilsonian renormalization: the macro selection threshold sigma_X* = mu_C - b_1 is the same boundary-equilibrium type one scale up, an inclusion gain crossing unity against a loss rate, and the macro order parameter is literally composed of firm-scale outcomes, conditional on capital-gated autocatalytic formation (b_1 > 0). The mind and the community are partial, near-genuine: the firm equations transfer under a substrate-faithful variable swap, and the boundary-equilibrium corner is derived at both, from a robust generative likelihood (in cognition, outlier-robust perception; in the public, identity-protective reasoning, which is the same bounded-influence updating). The numerical checks against the firm's own fixed points are a transcription guard; the upgrade past mere resemblance rests on that corner derivation, which could have failed. The propagation operator that spreads the cure across a population is the same percolation threshold pqsz > 1 at every scale, and its link-attack piece is literally the same object at the community scale, where engineered distrust is bond dilution. The result is stated as a theorem with five named footnotes, so that "theorem" is exact and not triumphal: the critical gain is not the bare number one but a balance condition, the inclusion gain crossing the corruption channel's marginal gain, normalized to one at the firm and substrate-dependent elsewhere, and case-measured rather than calibrated; the corner at mind and community is derived conditional on a robust likelihood; minor analytic leftovers remain; and the macro bifurcation's existence is itself conditional on b_1 > 0. The unifying claim is that the rigid mind is the atom of the corruption channel, so the math, the essays, the company, and the legislation are one object; the keeper is that inclusion is the condition for reality-tracking stability, not charity, while coercion can hold the corrupted basin durably but only as a persistent decoupling from the truth; and the one hopeful asymmetry is that the gain is trainable at the mind scale, which makes "do not go numb" the boundary condition of the whole structure. A reader who has met none of the other parts can follow the result from this paper alone; the four parts it synthesizes are cited where each is needed.

title: Is Human Attention Still Necessary? A Synthesis for Navigating the AI-Attention Transition

detail.title: Is Human Attention Still Necessary? A Synthesis for Navigating the AI-Attention Transition
detail.abstract: Artificial intelligence is automating cognitive work fast enough to force a question older economic transitions never had to ask so directly: if machines can replicate human thinking, are people becoming less relevant? This paper synthesizes results from decades of economics and control theory to map that transition. It composes several wellestablished results into a single, navigable account of where human value goes as AI grows abundant, and what institutions must do to keep that value from being lost. We stand on three foundations. From the theory of production (Krusell et al., 2000), AI-augmented capital and skilled human judgment are complements, not substitutes: more of one raises the value of the other. From growth theory (Baumol, 1967; Aghion et al., 2019), an essential input that cannot be automated becomes the bottleneck that governs how much an economy can produce: output is limited by the weakest link, not the strongest. Composing these, we identify that weakest link in the AI era as productive human attention: the judgment, oversight, creativity, care, leadership, and synthesis that remain when routine cognitive work is automated. We keep the claim falsifiable: it holds only if attention and AI-capital are gross complements (an elasticity of substitution below one, σ 2 < 1). Two consequences follow. First, institutions that treat human attention as a free input, the default in conventional corporate governance, are not merely unfair. As optimal-control solutions in the new regime they are provably inadmissible, a one-line contradiction in the planner's costate; and where attention is a depreciable stock, sustained mis-encoding drives output toward zero, asymptotically. Second, who owns AIproductive systems, decided at company formation, not corrected by redistribution afterward, will set which future the economy converges to. We give a governance design (an investor-share cap, contribution-gated equity, and an anti-stagnation rule) built to converge to durable employee co-ownership. Beneath this sits the claim we care about most, and we are precise about its status. We argue that the divide between a society which collapses under mis-encoded governance and one which stays structurally stable is a genuine bifurcation: a threshold across which the whole coupled system of ownership, attention, and production converges to qualitatively different fates. The discrete ownership dynamics already converge to opposite fixed points on either side of a 50%-control line; we locate the bifurcation in the nonlinear coupling of ownership and attention, and commit the companion paper to proving it. This paper establishes the foundation for that work.

title: Environmental Design and Digital Well-being Among Youth: An Interdisciplinary Review Integrating Neuroscience, Environmental Psychology, and Traditional Spatial Practices Author

detail.title: Environmental Design and Digital Well-being Among Youth: An Interdisciplinary Review Integrating Neuroscience, Environmental Psychology, and Traditional Spatial Practices Author
detail.abstract: The rapid expansion of digital technologies has profoundly transformed the educational, social, and psychological experiences of children, adolescents, and young adults. While digital devices provide unprecedented opportunities for learning, communication, creativity, and global connectivity, excessive and poorly regulated digital engagement has emerged as an important public health concern. Research increasingly associates problematic digital technology use with impairments in attention, executive functioning, emotional regulation, sleep quality, academic performance, and psychological well-being. At the same time, growing evidence from neuroscience, environmental psychology, and building science suggests that the physical characteristics of learning and living environments-including natural lighting, indoor air quality, thermal comfort, acoustics, exposure to nature, and spatial organisation-may influence cognitive performance, emotional resilience, and technology-use behaviours. This interdisciplinary review synthesises current evidence regarding the relationships among environmental design, brain function, cognitive performance, and digital well-being in young people. Drawing upon findings from neuroscience, environmental psychology, education, architecture, public health, and behavioural science, the review examines how environmental conditions may support healthier patterns of technology use while enhancing learning, attention, emotional regulation, and overall well-being. The review also discusses traditional spatial practices, including Vastu Shastra, from cultural and architectural perspectives, highlighting areas where empirical evidence is limited and further scientific investigation is warranted. Based on the available evidence, the paper proposes the Environmental Digital Well-being Model (EDWM), an integrative conceptual framework describing potential pathways linking built environments, brain function, digital behaviour, and health outcomes. The review concludes with evidence-informed recommendations for educational institutions, architects, policymakers, healthcare professionals, families, and researchers aimed at creating environments that promote healthier digital habits and improved cognitive and psychological well-being among youth.

title: The Enforcement Gap: Why Africa's AI Regulations Need Runtime Enforcement

detail.title: The Enforcement Gap: Why Africa's AI Regulations Need Runtime Enforcement

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author is the founder and maintainer of Comply54, an open-source AI governance framework discussed in this paper. The views expressed are the author's own, and no commercial entity influenced the research or its conclusions.
declarations.ethicsApproval: This work is a technical and conceptual study based on publicly available laws, regulations, technical documentation, and software implementations. It did not involve human participants or require institutional ethics approval.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding. The work was independently conducted and self-funded by the author.

detail.abstract: Africa is not facing an AI regulation gap; it is facing an AI enforcement gap. Nigeria, Kenya, South Africa, and the African Union have all moved quickly on data protection, financial conduct, and AI-specific rules, with real enforcement to back them, including a $220 million penalty against Meta and a ₦766.2 million penalty against MultiChoice Nigeria. At the same time, AI agents are already approving loans, screening transactions, and accessing patient records at production scale, built on frameworks (LangChain, LangGraph, CrewAI, AutoGen) with no built-in awareness of the jurisdiction they operate in. This paper argues that the resulting accountability gap is not a policy problem to be solved with more legislation, but an infrastructure problem, requiring a runtime enforcement layer that evaluates AI agent actions against jurisdiction-specific policy before execution. Drawing on firsthand experience translating Nigerian, Kenyan, and South African regulatory frameworks into machine-checkable policy, including a contribution merged into Microsoft's Agent Governance Toolkit that was outdated by a change in Nigerian law eight days later, the paper documents where legal requirements map cleanly onto code, where they don't, and what an operative runtime enforcement model looks like in practice. It closes with specific recommendations for developers, fintechs, and regulators, including the African Union's Continental AI Strategy Phase 2.

title: Who Shares Data? Bounded Rationality and Strategic Disclosure in Data Markets *
affiliations: and

detail.title: Who Shares Data? Bounded Rationality and Strategic Disclosure in Data Markets *
detail.abstract: Privacy regulation relies on informed consent, delegating consumer protection to consumer choice. But the payoff to sharing depends on how firms use data and on who else shares, so disclosure is a strategic decision, and consumers differ in their ability to reason through it. This paper studies how bounded rationality changes the welfare consequences of transparency-based privacy regulation. We model data disclosure as a simultaneous strategic game in which a consumer’s payoff depends on both firm use of the data and the composition of the pool that agrees to share. We estimate a cognitive-hierarchy model using a data-sharing study fielded through the Dutch LISS panel, in which 3,598 respondents rated their trust in nine organizations and made a real decision whether to share their data with academic researchers. The estimates imply substantial heterogeneity in strategic sophistication: most consumers do not fully internalize the strategic consequences of disclosure, and beliefs about downstream data use differ sharply across organizations. We then evaluate a transparency policy that improves consumers’ understanding of disclosure and shifts the population toward higher cognitive sophistication. The policy generates a direct welfare gain for previously naive consumers by correcting their disclosure mistakes, but it also induces adverse selection in the disclosure pool, lowering realized payoffs through an equilibrium channel. This sorting creates a privacy externality whose extent is bounded by the cognitive distribution. Whether transparency increases average welfare, therefore, depends on the joint distribution of cognitive types and data values in the population.

title: Deep Sequence Architectures in High-Frequency Finance: Benchmarking TimesNet and Classical Machine Learning Across Volatility Regimes
affiliations: Independent Researcher

detail.title: Deep Sequence Architectures in High-Frequency Finance: Benchmarking TimesNet and Classical Machine Learning Across Volatility Regimes

keywords: Independent Quantitative Researcher Financial Time Series

detail.abstract: Forecasting high-frequency intraday financial time series is a notoriously challenging task due to extreme volatility, low signal-to-noise ratios, and persistent regime shifts. Traditional machine learning (ML) models, heavily reliant on manually engineered technical indicators, often treat historical observations as independent and identically distributed (i.i.d.), thereby failing to capture complex, non-linear temporal dependencies. While recurrent neural networks (RNNs) address sequential memory, they frequently struggle with long-range dependencies and multi-scale volatility clustering in financial data. This paper presents a comprehensive empirical evaluation of state-of-the-art deep sequence architectures-specifically TimesNet, PatchTST, and recurrent models (LSTM/GRU)-benchmarked against classical tree-based models (Random Forest, XGBoost). Using twelve years of 5-minute intraday data for the XAUUSD (Gold/USD) market (2013-2025), we evaluate predictive performance through a leakage-free, chronologically split pipeline. Our analysis indicates that reframing 1D financial time series into 2D tensors through multi-periodicity (the TimesNet approach) significantly enhances forecasting reliability. Under a three-class Triple-Barrier labeling scheme, TimesNet attained a predictive accuracy of 78.7%, consistently outperforming classical baselines (~35%). Rather than solely relying on standard classification metrics, we incorporate these forecasts into a risk-adjusted trading simulation. The outcomes illustrate the specific market conditions where deep temporal models thrive, highlighting their adaptability across changing volatility regimes and structural breaks compared to traditional feature-engineered methods.

title: From Excellence to Viability Why Enduring Corporate Success Depends on Systemic Capabilities, Not on Time Horizons

detail.title: From Excellence to Viability Why Enduring Corporate Success Depends on Systemic Capabilities, Not on Time Horizons
