detail.abstract: This paper examines the limits of classical management studies on corporate excellence and enduring performance. It takes as its point of departure Peters and Waterman's In Search of Excellence and Collins and Porras' Built to Last. Peters and Waterman's book is publicly described as being based on a study of forty-three American companies and as presenting eight basic management principles associated with excellence. Collins and Porras' work is described by Stanford Graduate School of Business as drawing on a six-year research project in which eighteen exceptional and long-lasting companies were studied in direct comparison with leading competitors. 12 The central argument of this paper is that neither momentary excellence nor observed longevity is a sufficient proxy for strategic viability. Excellence describes superior performance in a given context. Endurance describes historical persistence over time. Viability, however, describes a firm's systemic capability to regenerate relevance, value creation, governability, and legitimacy when its relevant environment changes. The paper grounds this distinction in Christoph Ph. Schließmann's strategy work, especially "Die neue Dimension strategischen Denkens" and Das Konzept Interdependency: Chancen und Risiken systemischer Komplexität erkennen und steuern. Schließmann's Strategy Cube adds viability in the relevant system to market-based strategy analysis and thereby shifts the diagnostic focus from industry position and performance toward systemic life-capability. 67 Drawing on strategy theory, dynamic capabilities, organizational learning, resilience theory, business model research, and Schließmann's system-oriented approach, the paper develops Corporate Viability as a strategic category. Viability is conceptualized as a dynamic relation between agility, robustness, and complexity, and further specified through capabilities of strategically relevant market sensing, complexity processing, business-model evolution, ambidextrous learning, and strategic reflexivity. The paper's core thesis is that firms are not viable because they have lasted; rather, they last if they repeatedly mobilize viability-relevant capabilities.

title: Internalizing the Public Good Production in Space Industry: An Unexpected Convergence

detail.title: Internalizing the Public Good Production in Space Industry: An Unexpected Convergence
detail.abstract: This working paper presents selected results of research applying the Public Goods Input Chain (PGIC) framework to the historical and crosscountry evolution of space exploration value chains. Two boundaries are considered in the space projects' lifecycle: one between private-goods production and their consequential transformation into perfect or imperfect public goods (PG-boundary), and another separating corporate-controlled and governance-controlled elements within the same value chain (CG-boundary). The crosscountry historical dynamics comparison demonstrates the convergence in PG-CG architectures, underscoring the need to strengthen the public strategic component of the institutional environment. The construction of a non-profit transnational corporation with a public ownership structure is suggested as a development of the elaborated approaches. The Working Paper presents the main directions and components, while in-depth explanations, detailed structural descriptions, and other necessary elements of a research article will be integrated to build a full-fledged research paper.

title: Proximity as a Substitute of Contract Enforcement in Specialized Trade
affiliations: and Tecnológico de Monterrey

detail.title: Proximity as a Substitute of Contract Enforcement in Specialized Trade
detail.abstract: We examine how geographic proximity substitutes for contractenforcement institutions in enabling trade in specialized goods. When products require customization, successful trade depends on either strong contract enforcement or close buyer-seller relationships enabling monitoring and trust. Proximity facilitates such relationships by reducing business travel costs. Our theoretical framework predicts institutional quality primarily affects specialized trade at longer distances, where relationship-building becomes prohibitively expensive. Using bilateral product-specific export data in a gravity model, we find strong empirical support for this prediction. Consistent with our theory, business travel and passenger flights decline more sharply with distance toward destinations with weak contract enforcement institutions.

detail.abstract: Organizations increasingly use AI systems to generate draft outputs that are reviewed by humans before downstream use, particularly in high-stakes settings such as healthcare. As AI systems become more accurate, however, their errors become increasingly rare, making reviewers less vigilant while simultaneously making reviewer performance difficult for organizations to observe. We study whether intentionally inserting realistic errors into selected AI outputs before review, a practice we refer to as controlled error injection, can improve human oversight while creating observable opportunities to measure reviewer performance. We investigate this question through a preregistered, double-blind, 12-week randomized experiment in AI-assisted pharmacovigilance review. Seventeen Doctor of Pharmacy (PharmD) reviewers evaluated AI-generated summaries of adverse event reports under a control condition and three levels of error injection. We find that the effect of controlled error injection is nonmonotone. Relative to the control condition, low-frequency error injection reduced true-error detection by 6 percentage points, whereas high-frequency error injection increased true-error detection by 9 percentage points. False-positive detection did not differ significantly across conditions. Higher levels of error injection also increased review time and reduced trust in the AI system. Finally, reviewers who identified more injected errors were also more likely to identify naturally occurring AI-generated errors. These findings suggest that controlled error injection can improve oversight in AI-assisted workflows while simultaneously providing organizations with a practical signal of reviewer vigilance. At the same time, the effectiveness of the intervention depends critically on the frequency of injected errors. Low levels of error injection reduced true-error detection, whereas higher levels improved it, suggesting that organizations should carefully calibrate the prevalence of injected errors when deploying this intervention.

title: Contract Enforcement and International Trade: A New Look

detail.title: Contract Enforcement and International Trade: A New Look
detail.abstract: This paper reexamines the role of contract-enforcement institutions in international trade. The standard view is that countries with stronger domestic institutions specialize in contract-intensive sectors because weak enforcement discourages relationship-specific investment. I argue that this view is incomplete in an open economy: firms may source specific inputs from abroad, and contracting frictions may depend on the institutions of both the input supplier and the input buyer. I develop a multi-country model in which incomplete contracts generate an industry-specific bilateral cost wedge for relationshipspecific inputs. The model distinguishes two channels. First, contracting frictions raise the effective trade cost of specific inputs. Second, they raise production costs in sectors that rely heavily on those inputs. The model also implies that exporter and importer institutions are substitutes, and that access to foreign suppliers may partly mitigate weak domestic institutions. Using bilateral product-level trade data and measures of rule of law, I find evidence for both cost channels. Trade in specific inputs is increasing in the quality of contract enforcement in both origin and destination countries, and the marginal effect of one country's institutions is weaker when the other country's institutions are stronger. Domestic institutions also matter more in sectors that rely heavily on domestic specific inputs and in industries where know-how transfers are important. However, the direct evidence that access to foreign institutions offsets weak domestic institutions is limited. The results suggest that domestic institutions remain central to comparative advantage, but their effects operate through global input sourcing as well as domestic production.

detail.abstract: Strategic management has traditionally assessed corporate strength through market position, competitive advantage, growth and profitability. These dimensions remain essential, but they are increasingly insufficient in environments shaped by technological acceleration, interdependence, regulatory shifts, platform dynamics, supply-chain fragility and systemic complexity. A firm may hold a strong market position and generate attractive financial performance while simultaneously losing its ability to remain viable in the system in which it actually operates. This conceptual paper develops systemic viability as a third dimension of strategic management. It integrates the Schließmann Strategy Cube and the Schließmann Viability Matrix into a theorybuilding framework for assessing corporate strategy under conditions of complexity. The Strategy Cube extends strategic positioning beyond relative market strength and market performance by adding viability in the relevant system. The Viability Matrix clarifies that complexity is not only a source of risk, but also a source of variety, recombination, innovation and strategic renewal, provided that an organization possesses sufficient agility and robustness to process and use it.

title: The Cost of Continuous-Time Illusions: Empirical Failures of the Avellaneda-Stoikov Model in Hawkes-Driven Limit Order Books
affiliations: Independent Researcher

detail.title: The Cost of Continuous-Time Illusions: Empirical Failures of the Avellaneda-Stoikov Model in Hawkes-Driven Limit Order Books
detail.abstract: The Avellaneda-Stoikov (A-S) framework (2008) remains a foundational pillar for algorithmic market making, providing elegant closed-form solutions for dynamic inventory management under liquidity constraints. However, its core tractability relies on two restrictive assumptions: independent Poisson order arrivals and continuous mid-price standard Brownian motion. This paper utilizes high-precision, live-fire execution data from a custom matching engine to empirically dismantle these assumptions. By applying Maximum Likelihood Estimation (MLE) to tick-level trade logs, we demonstrate that aggressive order flow operates near criticality, characterized by a self-exciting Hawkes process with a branching ratio of α β = 0.9970. We leverage vectorized Maximum Adverse Excursion (MAE) and Maximum Favorable Excursion (MFE) analytics to quantify the exact financial penalty of assuming a memoryless market. Our findings prove that during order-flow clustering, the AS reservation price formula lags physical reality, structurally forcing market makers to quote directly into toxic adverse drift and capture severe tail-risk drawdowns.

title: Price Cuts Without Savings: Moral Hazards in Volume-Based Centralized Procurement
affiliations: , Tongji University, Tongji University - Advanced Institute of Business, Tongji University and Tongji University

detail.title: Price Cuts Without Savings: Moral Hazards in Volume-Based Centralized Procurement
detail.abstract: Centralized procurement is designed to lower input prices by pooling demand across downstream providers. Whether these price reductions translate into lower spending for final users, however, is unclear when procurement covers only one component of a product bundle and does not fully specify the product's post-award quality. In this paper, we study this question in the context of China's National Volume-Based Procurement (NVBP) reform, a national government-run group purchasing program for pharmaceuticals. Using a difference-indifferences design, we analyze a unique patient-visit-level panel of outpatient visits from multiple hospitals in a Chinese province. We find that NVBP reduces patients' spending on the contracted core drugs by 10.1%, yet patients' total medical expenditure does not decline by a statistically or economically meaningful amount. We identify two channels that help explain this limited pass-through. First, providers expand the quantity of non-procured auxiliary prescriptions, consistent with downstream agents shifting toward the margins that remain outside the procurement contract and retain positive markups. Second, patients visit hospitals more frequently and experience more active adjustment of their core-drug regimens, with more core-drug items changed between consecutive visits and more items new to their prescription histories, consistent with an upstream quality response under price-and-volume auctions with limited post-award quality monitoring. We further show that savings concentrate among patients with low historical visit frequency and among those treated in non-tertiary hospitals located in the provincial capital. Taken together, our findings suggest that centralized procurement design should not focus on price reductions alone. When the buyer contracts on only part of a treatment bundle and is not the final user, realized savings depend on both upstream quality incentives and downstream substitution toward non-contracted margins.

detail.abstract: Traditional Revenue Management metrics-RevPAR, GOPPAR and CPOR-describe the financial efficiency of a hospitality property but do not incorporate guest satisfaction as a calculation variable, allowing financially equivalent hotels to follow very different reputational sustainability paths. This paper presents two original metrics developed by the author from continuous consulting practice since 2003: the Satisfaction Coefficient (CS), a composite index that normalizes and weights Net Promoter Score, aggregated public review scores, and guest return rate; and the Hotel Efficiency Index (HEI), which multiplies the GOPPAR-to-CPOR ratio by CS, producing a single measure of operational efficiency adjusted for satisfaction. The paper describes the theoretical foundation of the metrics, their mathematical formulation, sample-validity criteria, and a numerical example applied to two hypothetical hotels with identical RevPAR, demonstrating how HEI reveals real efficiency differences that isolated metrics fail to show.

detail.abstract: The vision of India to become a developed country by 2047, called Viksit Bharat @2047, requires proper strategic planning, effective governance systems, sustainable economic development, and organizational restructuring. The major economic, social, technological, environmental, and administrative challenges that must be addressed by the Government of India for achieving the status of a developed nation are discussed in this paper. Strategic management concepts such as the Strategic Management Process, Boston Consulting Group (BCG) Matrix, and Porter's Five Forces Model are used to analyze India's developmental landscape and identify priority sectors for longterm growth. This study highlights employment generation, infrastructure development, skill enhancement, healthcare accessibility, digital governance, and technological innovation as key drivers for national development. Furthermore, an organizational framework based on decentralized decision-making supported by strong central coordination is proposed to improve governance efficiency and policy implementation. The findings suggest that technology-driven administration, collaborative federalism, organizational reforms, and long-term strategic planning will play a crucial role in transforming India into a globally competitive, inclusive, and sustainable developed nation by the year 2047.

title: A Crisis of Governance, Not Scarcity Diagnosing Libya's Water Sector through the Six Building Blocks of Good Water Governance

detail.title: A Crisis of Governance, Not Scarcity Diagnosing Libya's Water Sector through the Six Building Blocks of Good Water Governance

detail.abstract: Libya is among the most water-stressed countries on earth, with roughly 105 cubic metres of renewable water per capita per year, yet it built the largest fossil-groundwater transfer scheme ever constructed. This paper argues that the country's deepening water insecurity is not, in essence, a problem of physical scarcity but of governance, and that the centralised, extraction-oriented and short-horizon model long applied to oil is being reproduced in water. To move beyond description, the paper applies a recognised diagnostic framework, the six building blocks of good water governance, read alongside the OECD Principles on Water Governance, to the Libyan case. Drawing on authoritative data and recent field research, it maps systematic gaps across the administrative, legal, planning, financing, participation, and cooperation dimensions of the sector. It reads the 2023 Derna dam disaster, which peer-reviewed studies have shown was foreseeable and amplified roughly twentyfold by dam failure, through a disaster-risk-management lens, and it situates water service delivery as a potential peace dividend in a conflict-affected state. The paper closes with a phased, four-pillar reform framework and a three-tier institutional architecture calibrated to what is realistically actionable in the current Libyan context.

title: Dynamic Prediction of Airport Taxiway Hotspots Using Spatio-Temporal Traffic and Kinematic Risk Modeling
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN, affiliation not provided to SSRN, affiliation not provided to SSRN and University of California, Berkeley

detail.title: Dynamic Prediction of Airport Taxiway Hotspots Using Spatio-Temporal Traffic and Kinematic Risk Modeling
detail.abstract: At busy airports, airfield operations are among the most safety-critical phases of flight, during which aircraft maneuver through a complex network of taxiways and runway crossings. Despite investments in ground surveillance technologies, taxiway conflicts remain a safety concern. To address this concern, our study develops a traffic-based method for dynamic taxiway hotspot prediction that identifies conflict-prone locations without needing historical incident and accident records. Unlike current FAA-defined hotspots, which are reactive and static, our method models the airfield infrastructure as a directed graph and identifies critical intersections using agglomerative clustering. Hotspot scores are computed by combining (1) spatial utilization probabilities derived from Runway–Gate routing patterns, (2) temporal conflict likelihoods estimated by kernel density estimation of intersection arrival times, and (3) aircraft kinematic characteristics, including speed and acceleration profiles. Validated with one month of data from Hartsfield–Jackson Atlanta International Airport, the proposed model successfully identifies high-risk intersections that match FAA hotspots and reveals additional conflict-prone locations not captured in official FAA airport diagrams. Separating arrival and departure operations yields distinct hotspot distributions, with arrival risks concentrated at runway exit locations and departure risks at runway entry merge points. The proposed method enables dynamic hotspot prediction by using sliding windows to capture variations in temporal conflicts. Our study bridges offline analyses and real-time conflict alerts by successfully combining a traffic-driven hotspot detection approach, kinematic risk integration, operation-specific hotspot analysis, and a collision risk score to evaluate aircraft taxiway trajectories.

title: Cognitive Asymmetry and Volitional Aphasia: Theory of the New Imperium

detail.title: Cognitive Asymmetry and Volitional Aphasia: Theory of the New Imperium

detail.abstract: Contemporary power exercise has transcended traditional vectors of coercion and ideological persuasion, crystallizing instead into an architecture of structural opacity. This paper investigates the consolidation of "Cognitive Asymmetry" as the foundation of a new political and economic Imperium. Moving beyond the descriptive mapping of epistemocracy, this analysis dissects the actionable mechanisms through which technical, financial, and scientific elites permanently convert informational differentials into unchallenged leverage. Crucially, this work posits that such asymmetry is not a systemic anomaly violently imposed from above, but a rather stable equilibrium actively sustained from the bottom up: confronted with the unsustainable cognitive capital required to navigate algorithmic governance, advanced biotechnology, and hyper-financialization, the general population actively retreats into a state of "Volitional Aphasia." Mirroring the medieval delegation of scriptural interpretation to an exclusive clergy, modern citizens execute a rational choice: surrendering their epistemic agency in exchange for psychological comfort, cognitive relief, and the illusion of risk removal. Consequently, the new Imperium operates without friction or formal tyranny, it is maintained by a tacit transactional pact. By abandoning normative and moralizing critiques in favor of a clinical perspective, this paper provides a structural blueprint of a permanently stratified paradigm. It outlines a society divided between an elite vanguard that actively engineers the variables of reality, and a voluntarily muted substratum that merely consumes its optimized outputs.

detail.abstract: Budziszewski's The Line Through the Heart presents natural law as fact, as theory, and as a sign of contradiction. It is written into creation and into the human person, and fallen reason resists it. This review extends the diagnosis from the soul to the institution. If a person suppresses what he knows, an institution of persons can suppress what it knows as well, spreading responsibility across offices, boards, and procedures until no one has to own the evasion. What conscience is to the soul, mission integrity is to the community. Heritage communities and religious institutions therefore require standing, stewardship, and protection while they are still alive.

title: From Resource Rent to Science Endowment: Institutional Design for Capitalising National Science Systems in Small Resource-dependent Economies

detail.title: From Resource Rent to Science Endowment: Institutional Design for Capitalising National Science Systems in Small Resource-dependent Economies

keywords: national academy of sciences JEL Classification: H54

detail.abstract: This paper develops an institutional-design framework for financing national science systems in small resource-dependent economies through permanent endowments capitalised from extraction rents. The principal contribution is the licensing mechanism: a policy instrument that redirects the pre-existing social obligations of extractive licence holders into named perpetual contributions to a national science endowment. Unlike community development agreements (World Bank 2012), which channel such obligations into local community funds, the licensing mechanism routes them into a national-scale science endowment with donornamed sub-funds, introducing no new fiscal burden. The paper proposes a complementary two-track legal architecture-a pilot fund under existing charitable-organisation law and a dedicated enabling statute modelled on Kazakhstan's Law No. 199-VIII (2025)-and calibrates a three-scenario financial model to the conditions of thin local-currency bond markets. Building on the Hartwick rule (1977), we specify the corpus-sustainability condition for such markets, under which investment income alone cannot preserve real corpus value and continuous rent inflows are therefore structurally required. The framework is situated against the sovereign wealth fund literature, the established resource-financed education permanent funds (Texas, Norway, KAUST), and the post-Soviet endowment statutes of Russia and Kazakhstan. It represents, to our knowledge, the first proposed application of the endowment instrument to a national academy of sciences in the post-Soviet space. Implications for science governance and resource-curse mitigation in Central Asia are discussed.

title: Sequencing and Stacking Policies to Strengthen U.S. Energy Security
affiliations: Georgia Institute of Technology, Georgia Institute of Technology and Georgia Institute of Technology

detail.title: Sequencing and Stacking Policies to Strengthen U.S. Energy Security
detail.abstract: We examine how sequentially stacking seven energy policies, with and without renewable energy subsidies, affects energy security. We evaluate each stack using a multidimensional definition of energy security and the Energy Information Administration's National Energy Modeling System (NEMS). Unlike analyses that evaluate policies individually, we assess the incremental contribution of each policy as it is added to an evolving policy portfolio. Policies promoting domestic oil and gas supplies (HO&GS) deliver numerous benefits: decreasing imports, increasing incomes, reducing energy bills, and expanding the economy, but at the expense of environmental externalities and public health consequences. By stacking HO&GS with renewable energy (RE) subsidies, negative externalities are reduced energy affordability is improved. However, RE subsidies could also crowd out small modular reactors (SMRs), particularly when paired with demand-side management (DSM), reducing energy affordability after 2035. Also, only in the base case without renewables, do SMRs with DSM reduce the concentration of natural gas in the energy mix-boosting energy security. Secondary energy security benefits of EV standards are also revealed: decreased energy imports and increased energy exports, lower energy costs even for households who continue to depend on gasoline, and lower pollution. Results indicate that household energy expenditures and burdens could decline through 2050, with the largest reductions in the Pacific region where electric vehicle (EV) standards were born and in New England where energy expenditures have historically been highest. Overall, the results demonstrate that both the sequencing and composition of energy policies shape long-term energy security outcomes.

title: When GenAI Increases Inequality: Evidence From a University Debating Competition
affiliations: Instituto de Empresa Business School

detail.title: When GenAI Increases Inequality: Evidence From a University Debating Competition
detail.abstract: Research on Generative AI (GenAI) and work reports both productivity-compressing and inequality-expanding effects, leaving open a central question for organizations: who benefits from GenAI, and on which specific tasks. I address this question through a randomized controlled trial in competitive university debating, where participants are randomly assigned access to GenAI. While most previous experimental work examines the impact of GenAI on written activities and across individuals, this setting allows me to study the impact of GenAI on a knowledge-intensive spoken activity and to identify heterogeneous effects across subtasks. I find that GenAI expands performance inequality in this setting. Consistent with recent theories on GenAI and work, results show that high-ability participants experience significantly larger gains from GenAI usage than their lower-ability counterparts in judgment-intensive subtasks, while lower-ability individuals only improve their performance in less expert components of debating, where GenAI can be used as a substitute. If these inequality-expanding effects generalize to similar spoken settings where complex ideas must be internalized and explained, rather than simply written, they would have important implications for understanding the impact of GenAI on work and inequality.

detail.abstract: As AI systems assume greater roles in organizational decision-making, the human structures governing their use have become as consequential as the systems themselves. This paper examines a critical and under-theorized gap in practice: strategic decision-makers and senior individual contributors in AI-enabled organizations lack a consistent, strategy-aligned framework for establishing and maintaining leadership authority and accountability when AI-generated insights influence decisions. Drawing on a grounded theory qualitative approach, this study investigates how leaders construct and enact leadership identity, authority, and accountability within AImediated decision environments. The research addresses dimensions of scalable oversight, human-AI governance, and organizational alignment areas central to Anthropic's mission of building AI systems that are safe, interpretable, and beneficial. Findings are expected to produce a transferable, practice-relevant theoretical framework with direct implications for AI governance, policy development, and the design of human oversight structures in high-stakes organizational contexts.

title: Causal Inference With Endogenous Price Response
affiliations: University of California, Berkeley - Haas School of Business, University of California, Berkeley - Haas School of Business and Imperial College Business School

detail.title: Causal Inference With Endogenous Price Response
detail.abstract: We study the estimation of causal treatment effects on demand when treatment is randomly assigned but prices adjust in response to treatment. We show that regressions of demand on treatment or on treatment and price lead to biased estimates of the direct treatment effect. The bias in both cases depends on the correlation of price with treatment and points in the same direction. In most cases including an endogenous price control reduces bias but does not remove it. We show how to test whether bias from an endogenous price response arises and how to recover an unbiased direct treatment effect using a price instrument. We apply our approach to the estimation of feature advertising effects across several product categories using supermarket scanner data and show that the bias when not instrumenting price can be substantial.

title: Surrogate Subjecthood: Think Tank Networks as Agents of Regional Identity Formation in Central Asia

detail.title: Surrogate Subjecthood: Think Tank Networks as Agents of Regional Identity Formation in Central Asia
detail.abstract: Central Asia's five states — Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, Tajikistan, Turkmenistan, and Uzbekistan — exist as a recognized geographic and geopolitical unit, yet produce no collective voice, no shared analytical framework, and no self-generated regional agenda. This paper argues that C5's lack of subjecthood is not an accidental product of leadership failures or transitional dysfunction, but a structurally reproduced condition sustained by three mutually reinforcing forces: the political economy of rentier states, the infrastructural antagonism inherited from Soviet spatial planning (theorized here through the author's InfrastructurePolitical Geography framework), and the competitive hub logic that makes regional integration structurally costly for every member simultaneously. The paper further introduces the double dispossession thesis: C5 subjecthood is simultaneously eliminated by Washington's bilateralism-in-multilateral-costume and by Moscow's civilizational hierarchy of post-Soviet space — two actors operating through entirely different mechanisms but producing an identical structural outcome. Neither actor conspires against C5 agency; the fragmentation emerges from independent rational strategies that happen to converge. Against this diagnosis, the paper proposes the concept of surrogate subjecthood: the capacity of a distributed think tank network — one anchored institution per country, operating under a shared analytical protocol — to produce regional agency that state mechanisms cannot. Drawing on the author's T-Notation typology of think tank interaction modes, the paper specifies the network architecture, product logic, and activation sequence for a C5 think tank protocol with the Institute for Strategic and Academic Studies (ISAS, Bishkek) as intellectual secretariat. The paper contributes to regional integration theory by extending the structural diagnosis tradition (Krapohl and Vasileva-Dienes, 2020) with an operational instrument, and to think tank studies by formalizing the surrogate subjecthood function as a distinct mode of regional identity production distinct from conventional Track II diplomacy.

title: Requirement Elicitation Engine (REE): A Three-Phase Protocol for Autonomous Enterprise Requirement Disambiguation

detail.title: Requirement Elicitation Engine (REE): A Three-Phase Protocol for Autonomous Enterprise Requirement Disambiguation
detail.abstract: Enterprise software delivery is failing at its source. Despite the proliferation of AI-assisted development tools, the fundamental input to all code generation-the software requirement-remains structurally deficient in enterprise environments: contradictory across documents, under-specified at edge cases, laden with implicit assumptions, and temporally inconsistent across versioned artefacts. Every existing AI code generation system treats this as an unsolvable given. The Requirement Elicitation Engine (REE) treats it as the core problem. REE is a three-phase autonomous protocol-semantic parsing into a requirement knowledge graph, graph-traversal-based ambiguity detection with impact-weighted priority scoring, and a live runtime stakeholder Q&A session with real-time answer validation against the knowledge graph state-that produces a machine-executable Complete Requirement Specification (CRS) before any code generation commences. This paper presents three architectural contributions: (1) a three-phase disambiguation protocol applied to enterprise multi-artefact requirements, (2) an impact-weighted scoring formula with parameterised weight ranges, and (3) a live runtime state machine that validates stakeholder answers against a dynamic multi-document semantic graph during an active elicitation session. REE aims to reduce AI code hallucination at source by replacing ambiguous human prose with a mathematically consistent, verified JSON schema as the input to AI build agents. A proof-of-concept implementation is underway. Aiming at resolving systemic cross-document structural contradictions and graph node state conflicts within a dynamically mutating semantic database before execution by automated digital agent parsers.

title: The Age Bias Decomposition Matrix: A Sequential Audit Method for Locating Age Disparities Across Hiring Pipelines.

detail.title: The Age Bias Decomposition Matrix: A Sequential Audit Method for Locating Age Disparities Across Hiring Pipelines.

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author is considering whether future software or agent implementations related to this method may be protected or commercialized. This preprint discloses only the public conceptual and economic matrix, not a proprietary implementation. No external organization influenced the analysis.
declarations.ethicsApproval: This manuscript is a conceptual and methodological paper based on public literature, legal materials and a hypothetical illustrative example. It did not involve human subjects, patients, participant recruitment, private personal data or intervention with individuals. Ethics approval was therefore not sought.
declarations.funderStatement: No external funding was received for this research. The work was prepared independently by the author.

detail.abstract: Age related disparities in hiring are often summarized with one final rate. That measure can show that an outcome deserves attention, but it does not identify the transition where the disparity appeared or the process that produced it. This paper develops the Age Bias Decomposition Matrix, abbreviated ABDM, as a public method for sequential audit analysis. ABDM separates funnel location, mechanism hypothesis, evidence status, economic consequence and bounded response. It also introduces an exact descriptive decomposition in which the final selection rate ratio equals the product of conditional stage rate ratios. The method then directs evidence collection across representation, measurement, label, proxy, model, threshold and human process mechanisms. A synthetic hiring example shows that a favorable offer rate can coexist with earlier exclusion because later stages cannot recover people removed upstream. The method is not a causal estimator or liability test. Its contribution is to locate disparities, organize competing explanations and specify the evidence required before an institution selects a response.

title: The Inextinguishable Right: The Administered Union, Measured Against Three Constitutions and the Critics Who Named It

detail.title: The Inextinguishable Right: The Administered Union, Measured Against Three Constitutions and the Critics Who Named It

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author is the self-represented litigant in the matter the essay discusses and was a dues-paying member and steward of the union (COWINS) it examines. The essay is written from that standpoint, which it discloses throughout; it is offered as criticism and interpretive analysis, imputes no bad faith to any person, and acknowledges the union's reported gains as real.
declarations.ethicsApproval: Not applicable; no human-subjects research.
declarations.funderStatement: None. This research received no external funding.

keywords.keywords: public-sector labor relations; duty of fair representation; right to strike; comparative constitutional law; law and political economy; Marxian political economy; worker self-government; access to justice

detail.abstract: An administered union — one chartered, bounded, and "partnered" by the state employer rather than constituted by the workers — administers the worker where a fighting union would represent her. This essay develops that thesis through a public-sector model, Colorado Workers for Innovative and New Solutions (COWINS) and its 2024–2027 Partnership Agreement, read against the union's enabling statute and the author's own pro se litigation. The model is recognizably Lassallean — the arrangement Marx attacked from the left in 1875 — and, because it is run by institutions that outlive everyone who fights them and because, as Capital says, "between equal rights force decides," it does not hold ground but erodes toward a hollow the essay names a SHAM: a Standstill-bound, Hollow, Administered "Membership," a sham of representation. The argument is measured against three constitutions — Estonia, Colorado, and the United States — and against Marx and Engels, used as interpretive frames rather than as legal authority. The worker's own charters, it turns out, already contain most of the cure: power vested in the people, published and binding law, the right to withhold labor, open courts, separated powers, a constitutional merit forum, and rights retained by the people. What they lack is the machinery that makes a page bind. The essay shows that the arrangement reproduces, by contract, the same inverted mechanism a one-party state ran by command — the worker's own organization turned to administer the worker, in the worker's name — and argues the cure is self-government, durable enforceable rules, and the legal-research and AI tools now within a layperson's reach. Not legal advice.

title: Auditing Token Padding and Token Accounting in Large Language Models: A Constraint-Adherence Metric and a Multi-Provider Empirical Study
affiliations: Maharishi International University and

detail.title: Auditing Token Padding and Token Accounting in Large Language Models: A Constraint-Adherence Metric and a Multi-Provider Empirical Study
detail.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) frequently emit more tokens than a task requires, inflating cost and latency even when the extra text adds no information and violates explicit user constraints. We introduce the Token Padding Index (TPI), a reference-anchored metric that penalises verbosity, constraint violation, and semantic drift relative to a minimal control answer, plus an optional correctness term. We pair TPI with an adversarial battery of 106 trap prompts-each carrying an explicit negative constraint (e.g. "answer with a single word; no explanation")-and audit seven production models across three providers (OpenAI, Google, Anthropic) over 6970 trials. Our central finding is a dissociation between the tokens a provider bills and the content a model generates. On raw provider tokens the three Anthropic models appear extreme-3.6-3.8× the control-but recounting every response with one shared tokenizer collapses them to 1.09-1.28×, comparable to OpenAI and Gemini. We trace this to token accounting: the single word "Tokyo" is billed as 1 completion token by OpenAI and 7 by Anthropic for character-identical text (with zero reported thinking tokens) under the provider accounting we observed in mid-2026. This provides evidence for two separable sources of token overhead-content verbosity and tokenizeraccounting-and shows raw cross-provider token audits are misleading unless normalised: after normalisation only 1 of 21 model pairs differs significantly, versus 15 of 21 on raw tokens. We release the metric, trap battery, and pipeline as open source.

title: Confidently Wrong: Detecting Hallucinations in Financial Question Answering from LLM Internal States

detail.title: Confidently Wrong: Detecting Hallucinations in Financial Question Answering from LLM Internal States
detail.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) in financial applications fail most consequentially when they are confidently wrong. Hedged, uncertain answers invite scrutiny, whereas confident errors silently degrade downstream decisions without warning. We ask how reliably such confidently wrong answers, or confident hallucinations, can be detected from a model's internal activations, and whether those activations carry information beyond its observable outputs. We train linear probes on the residual stream and evaluate them on two established question-answering (QA) benchmarks built from real filings, FinQA and TAT-QA. Behavioral confidence is measured as the agreement among eight resampled answers to the same question, and probe effectiveness is compared against baselines, such as token log-probabilities and the model's own True/False self-assessment of its answer. Our findings show that among confident answers, those for which all eight resamples agree, 15-23% are wrong on FinQA. There the probes have a significant advantage over baseline methods in detecting hallucinations, holding 0.68-0.77 AUROC while the best baselines fall to 0.55-0.63, across Qwen3-8B, Llama-3.1-8B, and Gemma-2-9B. Our results suggest that probing can be a cost-effective triage mechanism for routing LLM answers to human review and quality control procedures in high-stakes financial applications.

title: Digitalization and Healthcare: Data, Telemedicine, and Patient-Centered Innovation
affiliations: TEXAS, Center for Migration Studies of New York, Inc. and TEXAS

detail.title: Digitalization and Healthcare: Data, Telemedicine, and Patient-Centered Innovation
detail.abstract: This article explores digitalization in healthcare, focusing on telemedicine, electronic health records, remote monitoring, and data-driven clinical support. It argues that digital health can improve access, coordination, and prevention when designed around patient needs and professional workflows. The article also addresses privacy, interoperability, equity, and the limits of technology in care relationships.

title: Remote Work: Driver or Deterrent of Digital Product Innovation
affiliations: University of Texas at Austin - McCombs School of Business, China Europe International Business School (CEIBS) and University of Texas at Austin - McCombs School of Business

detail.title: Remote Work: Driver or Deterrent of Digital Product Innovation
detail.abstract: As firms adopt divergent policies regarding work-from-home (WFH), the implications of remote work for collaborative and interdependent outcomes such as digital product innovation remain uncertain. This study examines how remote work adoption affects continuous digital product innovation using a panel dataset of mobile applications. We identify firm-level remote work adoption from job postings data and estimate its effects on app innovation using a staggered difference-indifferences design. We find that remote work significantly increases both major releases and new feature introductions per app, indicating enhanced digital product innovation performance. To assess whether these gains come at the expense of originality, we distinguish between novel and imitative feature introductions and show that remote work does not reduce the originality of digital product innovation. Moreover, improvements in digital product innovation translate into greater market success, as reflected in increased app downloads. The positive effects of remote work are stronger for app development teams with prior modular collaboration experience through open-source participation, suggesting that teams with greater experience coordinating modular work can better leverage remote work arrangements. We also find that remote work enables teams to expand their workforce and increase their collective skill capacity, both of which are associated with improved digital product innovation outcomes. In contrast, reductions in commuting time and app maturity do not explain the observed digital product innovation gains. Overall, our findings suggest that remote work can enhance continuous digital product innovation at the team level without compromising innovation novelty.

title: Generative AI and the Informational Value of Educational Credentials: Evidence from the Master's Margin
affiliations: Boston University, Boston University, Questrom School of Business - Department of Information Systems and

detail.title: Generative AI and the Informational Value of Educational Credentials: Evidence from the Master's Margin
detail.abstract: Educational credentials derive value both from the skills they certify and from the information they provide about worker ability. We study how generative AI affects both channels using employer demand for master's degrees as a setting. Unlike undergraduate degrees, which primarily signal broad capabilities, master's programs are designed to develop and certify specialized analytical skills-such as information synthesis, business analysis, forecasting, writing, and coding-that overlap closely with the capabilities of generative AI systems. Using worker-flow data from Revelio Labs covering U.S. hiring between 2018 and 2025, we exploit variation in occupational exposure to generative AI and the introduction of ChatGPT to examine changes in employer reliance on master's credentials. We find that occupations more exposed to AI experienced a significant post-2022 decline in the share of entry-level hires holding master's degrees. The decline is concentrated in business and other non-STEM master's degrees, emerges only after 2022, and is strongest at firms most likely to adopt AI. Importantly, it appears among experienced external and internal hires but not among first-job entrants. This pattern suggests that generative AI both reduces the value of some graduate-trained skills and lowers the informational value of the credentials that certify them when employers can rely on alternative signals of worker quality. More broadly, the results show that technological change can reshape not only the value of skills but also the value of educational credentials as signals in the labor market.

title: AI Sovereignty as Control Sovereignty

detail.title: AI Sovereignty as Control Sovereignty

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no personal, financial, institutional or other relationships that could have influenced, or could reasonably be perceived to have influenced, the research, analysis or conclusions presented in this paper.
declarations.ethicsApproval: Ethics approval was not required for this paper, as it is a conceptual and doctrinal working paper and does not involve patients, human participants, personal data collection, interviews, experiments or case-study subjects requiring consent.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no specific grant or external funding from any public, commercial or not-for-profit funding agency.

detail.abstract: This working paper develops the concept of control sovereignty as the next step in the legal and institutional theory of artificial intelligence. It builds on the thesis that advanced AI systems increasingly require machine-scale control architectures at the operational level, while normative, 2 constitutional and professional standards of control remain non-delegable to machines. The paper argues that democratic institutions face a double deficit. If they lack operational AI capability, they lose the capacity to act, learn, defend, administer and decide under conditions of machine-speed complexity. If they deploy AI systems without contestable legal control, they risk surrendering the conditions of human judgment, institutional accountability and democratic legitimacy. Control sovereignty is therefore defined as the institutional capacity to understand, procure, integrate, test, monitor, challenge, limit, replace and legally contest AI-based control infrastructures. Drawing on cybernetics, AI-control research, European and international AI governance instruments, riskmanagement frameworks and legal-AI evidence, the paper proposes a dual architecture: operational capability must pass a stress-condition capability test, and normative governance must pass a rule-oflaw contestability test. The central claim is that AI sovereignty cannot mean technological autarky, regulatory abstinence or uncritical adoption of powerful systems. It must mean contestable capability: the ability to use machine control without losing the institutional power to control the control of machines.

title: Securing Medical IoT: An MBSE Approach to the Asset Discovery Blind Spot in VPN and SASE Dependent Networks Under FDA Section 524B

detail.title: Securing Medical IoT: An MBSE Approach to the Asset Discovery Blind Spot in VPN and SASE Dependent Networks Under FDA Section 524B

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no conflicts of interest related to this research.
declarations.ethicsApproval: Not applicable. This study did not involve human participants, patient data, or clinical trials.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding.

keywords: medical device security and healthcare cybersecurity

detail.abstract: Healthcare organizations have spent a decade layering compensating controls, from VPN to SASE to agentless asset management, in response to a security problem that keeps resurfacing in a new form. Each layer solved the problem in front of it while quietly introducing the next one. This paper traces that chain to its current endpoint: the network based identification methods underlying widely deployed asset management platforms rest on a single, spoofable signal, leaving no independent means of confirming that a device is what its traffic claims to be. Under the FDA's February 2026 final guidance for Section 524B, which now requires manufacturers to demonstrate traceable, exploitability-focused assurance rather than network-level visibility alone, this gap has now been converted from a hypothetical concern to a compliance liability. This paper introduces the MIoT Behavioral Assurance Framework (MBAF), a three layer model combining Model Based Systems Engineering derived behavioral conformance, hardware rooted identity, and direct regulatory alignment, offering a verification signal that does not originate from the traffic an adversary is attempting to imitate. An illustrative risk analysis grounded in documented CVEs across representative device classes demonstrates the framework's potential impact.

title: From Reviews to Measures: Construct-Anchored Text Measurement of Restaurant Experience Quality in Tourism Management
affiliations: ,  and International University of Rabat

detail.title: From Reviews to Measures: Construct-Anchored Text Measurement of Restaurant Experience Quality in Tourism Management
detail.abstract: Tourism management increasingly relies on platform reviews to understand visitor and customer experiences, yet most review analytics convert text into sentiment, topics, or rating predictions rather than defensible measures of theoretically defined constructs. This study develops and evaluates a construct-anchored text measurement framework for restaurant experience quality. Treating review language as a selectively generated observation channel, the framework links construct blueprinting, admissible ACOS evidence units, weak-supervision/reference separation, calibrated extraction, pre-specified score construction, and cumulative validity and robustness evaluation. In the ACOS unit, category anchors an expression to a service-quality facet, sentiment supplies an ordered evaluative code, and aspect and opinion preserve traceability to source text. We demonstrate the framework using 217,139 platform-rendered English Google Maps restaurant reviews from four urban destinations in northern Spain. A calibrated FLAN-T5large extractor achieved a held-out category-sentiment F1 of .725 and recovered 578,873 facetlinked observations to construct perceived food quality, perceived service quality, and perceived environment quality scores. The scores showed differentiated evidence coverage, coherent associations with platform-based overall evaluations, rating-defined group differentiation, and robustness across observed operational conditions. The fixed extractor and supporting materials are released on Hugging Face, turning the framework into reusable measurement infrastructure for future restaurant-review research and facet-level service diagnosis while preserving coverage, traceability, and platform-bounded score interpretation.

title: The Sovereignty Trap: National AI Strategies, Compute Nationalism, and the Fragmentation of the Global AI Supply Chain

detail.title: The Sovereignty Trap: National AI Strategies, Compute Nationalism, and the Fragmentation of the Global AI Supply Chain
detail.abstract: Nations are increasingly treating artificial intelligence capabilities as matters of sovereignty-triggering a global wave of national AI strategies that combine industrial policy, compute infrastructure investment, data governance rules, and talent retention mechanisms into comprehensive programs designed to ensure that no nation is dependent on foreign AI capabilities for its economic competitiveness, national security, or democratic governance. India's IndiaAI Mission invests in sovereign compute capacity and indigenous foundation models. The European Union's compute sovereignty proposals aim to reduce dependence on US cloud hyperscalers. Gulf states are constructing AI cities as geopolitical positioning instruments. And US export controls on advanced semiconductors are reshaping the global compute supply chain by restricting China's access to frontier AI hardware. This paper examines how this emergent 'compute nationalism' affects multinational enterprise AI strategy across three dimensions: infrastructure access and cost, talent flows, and market fragmentation. The paper introduces the Compute Sovereignty Impact Model (CSIM), which maps how sovereign AI initiatives create three enterprise-level disruption mechanisms: infrastructure bifurcation (separate compute stacks for different jurisdictions), talent pool fragmentation (national strategies competing for fixed global AI talent), and compliance multiplexing (maintaining parallel governance and deployment architectures per jurisdiction). Using evidence from India, the EU, the Gulf states, and the US-China technology decoupling, the paper demonstrates that the current trajectory leads to a fragmented global AI supply chain that increases enterprise infrastructure costs by an estimated 25-40%, reduces cross-border innovation velocity, and creates new forms of geopolitical risk. The paper proposes the Sovereign-Ready Enterprise Architecture (SREA)-a three-principle design framework for multinational AI systems that enables operation across sovereign compute environments while maintaining operational coherence. The paper concludes with implications for corporate geopolitical risk teams, government AI strategy advisors, and venture investors with cross-border AI portfolios.

title: Imperfect Self-knowledge about Skills and Skill Mismatch
affiliations: University of Bern, University of Konstanz - Department of Economics and

detail.title: Imperfect Self-knowledge about Skills and Skill Mismatch
detail.abstract: Why do people sort into poorly fitting occupations? This paper shows that imperfect self-knowledge about skills is an important source of skill mismatch at labor market entry. We use unique data from standardized professional aptitude tests linked to administrative records on educational trajectories and early labor market outcomes in Switzerland. The data allow us to observe objective skills and subjective skill beliefs for many productivity-relevant skills in a high-stakes setting. We document large differences among individuals in how well their beliefs align with their skills. Imperfect self-knowledge predicts misaligned occupational aspirations, higher realized skill mismatch, and a higher probability of dropout. Guided by a Roy-style model of occupational choice with imperfect self-knowledge, we interpret these findings as evidence that distorted self-assessments at the school-to-work transition contribute to the misallocation of talent.

title: A Simple Model of Government Decision-Making and Plurilateral Cooperation on Critical Materials
affiliations: University of Nottingham - School of Economics, European University Institute - Robert Schuman Centre for Advanced Studies (RSCAS) and Tulane University - Department of Economics

detail.title: A Simple Model of Government Decision-Making and Plurilateral Cooperation on Critical Materials
detail.abstract: We develop an integrated framework to characterize multi-objective policymaking and apply it to the case of critical materials. The model considers that national policy decisions will be influenced by domestic agencies with different priorities and goals and be informed by actions taken by other countries pertaining to critical materials. This creates a potential basis for a group of countries to form a critical materials club to reduce the probability of supply shocks and/or their consequences. We show that in an environment with multiple policy-active governments, criticality assessments embedded in a multi-objective government with domain-specific bureaucracies and multiple instruments can rationalize divergent policy choices under similar risk environments, provide conditions under which international coordination is more or less likely and apply the model to consider the design and political economy of plurilateral arrangements for critical materials.

title: Taxi Market Deregulation: Effects on Market Outcomes, Tax Evasion and Crime
affiliations: ,  and Tampere University

detail.title: Taxi Market Deregulation: Effects on Market Outcomes, Tax Evasion and Crime
detail.abstract: We study the effects of taxi market deregulation in Finland, which removed price controls and lowered barriers to entry. The reform led to a surge in firm entry and a modest increase in exit, indicating substantial changes in market structure. Average taxi prices increased slightly according to price indices, while monthly firm-level reported sales and VAT declined by over 10 percent. Operating costs and mileage remained largely unchanged, suggesting limited demand responses. These findings point to increased tax evasion following deregulation. Consistent with this interpretation, we document a small rise in property crime, with no effects on other criminal offenses.

title: Evaluation and Assignment with Networked Competition and Spillovers
affiliations: University College London - Department of Economics and

detail.title: Evaluation and Assignment with Networked Competition and Spillovers
detail.abstract: This paper studies how organizations should jointly design evaluation rules and assign workers when performance depends on both effort and non-discretionary advantage. Agents choose effort in positions linked by a competition network, while their effective advantage depends on own type and spillovers through a second network. The planner chooses both the assignment and the effort weight in evaluation. Equilibrium effort rises with a position's Katz-Bonacich centrality and falls with effective advantage. The optimal evaluation rule generally differs from true output. When effort is more important in production, the planner lowers the effort weight and uses negative assortative assignment to strengthen incentives. When advantage is more important, the planner raises the effort weight and uses positive assortative assignment to exploit spillovers. We also study a constraint requiring assignments to be pairwise stable, which creates an output loss depending on the intensity of competition.
